units.name: Hadean
units.tagline: A molten world gains a Moon and oceans
units.world: There were no continents as we know them. The newborn Earth was covered at first by an ocean of molten rock. Early on, a Mars-sized body probably struck it, and the debris formed the Moon. As the surface cooled, a crust hardened and water gathered, perhaps into a world-wide ocean. Almost no rock survives; tiny zircon crystals from Western Australia are the main witnesses.
units.climate: Scorching at first, under thick steam and carbon dioxide, with no free oxygen. Zircon crystals suggest liquid water by about 4.4 to 4.3 billion years ago. The young Sun was much fainter than today, and just after the Moon formed a day may have lasted only five hours.
units.life: No fossils are known. Life may have begun in this eon: comparisons of DNA place the last common ancestor of all living things at about 4.2 billion years ago, and carbon sealed in one 4.1-billion-year-old zircon may be a trace of living things. Both claims are debated, and large asteroid impacts would have made survival hard.

changes.title: First solids in the Solar System
changes.text: The oldest grains in meteorites are 4,567 million years old. The international time scale uses this age as the start of the Hadean.

changes.title: The Earth reaches nearly full size
changes.text: Uranium-lead dating of meteorites gives the Earth an age of about 4.54 billion years, give or take 50 million.

changes.title: A giant impact forms the Moon
changes.text: A Mars-sized body, nicknamed Theia, probably hit the young Earth, and the debris gathered into the Moon. The date and the details of the collision are disputed.

changes.title: Oldest known mineral grain forms
changes.text: A zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia is 4,404 million years old. Its chemistry points to a solid crust and probably liquid water.

changes.title: A possible first trace of life
changes.text: Carbon inside a 4.1-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircon has the light make-up that living things produce. Whether life made it is disputed.

changes.title: Oldest surviving rocks form
changes.text: The Acasta Gneiss of northern Canada is about 4.03 billion years old. Its age marks the end of the Hadean.

units.evidenceNote: No rock survives from this time, so we rely on meteorites, Moon rocks and tiny zircon crystals dated by radioactive decay; no reliable figures exist for day length, air or temperature.

units.name: Archean
units.tagline: A water world where microbes take hold
units.world: The Earth was mostly ocean, dotted with volcanic islands and small early continents called cratons, such as the Pilbara in Australia and the Kaapvaal in southern Africa. The interior was hotter and volcanoes more active than today. When plates began to move as they do now is disputed; many geologists place it between 3.2 and 2.5 billion years ago. The proposed first supercontinents (Vaalbara, Ur, Kenorland) are uncertain.
units.climate: Mild enough for liquid oceans, probably somewhere between 0 and 40 degrees Celsius, although the Sun gave 20 to 25 percent less light. Extra carbon dioxide and methane kept the planet warm. The air held almost no free oxygen. The oldest known ice age came about 2.9 billion years ago.
units.life: Only single-celled microbes, bacteria and archaea, existed. The oldest widely accepted fossils are 3.48-billion-year-old stromatolites, layered mounds built by mats of microbes, in Western Australia; older claims from Greenland and Canada are disputed. By about 3.2 billion years ago microbes also lived on land. At some point cyanobacteria began to make oxygen from sunlight and water.

changes.title: Possible fossil microbes in Quebec
changes.text: Tiny iron-oxide tubes in rocks at least 3.77 billion years old at Nuvvuagittuq may be microbes from sea-floor hot vents. Both the age of the rocks and the fossils are disputed.

changes.title: Isua rocks hold possible signs of life
changes.text: Light carbon and mound-like structures in 3.7-billion-year-old Greenland rocks have been read as traces of microbes. Later studies argue that heat and squeezing made them.

changes.title: Stromatolites grow in the Pilbara
changes.text: Layered mounds in the Dresser Formation of Western Australia are the oldest fossils that most researchers accept.

changes.title: Signs of drifting plates
changes.text: Magnetic records show part of the Pilbara moved at modern plate speeds 3.2 billion years ago. Many geologists think plate tectonics took hold between then and 2.5 billion years ago.

changes.title: The first known ice age
changes.text: Glacial deposits in the Pongola rocks of South Africa and Eswatini, about 2.9 billion years old, record the oldest known glaciation.

changes.title: Continents grow and may merge
changes.text: Around 2.72 billion years ago several old continental cores grew and may have joined in a landmass called Kenorland. It remains a hypothesis.

changes.title: A whiff of oxygen?
changes.text: Metals in 2.5-billion-year-old Australian shale were read in 2007 as a first brief pulse of oxygen. A later re-study argues the signal was added to the rock afterwards.

units.evidenceNote: Archean rocks are dated by the steady decay of radioactive elements in their minerals; the day length (from tidal layers 3.2 billion years old) and the near-zero oxygen figure (from rock chemistry) are approximate.

units.name: Proterozoic
units.tagline: Oxygen arrives and cells grow complex
units.world: The longest eon, lasting nearly two billion years. Oxygen built up in the air for the first time. Continents joined into the supercontinents Columbia (Nuna) and then Rodinia, and split apart again. Cells with a nucleus appeared, then seaweeds and, near the end, the first animals. At least twice, ice may have covered almost the whole planet.
units.climate: Two bursts of severe ice ages, near the start and near the end, with a long, warm, stable stretch between them. Oxygen rose in two main steps but stayed below today's level.
units.life: Microbes throughout; cells with a nucleus by about 1.65 billion years ago; many-celled seaweeds by about one billion; large soft-bodied creatures and the first animals in the last 40 million years.
units.evidenceNote: Dated volcanic rocks, the chemistry of ancient sea-floor mud and a thin record of mostly microscopic fossils tell this story; see the three eras inside it for figures.

units.name: Paleoproterozoic
units.tagline: Oxygen changes the air for good
units.world: Small continents collided and merged. Between about 2.1 and 1.8 billion years ago these collisions built the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna, raising long mountain belts. Two giant asteroids struck: at Vredefort in South Africa 2.02 billion years ago and at Sudbury in Canada 1.85 billion years ago. They left two of the oldest and largest impact structures known.
units.climate: Oxygen made by cyanobacteria first built up in the air between about 2.46 and 2.06 billion years ago, the Great Oxidation Event. Around the same time the planet froze in the Huronian ice ages, when ice reached the tropics at least once. Banded iron formations rusted out of the seas.
units.life: Still a world of microbes, but a changing one. Oxygen was toxic to many microbes, while others evolved to breathe it. The first cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes) appear as fossils by about 1.65 billion years ago. Centimetre-sized shapes in 2.1-billion-year-old rocks in Gabon may be early many-celled life, but this is disputed.

changes.title: The Great Oxidation Event begins
changes.text: Free oxygen starts to build up in the air and shallow seas, in fits and starts, between about 2.46 and 2.43 billion years ago.

changes.title: Ice reaches the tropics
changes.text: Glacial deposits in South Africa formed about 11 degrees from the equator around 2.43 billion years ago, part of the Huronian ice ages (about 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago).

changes.title: Gabon's puzzling large 'fossils'
changes.text: Lobed structures up to several centimetres across in black shale near Franceville may be the oldest large living things, or may be mineral growths.

changes.title: The Vredefort impact
changes.text: An asteroid perhaps 20 to 25 kilometres across struck what is now South Africa, leaving a crater 170 to 300 kilometres wide.

changes.title: The Sudbury impact
changes.text: A body 10 to 15 kilometres across hit what is now Ontario, Canada, scattering debris for more than 800 kilometres.

changes.title: Supercontinent Columbia is complete
changes.text: Collisions between 2.1 and 1.8 billion years ago joined nearly all the continental blocks into Columbia (Nuna).

changes.title: Oldest accepted cells with a nucleus
changes.text: Microscopic fossils from North China show that eukaryotes, the kind of cell that builds all animals and plants, already existed and were varied.

units.evidenceNote: The rise of oxygen is read from sulfur and iron chemistry in dated rocks; the 17-hour day is measured from rhythmic layers 2.46 billion years old, near the start of the era, so it is approximate for the era as a whole.

units.name: Mesoproterozoic
units.tagline: The quiet middle age of the Earth
units.world: Columbia slowly broke apart between about 1.5 and 1.35 billion years ago. Its pieces drifted, then came together again, and by about 1.1 to 0.9 billion years ago they had formed a new supercontinent, Rodinia. The collisions raised the Grenville mountains, whose worn-down roots run from Labrador through Quebec and the Adirondacks to Texas and Mexico.
units.climate: A long calm with no known ice ages, part of the so-called Boring Billion. Oxygen stayed low: somewhere between a thousandth and a tenth of today's level (researchers disagree), and the deep sea had little or none. A day lasted about 19 hours.
units.life: Bacteria still ruled the seas, while cells with a nucleus slowly diversified. Near the end of the era the red seaweed Bangiomorpha, found in Arctic Canada and dated to 1,047 million years ago, shows two great steps: a body built of many cells, and the first known sexual reproduction. On land there were at most thin crusts of microbes.

changes.title: Columbia starts to break apart
changes.text: The supercontinent splits into separate blocks between about 1.5 and 1.35 billion years ago.

changes.title: A day lasts under 19 hours
changes.text: Rhythmic layers in 1.4-billion-year-old rocks show a day of about 18.7 hours and a Moon about 341,000 kilometres away, closer than today.

changes.title: Grenville mountain building begins
changes.text: Continental blocks begin to collide with ancient North America (Laurentia), a process that lasts until about 980 million years ago.

changes.title: Rodinia assembles
changes.text: From about 1.1 billion years ago the drifting continents gather into a new supercontinent, Rodinia.

changes.title: Bangiomorpha, the first known sex
changes.text: A fossil red seaweed from Somerset Island, Canada, is the first known organism to reproduce sexually.

units.evidenceNote: Day length comes from rhythmic rock layers that record wobbles in the Earth's orbit; oxygen estimates come from metals in ancient mud and differ a hundredfold between studies, so no single figure is given.

units.name: Neoproterozoic
units.tagline: Rodinia splits, the Earth freezes, animals appear
units.world: The era opened with the supercontinent Rodinia lying across the equator. From about 750 million years ago it broke into pieces, and by the end the southern pieces were joining again as Gondwana. In between came the most severe ice ages known, the Snowball Earth glaciations of the Cryogenian, followed in the Ediacaran by the first large living things.
units.climate: Warm and stable at first, then two long world-wide freezes between about 717 and 635 million years ago, then warmth again with rising oxygen.
units.life: Seaweeds and other cells with a nucleus diversified; the first animals arose, known from disputed chemical traces and then from the soft-bodied Ediacaran fossils.
units.evidenceNote: Glacial rubble, dated volcanic ash and, late in the era, the first large fossils record these events; see the three periods inside it for figures.

units.name: Tonian
units.tagline: Rodinia holds, then starts to tear
units.world: Rodinia lay across the equator, surrounded by a single world ocean called Mirovia, and stayed in one piece until at least 900 million years ago. Late in the period it began to stretch and rift; the name Tonian comes from the Greek for 'stretch'. Most geologists date the start of the real break-up to about 750 million years ago.
units.climate: Mostly warm and free of ice, the last stretch of the long calm before the great freezes. Oxygen was still far below today's level. At the very end of the period the planet cooled towards the first Snowball Earth glaciation.
units.life: Seaweeds and single-celled eukaryotes diversified, and chemical fossils show that modern kinds of algae became common only from about 800 million years ago. DNA comparisons suggest the first animals arose in this period or the next, but no certain animal fossils are known. Sponge-like textures in 890-million-year-old reef rocks have been proposed as the oldest; this is disputed.

changes.title: Rodinia in one piece
changes.text: The supercontinent, assembled by about 900 million years ago, and its surrounding ocean Mirovia stay stable through the early Tonian.

changes.title: The oldest sponge fossils?
changes.text: Net-like textures in reef rocks about 890 million years old resemble the skeletons of horny sponges. If they are sponges, they are the oldest animal fossils known; many researchers are unconvinced.

changes.title: Modern kinds of algae spread
changes.text: Fossil fat molecules show that older, more primitive eukaryotes dominated until about 800 million years ago, after which modern groups took over.

changes.title: Rodinia begins to break up
changes.text: Rifts open across the supercontinent and its fragments start to drift apart.

units.evidenceNote: Dated volcanic rocks and rift deposits show where Rodinia tore; microscopic fossils and fossil fat molecules record life. No reliable figures exist for day length, air or temperature.

units.name: Cryogenian
units.tagline: Snowball Earth: ice reaches the tropics
units.world: Rodinia was breaking up, with most of its fragments near the equator. Twice, ice spread from the poles until glaciers reached sea level in the tropics: the Sturtian glaciation, about 717 to 660 million years ago, and the shorter Marinoan, which ended 635 million years ago. Rubble dropped by that ice is found on every continent.
units.climate: The coldest times the Earth has known. Whether the oceans froze over completely ('hard snowball') or kept open water near the equator ('slushball') is disputed. Each freeze ended when carbon dioxide from volcanoes built up, to perhaps a hundred times today's level, and the ice melted fast.
units.life: Life survived, perhaps in meltwater ponds on top of the ice or in patches of open sea. Algae and microbes carried on. Molecules in Oman rocks older than 635 million years have been read as the oldest sign of animals (sponges), but some single-celled organisms make the same molecules, so the claim is disputed.

changes.title: The Sturtian glaciation begins
changes.text: Volcanic ash dated to 716.5 million years ago lies among glacial deposits that formed near the equator in what is now north-west Canada.

changes.title: The Sturtian ice melts
changes.text: After about 57 million years the first Snowball Earth ends.

changes.title: Sponge molecules in Oman?
changes.text: Fossil fats of a kind made by sponges appear in rocks laid down before the end of the Marinoan glaciation. Whether sponges made them is disputed.

changes.title: The Marinoan glaciation begins
changes.text: A second world-wide freeze is under way by about 639 million years ago; its start is poorly dated and may be earlier.

changes.title: A sudden thaw
changes.text: The ice retreats quickly and an unusual 'cap' of limestone is laid down over the glacial rubble around the world. This marks the end of the period.

units.evidenceNote: Rocks dropped by ice, found in layers that formed near the equator, show how far the ice reached; the 21.9-hour day comes from tidal layers dated to about 620 million years ago, just after the period, and is approximate.

units.name: Ediacaran
units.tagline: The first large living things
units.world: The fragments of Rodinia were regrouping. Collisions across what are now Africa, South America, Arabia and India welded the southern continents into Gondwana by about 550 million years ago. Laurentia (North America), Baltica and Siberia drifted apart as the Iapetus Ocean opened. A short-lived supercontinent, Pannotia, may have existed along the way; many geologists doubt it.
units.climate: Warmer after the great freezes, with one more short ice age, the Gaskiers, about 580 million years ago. Oxygen rose in the sea and the air, though still below today's level and probably unevenly. A day lasted about 22 hours.
units.life: Soft-bodied creatures up to about a metre long appear from about 575 million years ago: fronds, discs and quilted mats such as Charnia and Dickinsonia. What they were is disputed; fat molecules preserved in Dickinsonia show that it was an animal, but others may have been something else. Late in the period, trails and burrows show animals that could move.

changes.title: The seas warm and gain oxygen
changes.text: Sea-floor muds laid down in South China just after the Marinoan ice record a rise in oxygen in the ocean.

changes.title: The Gaskiers ice age
changes.text: A short glaciation, lasting about 250,000 years, leaves thick glacial deposits in Newfoundland.

changes.title: Large life at Mistaken Point
changes.text: Frond-shaped and spindle-shaped creatures, the oldest large and complex organisms known, live on a deep sea floor now exposed in Newfoundland.

changes.title: Dickinsonia and Kimberella
changes.text: Volcanic ash in Russia dates a rich community of soft-bodied creatures, including the slug-like Kimberella, to before 555 million years ago.

changes.title: Gondwana is assembled
changes.text: The collisions that joined the southern continents are largely complete.

changes.title: The Ediacaran creatures fade
changes.text: Most of the soft-bodied forms disappear as burrowing animals spread, at the threshold of the Cambrian.

units.evidenceNote: Soft-bodied creatures left impressions in sandstone and under volcanic ash that can be dated; the day length comes from tidal layers about 620 million years old and is approximate.

units.name: Phanerozoic
units.tagline: The eon of visible life
units.world: The present eon, whose name means 'visible life'. Animals with shells and skeletons fill the seas, life spreads onto the land, and the continents gather into the supercontinent Pangaea and then break apart towards today's map. Five mass extinctions reshape the living world. It is divided into three eras: the Paleozoic, the Mesozoic and the Cenozoic.
units.climate: Swings between warm 'greenhouse' and cold 'icehouse' states; global average temperature has ranged from about 11 to 36 degrees Celsius over the last 485 million years.
units.life: From the Cambrian explosion of animal groups to forests, insects, reptiles, dinosaurs, mammals and, at the very end, people.
units.evidenceNote: From this eon onward rocks contain abundant fossils with hard parts, which, together with dated volcanic ash, let geologists divide time finely; see the periods for figures.

units.name: Paleozoic
units.tagline: From a burst of sea life to Pangaea
units.world: The era began with most land in the south as Gondwana, and smaller continents (Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia) scattered in warm latitudes. One by one the oceans between them closed, raising the Caledonian, Appalachian, Variscan and Ural mountains, until nearly all land was joined in Pangaea. Life left the sea, forests spread, and the era ended with the largest extinction known.
units.climate: Mostly warm with high seas, broken by two ice ages: a short one at the end of the Ordovician and a long one in the Carboniferous and Permian.
units.life: Animal groups appear in the Cambrian; fishes, land plants, insects, amphibians and reptiles follow; about 81 percent of marine species die out at the end.
units.evidenceNote: Fossils in layered rocks, tied to dated volcanic ash beds, give the order and timing of events; see the six periods inside it for figures.

units.name: Cambrian
units.tagline: Animal life explodes in the seas
units.world: Most land lay south of the equator. Gondwana (today's Africa, South America, Antarctica, India and Australia) was the giant, stretching from the far south to beyond the equator. Laurentia (North America) lay across the equator, with Siberia and Baltica (northern Europe) as separate continents and the Iapetus Ocean opening between them. Sea level rose through the period and shallow seas flooded the edges and interiors of the continents.
units.climate: Warm, with no significant ice: global average temperature was probably 23 to 25 degrees Celsius for most of the period. Sea level rose from near today's to about 90 metres higher. Oxygen was lower than now, perhaps 2 to 11 percent of the air.
units.life: Within about 13 to 25 million years most major animal groups appear in the fossil record: arthropods such as trilobites, molluscs, worms, echinoderms and the first fish-like vertebrates. Shells, eyes, hunting and deep burrowing become common. Chengjiang in China and the Burgess Shale in Canada preserve soft bodies in fine detail. The land was bare apart from microbes.

changes.title: Complex burrows mark the start
changes.text: The first branching burrows, called Treptichnus pedum, define the base of the Cambrian at Fortune Head, Newfoundland.

changes.title: Trilobites appear
changes.text: These armoured arthropods become some of the most common fossils of the Paleozoic and last almost 270 million years.

changes.title: Chengjiang: the first fish-like animals
changes.text: Fine mudstones in Yunnan, China, preserve soft-bodied animals including Haikouichthys, one of the earliest known vertebrates.

changes.title: The Burgess Shale is buried
changes.text: Mud buries a rich sea-floor community in what is now British Columbia, preserving soft-bodied animals as dark films.

changes.title: A new wave of diversity begins
changes.text: By one detailed count, the long build-up of sea life called the Great Ordovician Biodiversification starts about now.

units.evidenceNote: Fossils with hard parts, plus rare sites that kept soft bodies, record the burst of animal life; temperature, sea-level and oxygen figures come from rock chemistry and models and are approximate.

units.name: Ordovician
units.tagline: Seas brim with life, then ice strikes
units.world: Gondwana drifted over the South Pole. Laurentia lay across the equator, at first almost entirely under shallow sea. Baltica and the small continent Avalonia (which included England and Wales) moved north towards it, narrowing the Iapetus Ocean. A highland rose along Laurentia's eastern edge, the first stage of the Appalachians. North of the tropics the globe was almost all ocean.
units.climate: Hot for most of the period, with a global average near 30 degrees Celsius, carbon dioxide several times today's level and seas about 200 metres higher than now. Then came cooling, and at the very end an ice sheet spread across Gondwana and sea level fell sharply.
units.life: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification multiplied the variety of sea life several times over: corals, bryozoans, brachiopods, sea lilies, nautiloids, graptolites and jawless armoured fishes. Spores show that small moss-like plants had reached the land by about 470 million years ago. The period closed with the first of the five great mass extinctions.

changes.title: Sea life multiplies
changes.text: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification is under way, with new kinds of animals building reefs and filling open water.

changes.title: Plants reach the land
changes.text: Spores like those of primitive land plants appear in rocks of this age, for example in Argentina.

changes.title: Highlands rise on Laurentia's edge
changes.text: A highland rises along the eastern margin of Laurentia (the Taconic mountain building), where the Appalachians now stand, as the Iapetus Ocean narrows.

changes.title: Seas reach their highest level
changes.text: Sea level peaks about 220 metres above today's, the highest of the whole Paleozoic.

changes.title: Ice covers southern Gondwana
changes.text: In the Hirnantian age an ice sheet spreads over the polar parts of Gondwana, including what is now the Sahara, and the sea falls.

changes.title: The Late Ordovician mass extinction
changes.text: In two pulses, as the ice grows and then melts, about 85 percent of marine species die out.

units.evidenceNote: Fossils date the rocks and record the extinction; temperature and carbon dioxide are period averages from a 2024 reconstruction, and the sea-level and oxygen figures are approximate (oxygen especially so).

units.name: Silurian
units.tagline: Reefs recover and life edges onto land
units.world: The Iapetus Ocean closed. Baltica and Avalonia collided with Laurentia to begin a larger northern continent, Laurussia (also called Euramerica), raising the Caledonian mountains across what are now Scandinavia, Scotland, Greenland and eastern North America. Gondwana, with South America and Africa over the South Pole, filled the far south. The continents lay low and the sea stood high.
units.climate: Warmer and steadier once the ice had melted, though with sharp swings: the global average was about 25 degrees Celsius. Seas stood roughly 180 metres above today's. Oxygen was climbing towards modern levels.
units.life: Coral reefs spread widely. Fishes with jaws appeared beside the jawless kinds, among them some of the first bony fishes. On land, the first plants with water-carrying stems, such as Cooksonia, stood only a few centimetres tall, and millipede-like animals, among the oldest known land animals, lived among them.

changes.title: Ice melts and the seas flood back
changes.text: Sea level rises from its ice-age low through the first half of the period.

changes.title: Cooksonia, the first stemmed plants
changes.text: The oldest known plants with water-carrying tissue in their stems appear in the middle of the Silurian.

changes.title: One of the oldest bony fishes
changes.text: Guiyu, found in Yunnan, China, is one of the earliest bony fishes known from a nearly complete skeleton.

changes.title: The Caledonian collision peaks
changes.text: Baltica and Laurentia finally collide between about 425 and 415 million years ago, at the height of the Caledonian mountain building.

changes.title: The first wildfires
changes.text: Fossil charcoal appears in rocks from about 419 million years ago, showing there was now enough oxygen, and enough plant fuel, for fire.

units.evidenceNote: Reef, fish and early land-plant fossils date and describe the period; temperature and carbon dioxide are period averages from a 2024 reconstruction, and the oxygen figure is a rough reading of a model, so treat it as approximate.

units.name: Devonian
units.tagline: Age of Fishes and the first forests
units.world: Two great landmasses faced each other: Laurussia (Euramerica) near the equator, where the Old Red Sandstone was laid down, and Gondwana to the south, with Siberia to the north. The Rheic Ocean between them was closing, starting the collisions that would build Pangaea. The Acadian mountain building raised the northern Appalachians, and the Variscan belt began to form in Europe.
units.climate: Warm, with a global average of about 26 degrees Celsius. Carbon dioxide fell from roughly 2,000 to under 1,000 parts per million as forests spread. Sea level was high, near 190 metres above today's, and slowly falling. The period ended with cooling.
units.life: Fishes diversified hugely: armoured placoderms, sharks, ray-finned and lobe-finned fishes. Plants grew from ankle-high stems into the first trees and forests, about 385 million years ago, and evolved seeds. Early insects, mites and spider relatives lived among them. Lobe-finned fishes gave rise to four-limbed animals (tetrapods). Two extinction crises near the end destroyed the great reefs.

changes.title: The Rhynie chert
changes.text: Hot-spring water in what is now Scotland turns an early land community of plants, fungi and tiny animals to stone.

changes.title: Footprints before bones?
changes.text: Trackways in Poland almost 400 million years old suggest four-limbed animals were walking tidal flats about 18 million years before the oldest tetrapod bones.

changes.title: The first forests
changes.text: Fossil stumps at Gilboa, New York, are the remains of one of the earliest known forests.

changes.title: Tiktaalik
changes.text: A lobe-finned fish from Arctic Canada has a neck and wrist-like fin bones, a step between fishes and tetrapods.

changes.title: The Kellwasser extinction
changes.text: Oxygen-starved seas kill the great reefs and perhaps 40 percent of marine species.

changes.title: Tetrapods with fingers and toes
changes.text: Acanthostega, found in Greenland, has four limbs with digits but still lives mainly in water.

changes.title: The Hangenberg extinction
changes.text: A second crisis at the very end of the period wipes out the armoured placoderm fishes.

units.evidenceNote: Fossils record the fishes, forests and first tetrapods; daily growth lines in fossil corals show a year of about 400 days (a day of about 22 hours); the temperature, carbon dioxide, sea-level and oxygen figures are approximate.

units.name: Carboniferous
units.tagline: Coal swamps, giant insects, Pangaea assembles
units.world: Gondwana moved north and collided with Laurussia, closing the Rheic Ocean. From about 335 million years ago the two merged into the supercontinent Pangaea. The collision raised a mountain chain across its centre: the Variscan ranges of Europe and the Appalachians of North America. In the east, Siberia and Kazakhstania closed on Baltica and the Ural Mountains began to rise.
units.climate: Cooling into a long ice age: the global average was about 16 degrees Celsius, with ice sheets growing and shrinking over southern Gondwana and sea level swinging with them. Carbon dioxide fell to about 400 parts per million, while oxygen rose to 25 to 30 percent of the air.
units.life: Vast tropical swamp forests of giant clubmosses, horsetails and tree ferns laid down the peat that became much of the world's coal. Arthropods grew huge: the dragonfly-like Meganeura had a wingspan near 70 centimetres and the millipede Arthropleura reached about 2.6 metres. The first amniotes, animals that lay eggs on dry land, appeared; reptiles and the ancestors of mammals descend from them.

changes.title: Pangaea begins to assemble
changes.text: Gondwana and Laurussia meet, joining most of the world's land into one mass.

changes.title: The Late Paleozoic ice age sets in
changes.text: Between about 335 and 330 million years ago ice sheets start to spread across southern Gondwana.

changes.title: The Appalachians are pushed up
changes.text: Africa, as part of Gondwana, collides with North America in the Alleghanian mountain building, which lasts until about 260 million years ago.

changes.title: Hylonomus, the earliest known reptile
changes.text: A small lizard-like animal is preserved inside hollow tree stumps at Joggins, Nova Scotia.

changes.title: Mazon Creek
changes.text: Ironstone nodules in Illinois preserve the plants and soft-bodied animals of a coal-swamp delta.

changes.title: The rainforests collapse
changes.text: The great coal forests of the tropics break up into isolated patches, causing a minor extinction among plants and animals.

changes.title: Giant insects fly
changes.text: Meganeura, a dragonfly relative from the coal forests of France, has wings 32 centimetres long.

units.evidenceNote: Coal seams and their fossils record the forests, and glacial deposits record the ice; temperature and carbon dioxide are period averages from a 2024 reconstruction, and the oxygen and sea-level figures are approximate.

units.name: Permian
units.tagline: One supercontinent, then the Great Dying
units.world: Nearly all land was joined in Pangaea, a C-shaped supercontinent reaching from pole to pole, wrapped around the Tethys sea and surrounded by the world ocean Panthalassa. Mountain chains from the Appalachians to the Urals crossed it. Only parts of Asia remained separate. At the very end, huge eruptions in Siberia flooded millions of square kilometres with lava.
units.climate: The southern ice sheets shrank and Pangaea's vast interior grew dry, with strong seasons. The global average was about 19 degrees Celsius until the very end, when the Siberian eruptions drove rapid warming of roughly 10 degrees. Sea level fell to its lowest of the era.
units.life: Conifers and other seed plants replaced many swamp trees. Synapsids, the lineage leading to mammals, ruled the land: first sail-backed Dimetrodon, then the more mammal-like therapsids. Reptiles diversified and the first beetles appeared. At the end, the worst extinction on record killed about 81 percent of marine species and 70 percent of land vertebrate species.

changes.title: Dimetrodon, a sail-backed hunter
changes.text: This relative of mammals, not a dinosaur, lives from about 294 to 271 million years ago in what is now North America and Europe.

changes.title: The southern ice sheets shrink
changes.text: From about 290 million years ago the ice retreats and the long ice age eases.

changes.title: Therapsids appear
changes.text: More mammal-like synapsids appear around 275 to 272 million years ago and soon dominate the land.

changes.title: The Capitanian extinction
changes.text: Eruptions of the Emeishan lavas in China coincide with an extinction on land and in the sea; how severe it was is debated.

changes.title: The Siberian Traps erupt
changes.text: One of the largest volcanic outpourings of the last 500 million years begins in Siberia.

changes.title: The end-Permian mass extinction
changes.text: Within about 60,000 years most species in the sea die out. It is the largest extinction known.

units.evidenceNote: Fossils and precisely dated ash beds record the period and its catastrophic end; temperature and carbon dioxide are period averages from a 2024 reconstruction, and the oxygen figure is approximate.

units.name: Mesozoic
units.tagline: The age of reptiles; Pangaea breaks apart
units.world: At the start almost all land was joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea, surrounded by a single vast ocean. Over the next 186 million years it tore apart: the Atlantic opened, the southern landmass Gondwana split into Africa, South America, India, Antarctica and Australia, and shallow seas flooded the continents. By the end the map was starting to look familiar.
units.climate: Mostly a warm greenhouse world with little or no lasting ice at the poles. Average temperatures were about 10 °C or more above today's, and for much of the era the seas stood tens of metres higher, drowning low-lying land.
units.life: Life rebuilt itself after the worst extinction in Earth's history. Reptiles ruled: dinosaurs on land, ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs in the sea, pterosaurs in the air. The first mammals, birds and flowering plants all appeared. The era ended when an asteroid struck and about three quarters of species, including every dinosaur except the birds, died out.
units.evidenceNote: Fossils in the rock layers show what lived when, and volcanic ash between the layers is dated by the steady decay of radioactive elements inside its crystals.

units.name: Triassic
units.tagline: Life recovers; first dinosaurs and mammals appear
units.world: Nearly all land formed the C-shaped supercontinent Pangaea, stretching from pole to pole. The Tethys Sea cut into its eastern side, and one giant ocean, Panthalassa, covered the rest of the globe. Mountains rose along the western edge of the Americas. Late in the period rift valleys opened between North America and Africa: the first cracks of the future Atlantic.
units.climate: Hot and mostly dry, with no ice caps at the poles. The huge landmass drove fierce seasonal monsoons and its interior was desert. Sea level stayed low compared with later periods, so few shallow seas flooded the land.
units.life: Survivors of the end-Permian extinction, such as the plant-eater Lystrosaurus, spread across Pangaea. New groups followed: the first dinosaurs, pterosaurs, crocodile relatives, turtles and small early mammals on land, ichthyosaurs in the sea, and the first reefs built by modern-type corals. Conifers, cycads and ferns were the main plants. Dinosaurs stayed mostly small until the very end.

changes.title: Slow recovery from the Great Dying
changes.text: The period opens just after the end-Permian extinction, the worst in Earth's history. No coal is known from the earliest Triassic anywhere, a sign of how badly plant life had been hit.

changes.title: The Carnian Pluvial Episode
changes.text: For one to two million years the dry climate turned much wetter, probably because of huge eruptions. About a third of marine genera died out, and dinosaurs and many modern groups spread afterwards.

changes.title: Oldest well-dated dinosaurs
changes.text: Rocks at Ischigualasto in Argentina, dated to about 231 million years ago, hold some of the oldest known dinosaurs, including Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus.

changes.title: Early mammals appear
changes.text: In the Late Triassic small, probably night-active insect-eaters evolved from cynodonts, the mammal-like reptiles. Exactly which fossils count as the first true mammals is debated.

changes.title: Pangaea starts to crack
changes.text: Between about 225 and 200 million years ago the crust began to stretch and split where North America met Africa.

changes.title: The Central Atlantic eruptions
changes.text: Lava flooded more than 7 million square kilometres around the future Atlantic in four pulses over about 600,000 years.

changes.title: End-Triassic mass extinction
changes.text: Up to about half of marine species diversity was lost and most large land reptiles other than dinosaurs vanished, leaving the dinosaurs to take over.

units.evidenceNote: Fossils of each stage lie in rock layers whose ages come from uranium slowly turning to lead in zircon crystals from volcanic ash.

units.name: Jurassic
units.tagline: Giant dinosaurs, first birds, the Atlantic is born
units.world: Pangaea broke in two: Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south. A narrow young ocean, the central Atlantic, opened between North America and Africa. About 180 million years ago Gondwana itself began to split, as Africa and South America pulled away from Antarctica, India and Australia. The South Atlantic had not yet opened. Rising seas spread over low-lying land.
units.climate: Warmer than today, with no ice caps and forests growing close to the poles, though polar winters could be cold. Low latitudes had large dry regions. Sea level rose through the period, perhaps to more than 100 metres above today's near the end.
units.life: Dinosaurs took over the land. Long-necked sauropods such as Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus were the largest land animals ever, hunted by predators like Allosaurus. The first birds, including Archaeopteryx, evolved from small meat-eating dinosaurs. Ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and ammonites filled the seas and pterosaurs flew overhead. There were no flowers: forests were conifers, cycads, ginkgoes and ferns. Mammals stayed small.

changes.title: Dinosaurs inherit the land
changes.text: With many rival reptiles gone after the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs spread across the world and grew larger.

changes.title: The central Atlantic opens
changes.text: New sea floor began to form between North America and north-west Africa: the first ocean to split Pangaea.

changes.title: Karoo-Ferrar eruptions and an ocean crisis
changes.text: Lava floods in southern Africa and Antarctica coincided with the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, when large parts of the sea lost their oxygen and many marine species died.

changes.title: Gondwana begins to split
changes.text: East Gondwana (Antarctica, Madagascar, India and Australia) started to separate from Africa and South America.

changes.title: An early relative of placental mammals
changes.text: Juramaia lived about 160 million years ago and is the earliest known member of the group that includes today's placental mammals.

changes.title: Dinosaurs of the Morrison Formation
changes.text: From about 156 to 147 million years ago rivers in western North America buried Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus.

changes.title: Archaeopteryx, an early bird
changes.text: Fine limestone at Solnhofen in Germany preserved a feathered animal with wings, but also teeth and a long bony tail.

units.evidenceNote: Rock layers are matched worldwide by their ammonite fossils, which changed quickly through time, and dated by radioactive decay in volcanic ash.

units.name: Cretaceous
units.tagline: Flowers bloom, seas rise, an asteroid ends it
units.world: The continents moved towards their modern places. South America split from Africa, opening the South Atlantic from south to north; India broke from Madagascar and headed north; Australia was still joined to Antarctica. Seas were so high that at the peak about a third of today's land was under water, and a seaway cut North America in two. The Rocky Mountains began to rise.
units.climate: One of the warmest times of the last 500 million years: about 92 million years ago the global average probably topped 30 °C. There were no lasting ice sheets, forests grew near both poles, and sea level stood perhaps 100 metres or more above today's.
units.life: Flowering plants appeared and spread until they dominated most landscapes, alongside the oldest known ants, bees and butterflies. Dinosaurs included Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops and the duck-bills. Birds diversified and mammals stayed small. Mosasaurs, plesiosaurs and ammonites lived in the chalk-forming seas. The period ended with a mass extinction that killed about three quarters of all species.

changes.title: The South Atlantic starts to open
changes.text: Flood basalts erupted across what are now southern Brazil and Namibia 136 to 132 million years ago as South America began to tear away from Africa.

changes.title: First flowering plants
changes.text: The oldest fossil flowering plants date from about 130 to 125 million years ago; by 100 million years ago they were spreading fast.

changes.title: Feathered dinosaurs of Liaoning
changes.text: Lake beds in north-east China preserved dinosaurs with feathers, early birds and mammals in fine detail.

changes.title: An ocean without oxygen
changes.text: During Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a large parts of the sea ran short of oxygen and black carbon-rich mud covered the sea floor.

changes.title: Peak heat and highest seas
changes.text: Around 94 to 92 million years ago the Cretaceous hothouse reached its peak, the oceans again lost oxygen, and a shallow sea covered the middle of North America.

changes.title: India leaves Madagascar
changes.text: India broke away and began a fast journey north towards Asia.

changes.title: Asteroid impact and mass extinction
changes.text: An asteroid about 10 km wide struck at Chicxulub in Mexico while huge eruptions were under way in India. All dinosaurs except birds died out.

units.evidenceNote: Fossils of sea plankton and land animals, dated volcanic ash and flips of Earth's magnetic field recorded in the rocks together give the ages; a fossil shell with daily growth lines even shows how long a day was.

units.name: Cenozoic
units.tagline: The age of mammals; the world cools
units.world: The continents drifted into today's positions. India collided with Asia and pushed up the Himalayas and Tibet; Africa pressed into Europe, raising the Alps; the Atlantic kept widening; Australia broke from Antarctica and moved north; and North and South America were finally joined at Panama. New sea passages around Antarctica let a cold current circle it.
units.climate: A long slide from hothouse to ice age. The early era was 10 °C or more warmer than today, with no polar ice. Ice sheets formed on Antarctica about 34 million years ago and in the north about 2.7 million years ago.
units.life: With the big dinosaurs gone, mammals and birds diversified into whales, bats, horses, elephants, cats and primates. Grasslands spread as the climate cooled and dried, and grazing animals with them. Apes evolved in the Miocene, upright-walking apes by about 7 to 6 million years ago, and our own species about 300,000 years ago.
units.evidenceNote: Mud drilled from the deep sea floor holds tiny shells whose chemistry records temperature and ice volume, layer by layer, for the whole 66 million years.

units.name: Paleogene
units.tagline: Mammals take over a hothouse that slowly cools
units.world: Covers the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene epochs. The North Atlantic opened between Greenland and Europe, India met Asia, and Australia and South America parted from Antarctica, leaving it alone at the South Pole. The Alps and Himalayas began to rise. By the end a cold ocean current circled Antarctica and an ice sheet covered it.
units.climate: Very warm for the first half, peaking 56 to 50 million years ago with no polar ice and palms in the Arctic. Then came long cooling, and about 34 million years ago the first continent-wide Antarctic ice sheet.
units.life: Mammals grew from small survivors of the extinction into whales, bats, early horses, elephants' relatives and primates. Modern bird groups spread. Forests covered most land at first; as the climate cooled, more open country and the first widespread grasses appeared.
units.evidenceNote: Deep-sea mud cores record temperature and ice through the chemistry of tiny shells, and volcanic ash layers on land give dates in years.

units.name: Paleocene
units.tagline: Recovery after the asteroid
units.world: The continents were close to today's layout, but India was still an island continent crossing the ocean towards Asia, Australia was joined to Antarctica, and North and South America were separate. Greenland began to split from north-west Europe amid huge eruptions. The Rocky Mountains were still rising, and the shallow sea across North America drained away.
units.climate: Warm and largely ice-free, with palms and crocodiles living inside the Arctic Circle. The global average was around 25 °C or more, some 10 °C above today's. The epoch ended with a sudden extra burst of warming.
units.life: Forests regrew after the impact, and the survivors spread into an emptied world. Mammals, small at first, quickly became bigger and more varied, taking over roles the dinosaurs had filled. Birds diversified too: the ones that came through the extinction seem to have been mostly ground-dwellers. Crocodiles, turtles and many plants carried on much as before.

changes.title: Aftermath of the impact
changes.text: Forests were destroyed across the world, yet in western North America mammal communities were recovering within about 20,000 years.

changes.title: The Deccan eruptions end
changes.text: The lava floods in India went on until about 65.6 million years ago; by one dating study, about three quarters of the lava erupted after the impact.

changes.title: North Atlantic eruptions begin
changes.text: From about 62 million years ago lava poured out across what are now Greenland, Scotland and Northern Ireland as the crust stretched before the ocean opened.

changes.title: Sudden global warming
changes.text: At the very end of the epoch a huge release of carbon set off the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum.

units.evidenceNote: The epoch begins at the thin layer of asteroid debris found worldwide, dated by radioactive argon in volcanic ash just above and below it.

units.name: Eocene
units.tagline: Hothouse Earth; whales, horses and primates emerge
units.world: Greenland parted from Europe about 55 million years ago, opening the North Atlantic. India ran into Asia, starting the rise of the Himalayas and Tibet, and Africa's push against Europe began to build the Alps. Australia pulled away from Antarctica, and sea passages opened south of Tasmania and South America, leaving Antarctica isolated by the end of the epoch.
units.climate: The warmest time of the last 66 million years. Around 53 to 51 million years ago the world was more than 10 °C warmer than before industry, CO2 was about 1,400 ppm, and near-tropical forest grew on Antarctica. Then it cooled steadily.
units.life: The oldest known fossils of most modern groups of mammals appear early in the Eocene, all of them small: early horses, bats and primates among them. Whales evolved from land mammals; Basilosaurus still had tiny hind legs. Lake beds at Green River in Wyoming and Messel in Germany preserve fish, bats, insects and palms in fine detail.

changes.title: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
changes.text: Global temperature jumped by about 5 to 8 °C in under 10,000 years and stayed high for about 200,000 years.

changes.title: The North Atlantic opens
changes.text: Greenland separated from north-west Europe and sea floor began to form between them.

changes.title: Peak warmth
changes.text: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, about 53 to 51 million years ago, was the hottest long spell since the dinosaurs.

changes.title: India collides with Asia
changes.text: First contact is usually dated to about 55 to 50 million years ago, though the timing is disputed. The Himalayas began to rise.

changes.title: The Azolla event
changes.text: For about 800,000 years mats of a floating fern covered the Arctic Ocean, burying carbon as they died.

changes.title: A passage opens south of South America
changes.text: Pacific water first reached the Atlantic through the Drake Passage about 41 million years ago, by one estimate; the date is disputed.

changes.title: Antarctica starts to freeze
changes.text: As the epoch ended a continent-wide ice sheet grew on Antarctica and sea level fell by about 55 metres.

units.evidenceNote: Chemical signals in sea-floor shells and in drill cores from the Arctic and Antarctic record the warmth, and volcanic ash layers date the fossil beds.

units.name: Oligocene
units.tagline: Antarctica freezes; grasses and open country spread
units.world: Antarctica now sat alone over the South Pole, ringed by a cold current once deep water flowed past Tasmania and through the Drake Passage. The Alps were rising quickly as Africa pushed into Europe, and the Himalayas and Tibet kept growing. In East Africa floods of lava poured out and the Red Sea began to open, splitting Arabia from Africa.
units.climate: Much cooler than the Eocene. An ice sheet covered Antarctica from about 34 million years ago and sea level dropped by about 55 metres as it grew. The global average, around 23 °C, was still far warmer than today's.
units.life: Tropical forests shrank back towards the equator, and open woodland, scrub and grasses took their place. In Europe many older mammal families died out and newcomers replaced them, a turnover called the Grande Coupure. Early relatives of monkeys and apes lived in Africa. Horses and other mammals began adapting to life in open country.

changes.title: The Grande Coupure
changes.text: Cooling and falling seas brought a wave of extinctions; in Europe many native mammals were replaced by new arrivals.

changes.title: Deep water flows past Tasmania
changes.text: The sea passage between Australia and Antarctica became deep enough for ocean currents, 33.5 million years ago give or take 1.5 million.

changes.title: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current begins
changes.text: A cold current started to flow right around Antarctica about 30 million years ago, cutting it off from warmer waters.

changes.title: The Red Sea starts to open
changes.text: Volcanic eruptions in East Africa about 30 million years ago came with rifting that began to split Arabia from Africa.

changes.title: Mammals of Riversleigh
changes.text: From about 28 million years ago limestone in northern Australia began to record the continent's unique marsupials and other mammals.

units.evidenceNote: A sharp change in the oxygen chemistry of sea-floor shells marks the growth of Antarctic ice, and sand dropped by icebergs appears in sea-bed mud around the continent.

units.name: Neogene
units.tagline: Grasslands, great mountain ranges and the first hominins
units.world: Covers the Miocene and Pliocene epochs. The continents reached almost their present positions. Africa and Arabia met Eurasia, closing the old Tethys seaway and creating the Mediterranean, which dried out and refilled. The Himalayas, Tibet, Alps and Andes rose to great heights, and near the end North and South America were joined at Panama.
units.climate: Warm at first, with a peak 17 to 14 million years ago, then steadily cooler and drier. The East Antarctic ice sheet became permanent, and by the end large ice sheets were starting to grow in the north.
units.life: Grasslands spread across the continents and grazing mammals with them. Apes appeared and spread through Africa, Europe and Asia. The first upright-walking apes lived in Africa by about 7 to 6 million years ago, and the oldest known stone tools are 3.3 million years old.
units.evidenceNote: Sea-floor cores give a continuous climate record, and the regular wobbles of Earth's orbit recorded in the layers date them to within a few thousand years.

units.name: Miocene
units.tagline: Apes, grasslands and rising mountain chains
units.world: The map looked almost modern, except that North and South America were still apart. Arabia and Africa met Eurasia, closing the old Tethys seaway and leaving the Mediterranean. The Himalayas, Tibet, the Alps and the Andes all rose higher, and the East African Rift began to tear open. At the very end the Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic and largely dried out.
units.climate: Warm at first, peaking 17 to 14 million years ago, when floods of lava erupted in the north-western United States. Then it cooled: the East Antarctic ice sheet became large and permanent by about 13 million years ago, and the world grew drier.
units.life: Grasslands kept spreading and forests shrank, and grazing mammals multiplied. Apes arose early in the Miocene and spread through Africa, Europe and Asia. Kelp forests appeared in the seas, home to whales and seals. Plants and animals were recognisably modern. Near the end, the line leading to humans split from the line leading to chimpanzees.

changes.title: Apes appear
changes.text: The first apes evolved early in the Miocene and soon spread widely across the Old World.

changes.title: The East African Rift begins
changes.text: From about 25 to 22 million years ago the crust of East Africa began to pull apart along what is now the Rift Valley.

changes.title: The Tethys seaway closes
changes.text: Arabia's collision with Eurasia began to cut the sea link between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean about 20 million years ago.

changes.title: Lava floods and a warm spell
changes.text: The Columbia River basalts erupted, mostly 16.7 to 15.9 million years ago, during the warm Miocene Climatic Optimum.

changes.title: Antarctic ice expands for good
changes.text: Sharp cooling about 14 million years ago rebuilt the East Antarctic ice sheet, which has been permanent ever since.

changes.title: Upright apes and tropical grasslands
changes.text: Sahelanthropus, possibly the oldest known member of the human line, lived in Chad 7 to 6 million years ago, as tropical grasslands expanded.

changes.title: The Mediterranean dries out
changes.text: Cut off from the Atlantic, the Mediterranean partly or almost wholly evaporated between 5.96 and 5.33 million years ago.

units.evidenceNote: Deep-sea cores record temperature and ice volume, thick salt under the Mediterranean shows it dried, and volcanic layers date the fossil beds.

units.name: Pliocene
units.tagline: The Americas join; northern ice begins to grow
units.world: The continents lay within a few tens of kilometres of where they are now. At the start the Atlantic burst back into the dried-out Mediterranean in a giant flood. Rising land finally joined North and South America at Panama, about 2.8 million years ago by the usual estimate, separating the Pacific from the Caribbean. The Himalayas and Andes kept rising.
units.climate: A little warmer than today: about 2 to 4 °C above pre-industrial temperatures in its warm spells, with sea level 10 to 25 metres higher. Cooling late in the epoch let large ice sheets grow in the north from about 2.7 million years ago.
units.life: Animals were close to modern kinds. When the Panama land bridge formed, ground sloths, armadillos and opossums walked north while cats, horses and tapirs went south. In Africa, upright-walking Australopithecus lived in a landscape of woods and grassland, and the oldest known stone tools, from Kenya, are 3.3 million years old.

changes.title: The Mediterranean refills
changes.text: The Atlantic broke through at Gibraltar; most of the basin may have filled in as little as a few months to two years.

changes.title: Warm spells with high seas
changes.text: Between about 4.4 and 3.3 million years ago, cave deposits on Mallorca show sea level stood 16 to 24 metres above today's.

changes.title: Oldest known stone tools
changes.text: Stone tools 3.3 million years old were found at Lomekwi in Kenya, older than our own genus Homo.

changes.title: The Isthmus of Panama forms
changes.text: A complete land bridge joined the Americas about 2.8 million years ago, though some researchers argue for a much earlier date.

changes.title: Northern ice sheets and a great migration
changes.text: Ice sheets began to grow on northern lands, and animals started crossing between North and South America in large numbers.

units.evidenceNote: Old shorelines, cave deposits formed at sea level and sea-floor cores show how warm it was and how high the sea stood; volcanic ash dates the African fossil sites.

units.name: Quaternary
units.tagline: The ice ages and the rise of humans
units.world: Covers the Pleistocene and Holocene epochs. The continents were in their present places, but coastlines moved back and forth as ice sheets grew and melted. At cold peaks ice buried Canada and northern Europe, the sea fell by up to about 130 metres, and land bridges joined Asia to North America and Australia to New Guinea.
units.climate: An ice age still under way: long cold glacial periods broken by shorter warm ones like the present. The swings followed regular changes in Earth's orbit, about every 41,000 years at first and about every 100,000 years later.
units.life: Mammoths, giant sloths and other huge animals thrived and then mostly died out. Humans spread from Africa to every continent except Antarctica. In the last 12,000 years people took up farming and became the main force changing the planet's surface.
units.evidenceNote: Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica hold trapped air and yearly layers going back hundreds of thousands of years, and sea-floor cores extend the record further.

units.name: Pleistocene
units.tagline: Ice ages come and go; humans spread worldwide
units.world: The continents were where they are today, but coastlines kept shifting. In each cold phase ice sheets covered Canada, Scandinavia and much of Britain, and sea level fell by as much as 130 metres. Dry land then joined Siberia to Alaska, Britain to mainland Europe, and New Guinea to Australia. In warm phases the ice melted back and the seas returned.
units.climate: Cold on average, swinging between long glacial periods and shorter warm ones: every 41,000 years at first, then about every 100,000 years. At the last cold peak the world was about 6 °C colder than before industry, and ice covered about a quarter of all land.
units.life: The time of mammoths, giant ground sloths, sabre-toothed cats and other large 'megafauna', most of which died out between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago. Several kinds of human lived through the ice ages. Our own species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago and later reached every continent except Antarctica.

changes.title: The ice-age cycles set in
changes.text: With large ice sheets now in both hemispheres, the climate began to swing between cold and warm about every 41,000 years.

changes.title: Longer, deeper ice ages
changes.text: Between about 1.25 and 0.7 million years ago the cycles lengthened to about 100,000 years and the cold phases became more severe.

changes.title: Homo sapiens appears
changes.text: The oldest known fossils of our species, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 315,000 years old.

changes.title: People reach Australia
changes.text: Tools at Madjedbebe in northern Australia have been dated to about 65,000 years ago, though that early date is debated.

changes.title: The Last Glacial Maximum
changes.text: Ice sheets were at their greatest extent from 26,500 to about 19,000 years ago and sea level was about 125 to 134 metres lower.

changes.title: People in the Americas
changes.text: Footprints at White Sands in New Mexico are dated to 23,000 to 21,000 years ago; the dating is still argued over.

changes.title: A last cold snap
changes.text: The Younger Dryas, 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, returned the north to near-glacial cold before the final warming.

units.evidenceNote: Yearly layers in ice cores and the chemistry of sea-floor shells record each cold and warm swing, and radiocarbon dates the last 50,000 years of bones and campsites.

units.name: Holocene
units.tagline: The warm, steady time of farming and cities
units.world: Today's geography. As the ice sheets melted the sea rose by more than 100 metres, drowning the land bridges and coastal plains of the ice age: Britain and New Guinea became islands and the Bering Strait separated Asia from America. Most of the rise was over by about 8,000 years ago, and sea level has been nearly steady for the last few thousand years.
units.climate: Warm and unusually steady. By one reconstruction, global temperature peaked about 6,500 years ago at roughly 0.7 °C above the 1800s. CO2 stayed near 280 ppm until the industrial age; in late 2026 it is about 427 ppm.
units.life: Today's plants and animals, without most of the ice-age giants. People took up farming, built cities and now shape much of the land, the climate and the wildlife. A proposal to name a new human-made epoch, the Anthropocene, was rejected by geology's governing bodies in 2024, so officially we still live in the Holocene.

changes.title: The Holocene begins
changes.text: The epoch is defined as starting 11,700 years ago, when the last cold snap of the ice age ended, a moment recorded in Greenland ice.

changes.title: A sudden chill
changes.text: About 8,200 years ago global temperatures dropped rapidly for two to four centuries. The date is used to divide the Holocene.

changes.title: The warmest centuries
changes.text: By one reconstruction the warmest 200 years of the Holocene, before the present, fell around 6,500 years ago.

changes.title: The latest age begins
changes.text: Geologists start the Meghalayan Age, the present subdivision of the Holocene, 4,200 years ago.

changes.title: The Anthropocene proposed and rejected
changes.text: A new epoch starting in 1952 was proposed, but the responsible commission voted it down in March 2024.

units.evidenceNote: Yearly layers in Greenland ice, counted back one by one, mark the start of the epoch, and tree rings, lake mud and cave formations record the climate since.

events.title: The Earth forms
events.evidenceNote: Radioactive uranium turns into lead at a steady, known rate, so the amounts of each in meteorites show how long ago they formed.
events.text: The Sun and planets grew from a disc of gas and dust. The oldest solid grains in meteorites are 4,567 million years old, and the Earth reached nearly its full size some tens of millions of years later. The usual figure for the Earth's age, 4.54 billion years, give or take 50 million, comes from uranium-lead dating of meteorites, above all the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite, first measured by Clair Patterson in 1956.

sources.title: USGS: Geologic Time, Age of the Earth

International Commission on Stratigraphy: International Chronostratigraphic Chart, v2026/06

events.title: A giant impact forms the Moon
events.evidenceNote: Moon rocks brought back by the Apollo astronauts are chemically so like the Earth's that most scientists think the Moon was made from the debris of a collision; when and how exactly is still argued over.
events.text: Most scientists think a Mars-sized body, nicknamed Theia, struck the young Earth and the debris gathered into the Moon. Disputed: the details. Canup and Asphaug (2001) modelled a glancing blow by a Mars-sized body; Cuk and Stewart, and Canup (2012), proposed a fast-spinning Earth or a larger impactor to explain why Moon and Earth rocks are almost identical. Dates range from about 30 to 200 million years after the Solar System formed; Apollo zircons suggest by 4.51 billion years ago.

events.title: Oldest mineral grains hint at early oceans
events.evidenceNote: Zircon crystals trap uranium, which slowly decays to lead, so each grain carries its own clock; the oldest reads 4,404 million years, give or take 8 million.
events.text: Sand-sized zircon crystals, washed long ago into younger rocks of the Jack Hills, are the oldest known pieces of the Earth; one is 4,404 million years old. Their chemistry points to granite-like crust and to rock that had been in contact with liquid water, so the planet probably had a solid surface and oceans within about 150 million years of forming. Some researchers are cautious about reading so much from such tiny grains.

events.title: The last common ancestor of all life
events.dateLabel: c. 4.2 billion years ago (estimate from DNA)
events.evidenceNote: Scientists compare the DNA of living things and count the differences, using dated fossils to set the pace of this 'molecular clock'; the answer has wide error bars.
events.text: All living things descend from a single ancestor, known as LUCA. A 2024 study comparing genes across the whole tree of life estimated that it lived about 4.2 billion years ago (between 4.09 and 4.33), only a few hundred million years after the Earth formed, and that it was already a fairly complex microbe. A 2018 study placed it before 3.9 billion years ago. No fossil of this age is known, so the date rests on DNA alone.

sources.title: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution: The nature of the last universal common ancestor and its impact on the early Earth system

events.title: Carbon in a zircon: life's oldest trace?
events.evidenceNote: Living things prefer the lighter kind of carbon atom, and a speck of carbon rich in light atoms was found sealed inside a 4.1-billion-year-old crystal; chemistry without life can sometimes produce the same pattern.
events.text: In 2015 Elizabeth Bell and colleagues reported specks of graphite (pure carbon) sealed inside a 4.10-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircon. The carbon is rich in the light form that living things favour, and the team suggested that life may already have existed. Disputed: the authors themselves call it only 'potentially' biological; it is one crystal out of more than 10,000 examined, and light carbon can also form without life. The find still awaits confirmation.

events.title: The oldest surviving rocks
events.evidenceNote: Zircon crystals inside the rock act as radioactive clocks and give ages of about 4.02 to 4.03 billion years.
events.text: The Acasta Gneiss, about 300 kilometres north of Yellowknife, contains the oldest known rock that is still in one piece, about 4.03 billion years old. The international time scale uses this age to mark the end of the Hadean and the start of the Archean. Rocks on Hudson Bay in northern Quebec may be older still, but their age is disputed.

events.title: Nuvvuagittuq: oldest rocks, oldest fossils?
events.dateLabel: at least 3.77 billion years ago, perhaps 4.3
events.evidenceNote: Different radioactive clocks in these rocks give different ages, and tiny rusty tubes in them look like microbes but might have formed without life.
events.text: On the shore of Hudson Bay lie volcanic rocks at least 3.75 billion years old. O'Neil and colleagues (2008) and Sole and colleagues (2025) argue from neodymium isotopes that they are about 4.2 to 4.3 billion years old, which would make them the only known Hadean rocks; other teams accept only the younger zircon dates. In 2017 Dodd and colleagues described tiny iron-oxide tubes and filaments here as fossil microbes from sea-floor hot vents, a reading others question.

events.title: Isua: carbon and 'stromatolites' in Greenland
events.place: Isua Greenstone Belt, near Nuuk, south-west Greenland
events.evidenceNote: These rocks have been squeezed and heated so strongly that signs of life are hard to tell from marks made by the squeezing itself.
events.text: Isua holds some of the oldest sea-floor sediments on Earth. Mojzsis and colleagues (1996) and Ohtomo and colleagues (2014) found graphite rich in light carbon and read it as the remains of microbes; others think hot fluids could have deposited it. In 2016 Nutman and colleagues reported 3.7-billion-year-old stromatolites, mounds built by microbes. In 2018 Allwood and colleagues re-examined them and concluded that they formed when the rock was deformed, not by life.

events.title: Pilbara stromatolites: the oldest accepted fossils
events.place: North Pole Dome, Pilbara, Western Australia
events.evidenceNote: Layered mounds in these rocks match the shapes that mats of microbes build today, and volcanic layers around them have been dated.
events.text: Layered mounds called stromatolites in the 3.48-billion-year-old Dresser Formation, and a whole reef of them in the nearby 3.43-billion-year-old Strelley Pool Chert, are the oldest evidence of life that most researchers accept. Still disputed: whether every such structure was built by microbes, and the 3.46-billion-year-old 'microfossils' of the nearby Apex chert, which Brasier and colleagues (2002) argued are mineral artefacts, not cells.

events.title: The plates begin to move
events.evidenceNote: Magnetic minerals in old lavas record the latitude at which they cooled, and the kinds of rock made at plate edges first appear at different times; experts read this patchy record differently.
events.text: Today the Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that drift, collide and dive beneath one another. When this began is disputed, with estimates from over 4 billion to under 1 billion years ago. Hopkins and colleagues (2008) saw signs of it in Hadean zircons. Cawood and colleagues (2018) place the change between 3.2 and 2.5 billion years ago, and Brenner and colleagues (2020) found that part of the Pilbara was drifting at modern plate speeds 3.2 billion years ago.

events.title: Vaalbara and Ur: the first continents?
events.evidenceNote: Two very old blocks of crust, now in South Africa and Western Australia, have such similar rock layers that some geologists think they were once joined.
events.text: The Kaapvaal block of southern Africa and the Pilbara block of Western Australia are built of crust 3.6 to 2.7 billion years old. Some geologists join them in a single early continent, Vaalbara. A rival idea, Ur, proposed by John Rogers, groups rocks of India, Western Australia and southern Africa from about 3.1 billion years ago; the two ideas conflict in part. Both are hypotheses: too little rock survives to test them firmly, and either landmass would have been small.

events.title: Microbes start making oxygen
events.evidenceNote: Certain metals in old sea-floor rocks only behave as they did if some oxygen was present, but later changes to the rocks can leave the same signal.
events.text: Cyanobacteria learned to split water using sunlight, releasing oxygen: the source of nearly all the oxygen we breathe. When is disputed. Planavsky and colleagues (2014) found chemical signs of oxygen in 2.95-billion-year-old sea-floor rocks in South Africa, and Patry and colleagues (2025) date oxygen-making microbes in Canada to 2.87 billion years ago. Kopp and colleagues (2005) argue instead that the ability evolved only shortly before oxygen filled the air. Supposed 2.7-billion-year-old chemical fossils of cyanobacteria proved to be later contamination.

events.title: Kenorland, a possible early supercontinent
events.evidenceNote: The old cores of several continents formed or were welded together at about the same time, which may mean they were joined; how they were arranged cannot be checked directly.
events.text: Around 2.72 billion years ago several old continental cores, including parts of Canada, Scandinavia and Western Australia, grew quickly and may have merged into one landmass. It is called Kenorland after mountain-building rocks near Kenora in Ontario. It remains a hypothesis: geologists disagree about which blocks belonged to it, and some prefer several separate 'supercratons' to a single supercontinent (Mitchell and colleagues, 2021).

events.title: The seas rust: great iron formations
events.evidenceNote: Thin, regular layers in these iron-rich rocks follow known wobbles in the Earth's orbit, and volcanic ash between them gives the date.
events.text: Thick banded iron formations settled on the sea floor as iron dissolved in the oceans met oxygen, probably made by early cyanobacteria, and rusted out of the water. Rocks of this kind hold more than 60 percent of the world's iron reserves. Rhythmic layers in the Hamersley iron beds, dated to 2.46 billion years ago, also show that a day then lasted only about 17 hours and that the Moon was about 322,000 kilometres away, closer than today.

sources.title: Lantink et al. 2022, PNAS: Milankovitch cycles in banded iron formations constrain the Earth-Moon system 2.46 billion years ago
Wikipedia: Banded iron formation

events.title: The Great Oxidation Event
events.evidenceNote: Before this time, sulfur in rocks carries a chemical fingerprint that can form only in air without oxygen; afterwards the fingerprint disappears for good.
events.text: For the first time, free oxygen built up in the air and shallow seas: from almost nothing to a level still far below today's. The source was oxygen-making cyanobacteria, though the timing is debated. It began between 2.46 and 2.43 billion years ago, came in fits and starts, and settled by about 2.06 billion years ago. Oxygen was toxic to many microbes, let others evolve to breathe it, and may have helped to trigger severe ice ages.

events.title: The Huronian ice ages
events.place: North shore of Lake Huron, Ontario, Canada
events.evidenceNote: Layers of boulder-filled mud dropped by glaciers lie in rocks of this age near Lake Huron and in South Africa.
events.text: Three separate layers of glacier-dropped rubble north of Lake Huron record a series of ice ages. In South Africa, glacial deposits of about this age formed close to the equator, so at least one of these freezes may have been a 'Snowball Earth'. Kopp and colleagues (2005) proposed a cause: the new oxygen destroyed methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Later dating confirmed that oxygen began to rise before the tropical glaciation (Warke and colleagues, 2020).

events.title: Gabon's Francevillian 'fossils'
events.evidenceNote: Centimetre-sized lobed shapes sit in dated black shale; their regular form suggests living things, but minerals can grow into similar shapes.
events.text: Black shales near Franceville hold flattened, lobed and disc-like structures up to several centimetres across. El Albani and colleagues (2010) described them as the oldest large, many-celled organisms, living soon after oxygen first rose. Disputed: Adolf Seilacher regarded them as mineral growths of pyrite, not fossils, and a 2016 study of similar structures in Michigan found those to be mineral lumps. Nothing comparable is known from the following billion years.

sources.title: El Albani et al. 2010, Nature: Large colonial organisms with coordinated growth in oxygenated environments 2.1 Gyr ago
Wikipedia: Francevillian biota

events.title: The Vredefort impact
events.evidenceNote: Rock melted by the impact contains crystals that can be dated, and the surrounding rocks are shattered in ways that only an impact can cause.
events.text: An asteroid perhaps 20 to 25 kilometres across struck what is now South Africa 2,023 million years ago, give or take 4 million. The crater, since worn away by erosion, was between 170 and 300 kilometres wide, which makes Vredefort one of the largest impact structures known on Earth and one of the oldest. Only the deeply eroded central part of the structure can be seen today.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Vredefort impact structure

events.title: Grypania: coiled ribbons in Michigan
events.place: Empire Mine, near Palmer, Michigan, USA
events.evidenceNote: The coils are thin films of carbon in dated iron-rich rock; their regular shape suggests something living, but no cells are preserved to show what kind.
events.text: Hundreds of coiled ribbons of carbon, each more than a centimetre long, lie in the Negaunee Iron Formation at the Empire Mine. Han and Runnegar (1992) named them Grypania, a seaweed-like eukaryote, and dated them to 2.1 billion years; the rock has since been redated to about 1.87 billion. If they are eukaryotes, they are the oldest big enough to see without a microscope. Disputed: unlike younger Grypania from Montana, China and India, about 1.45 to 1.4 billion years old, they show no segments, and they could be giant bacteria or bacterial colonies.
