events.title: The Sudbury impact
events.evidenceNote: The basin's shattered and melted rocks can only be explained by an impact, and crystals in the melt give its age.
events.text: A body about 10 to 15 kilometres across hit what is now Ontario 1,849 million years ago, leaving one of the oldest and largest impact structures known. Debris was thrown more than 800 kilometres, as far as Minnesota. The rocks of the Sudbury Basin are rich in nickel, copper and other metals, which are mined there today.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sudbury Basin

events.title: Supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) comes together
events.evidenceNote: Belts of crumpled, once deeply buried rock of the same age on many continents mark the places where older landmasses collided.
events.text: Between about 2.1 and 1.8 billion years ago nearly all of the Earth's continental blocks collided and joined into what many geologists count as the first true supercontinent: Columbia, also called Nuna, first proposed in 2002. Its exact layout is uncertain. It began to break apart about 1.5 billion years ago, and its pieces later came together again as Rodinia.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Columbia (supercontinent)
Mitchell et al. 2021, Nature Reviews Earth & Environment: The supercontinent cycle
Wikipedia: Mesoproterozoic

events.title: The first cells with a nucleus
events.evidenceNote: Microscopic fossils of this age are too large and too elaborately shaped to be bacteria; DNA comparisons suggest that such cells arose somewhat earlier.
events.text: Eukaryotes are cells with a nucleus; all animals, plants and fungi are built of them. Their oldest widely accepted fossils are acritarchs: tiny organic cases, mostly a few hundredths to a tenth of a millimetre across, made by organisms nobody can name. Ornamented ones in the Changcheng Group of North China and in northern Australia, about 1.65 billion years old, are already varied. Disputed: plainer acritarchs about 1.8 billion and even 2.1 billion years old may be early eukaryotes or just bacteria. Molecular clocks place the last common ancestor of living eukaryotes between about 1.2 and more than 1.8 billion years ago.

events.title: The Roper Group: a sea of early complex cells
events.place: Roper River area, Northern Territory, Australia
events.evidenceNote: Crystals in a volcanic ash layer low in the rocks are dated to 1,492 million years, and many of the fossil cell walls are too ornate and varied to be bacteria.
events.text: Drill cores through more than 1,000 metres of mudstone and sandstone of the Roper Group hold 34 kinds of microfossil. Javaux and Knoll count five as certain eukaryotes, among them the acritarch Tappania, whose uneven, finger-like outgrowths suggest a growing cell; it has been compared with fungi. These early complex cells were commonest in shallow, well-oxygenated coastal seas. A 2026 study of rocks in northern Australia between 1.75 and 1.4 billion years old reached the same conclusion: the first complex cells lived on oxygen-rich sea floors near the shore.

events.title: Rodinia assembles and the Grenville mountains rise
events.place: Adirondack Mountains, New York, USA (Grenville Province)
events.evidenceNote: The deep roots of a worn-down mountain chain of this age run from Labrador to Mexico, and matching belts lie on other continents.
events.text: The fragments of Columbia came together again as a new supercontinent, Rodinia, complete by about 900 million years ago. Where other continents collided with Laurentia (ancient North America), in a collision compared with the one raising the Himalaya today, the Grenville mountains rose. Their eroded roots are exposed from Labrador through Quebec and the Adirondacks to Texas and Mexico, and in Scotland. How the continents fitted together inside Rodinia is still debated.

events.title: Bangiomorpha: the first known sex
events.evidenceNote: The fossil threads show the same cell patterns as a living red seaweed, and the rock layers that hold them have been dated.
events.text: Microscopic threads in Arctic Canadian rocks dated to 1,047 million years ago look almost exactly like the living red seaweed Bangia. Bangiomorpha is a red alga built of many cells and is the first organism known to have reproduced sexually. Sex shuffles genes in every generation, and many-celled bodies allow cells to take on different jobs; both steps opened the way to larger and more complex life.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bangiomorpha
Wikipedia: Mesoproterozoic

events.title: Rodinia breaks apart
events.evidenceNote: Rift valleys filled with sediment and lava of this age line the edges of the old continental blocks, showing where they tore apart.
events.text: Rodinia began to stretch and rift late in the Tonian, and from about 750 million years ago it split into separate continents. The break-up seems linked to what came next: the first Snowball Earth glaciation followed the break-up of a supercontinent that lay in the tropics, and many researchers think the changes it caused in the oceans and the air helped to tip the planet into the deep freeze.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rodinia
Wikipedia: Tonian

events.title: Snowball Earth I: the Sturtian glaciation
events.evidenceNote: Volcanic ash dated to 716.5 million years ago lies among glacier-dropped rubble in rocks that formed near the equator, so ice reached sea level in the tropics.
events.text: For about 57 million years ice sheets reached sea level even near the equator. The glaciation is named after glacial rocks at Sturt Gorge. Disputed: how complete the freeze was. Paul Hoffman and colleagues argue that the whole ocean froze over (a 'hard snowball'); climate models by Hyde and colleagues (2000) allow a belt of open water in the tropics (a 'slushball'), which would more easily explain how sunlight-dependent life survived.

events.title: Chemical traces of the first animals?
events.evidenceNote: Oil-like molecules in these rocks match fats made by living sponges, but some algae and single-celled organisms make the same molecules.
events.text: Love and colleagues (2009) found fossil fat molecules in Oman, in rocks laid down before the end of the Marinoan ice age, and argued that sponges made them: the oldest evidence of animals, 100 million years before the Cambrian explosion. Disputed: Nettersheim and colleagues (2019) showed that single-celled Rhizaria can make the same molecules, while Zumberge and colleagues (2018) reported a second molecule pointing to sponges. DNA-based estimates do place the first animals in or just before this period.

events.title: Snowball Earth II: the Marinoan glaciation
events.evidenceNote: Glacial rubble of this age is capped around the world by an unusual layer of limestone, the mark of a sudden swing from freezing to warm seas.
events.text: A second world-wide freeze, named after Marino near Adelaide, ended 635 million years ago. Its start is poorly dated; it lasted at least four or five million years. Carbon dioxide from volcanoes built up to perhaps a hundred times today's level before the ice gave way, and 'cap' limestones were then laid down over the glacial rubble. As with the Sturtian, whether open water survived at the equator is disputed. The thaw marks the start of the Ediacaran Period.

events.title: Pannotia: a brief supercontinent?
events.dateLabel: c. 630 to 570 million years ago (if it existed)
events.evidenceNote: The fit depends on where magnetic minerals say each continent lay, and those readings are sparse and uncertain for this time.
events.text: Some reconstructions gather the fragments of Rodinia briefly into a new southern supercontinent, Pannotia (named by Powell in 1995), with Laurentia lying against South America before the Iapetus Ocean opened between them. Disputed: a 2022 study argued that Pannotia never fully existed, because it had begun to break up before it was fully assembled. What is agreed is that the southern continents were merging into Gondwana at about this time.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pannotia
Wikipedia: Rodinia

events.title: Weng'an: spiny cysts and 'embryos'
events.evidenceNote: Calcium phosphate replaced soft cells before they rotted, so single cells survive; the clusters divide like embryos, but some algae and single-celled relatives of animals divide the same way.
events.text: Phosphate rock of the Doushantuo Formation at Weng'an preserves microscopic life in three dimensions, down to single cells. Among the fossils are large spiny acritarchs and balls of dividing cells, often found inside them, that Xiao and colleagues (1998) read as the embryos of early animals. Disputed: Bailey and colleagues (2007) proposed giant sulfur bacteria; Cunningham and colleagues (2017) reject that but find nothing that proves an animal, and others suggest algae or single-celled relatives of animals. Identical spiny cases occur in South China soon after the Marinoan ice, about 632 million years ago.

events.title: Mistaken Point: the oldest large living things
events.evidenceNote: Volcanic ash buried the sea floor and preserved the creatures where they lived; crystals in the ash give the date, and one layer is 565 million years old.
events.text: On a deep sea floor lived fronds, bushes and spindle-shaped creatures such as Fractofusus and Charniodiscus, among the oldest large and complex organisms known. Falls of volcanic ash buried whole communities where they stood. They appear a few million years after the short Gaskiers ice age of about 580 million years ago. The first fossil was found in 1967 by the student Shiva Balak Misra. Mistaken Point is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: Ediacara Hills: Dickinsonia and its neighbours
events.place: Ediacara Hills, Flinders Ranges, South Australia
events.evidenceNote: The soft bodies left clear impressions in sandstone; similar fossils in Russia lie beside volcanic ash dated to 555 million years, and fat molecules preserved in some show that they were animals.
events.text: The fossils that Reg Sprigg noticed here in 1946 gave the Ediacaran Period its name: flat, quilted Dickinsonia, discs and fronds, all soft-bodied. Disputed: what they were. They have been called early animals, giant single cells, lichens, or a lost branch of life (Adolf Seilacher's 'Vendobionta'). In 2018 Bobrovskiy and colleagues found cholesterol, a hallmark of animals, in Dickinsonia fossils from Russia. Other Ediacaran forms remain puzzles.

events.title: Gondwana is welded together
events.evidenceNote: Worn-down mountain belts of this age stitch together the old cores of Africa, South America, India, Antarctica and Australia.
events.text: A series of collisions, together called the Pan-African mountain building, joined the future southern continents (South America, Africa, Arabia, India, Antarctica and Australia) into one giant landmass, Gondwana. It began when India and Madagascar met East Africa, about 800 to 650 million years ago, and was complete about 600 to 530 million years ago. What is left of Gondwana makes up about two-thirds of today's continental area.

events.title: The Cambrian explosion begins
events.evidenceNote: Rock layers from this time onward suddenly contain shells, skeletons and complex burrows; the first such burrows, at Fortune Head, officially mark the start of the Cambrian.
events.text: Over about 13 to 25 million years most of the major groups of animals alive today appear in the fossil record, many with shells, legs and eyes. The start of the Cambrian is defined at Fortune Head by the first complex burrows, called Treptichnus pedum. Genes suggest that the groups had begun to split earlier, before any clear fossils. Why the burst came when it did (more oxygen, new predators, new genes) is debated.

events.title: The Chengjiang fossils
events.evidenceNote: Fine mud buried animals so quickly that soft parts such as legs and antennae were preserved; the rock layers are dated to about 518 million years.
events.text: Mudstones at Maotianshan preserve an early Cambrian sea floor in fine detail: soft-bodied worms, sponges, trilobites with their legs and antennae, and the earliest fish-like vertebrates, such as Haikouichthys. First recognised for its exceptional fossils in 1984, and about ten million years older than the Burgess Shale, Chengjiang shows that complex animal communities were established early in the Cambrian explosion. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

events.title: The Burgess Shale
events.place: Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
events.evidenceNote: Animals were buried in fine mud that kept their soft tissues as thin dark films; the rocks are dated to about 508 million years.
events.text: Discovered by Charles Walcott in 1909, high in the Canadian Rockies, the Burgess Shale preserves soft-bodied sea animals of the middle Cambrian as dark films on the rock. Walcott collected more than 65,000 specimens. Strange forms such as five-eyed Opabinia, spiny Wiwaxia and the predator Anomalocaris, one of the largest animals of its time, showed how varied early animals were. It is one of the most famous fossil sites in the world.

events.title: The Late Ordovician mass extinction
events.evidenceNote: Fossil counts show sea life crashing in two steps, and glacial deposits in North Africa and Arabia show a great ice sheet over the South Pole at the same time.
events.text: The first of the 'big five' extinctions removed about 85 percent of marine species in two pulses. The usual explanation: an ice sheet spread over Gondwana at the South Pole, cooling the seas and draining the shallow shelves, and a second pulse came as the ice melted and oxygen-poor water spread. Disputed: Finnegan and colleagues (2012) tie the losses to cooling and lost habitat, while some later studies blame volcanic eruptions and link the first pulse to warming instead.

events.title: The Caledonian mountains rise
events.evidenceNote: Folded and baked rocks of the same age run in one belt from Scandinavia through Scotland to Greenland, pieces of a single chain later split apart by the Atlantic.
events.text: As the Iapetus Ocean closed, the continents Laurentia (North America and Greenland) and Baltica (northern Europe) and the smaller Avalonia (which included England) collided. The result was a great mountain chain named after Caledonia, the Latin name for Scotland. Its worn-down remains form the Scottish Highlands and the mountains of Norway and eastern Greenland. The main collision between Baltica and Laurentia came about 425 to 415 million years ago.

events.title: The Rhynie chert
events.evidenceNote: Silica-rich water from hot springs flooded a patch of ground and turned the plants and animals to stone, cell by cell.
events.text: Hot-spring water rich in silica petrified an entire early land community where it stood, almost instantly, down to single cells. The chert, discovered by William Mackie between 1910 and 1913, preserves simple leafless plants with water-carrying cells, together with fungi, lichens, algae and small arthropods. It is one of the best windows we have on life's early steps onto land.

events.title: The first forests: Gilboa
events.evidenceNote: Fossil tree stumps still stand where they grew, in rock layers about 385 million years old.
events.text: Fossil stumps known at Gilboa since the 1870s are the remains of one of the oldest known forests. For over a century nobody knew what the trees looked like; in 2007 a complete fossil showed that they were Wattieza, tree-sized relatives of ferns with a crown of branches. Forests like this spread across the lowlands, and the growth of land plants is thought to have drawn carbon dioxide out of the air over time.

events.title: Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck and wrists
events.evidenceNote: The bones were found in rocks of known age and show a mix of fish features and those of four-legged animals.
events.text: Found in 2004 and described by Edward Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins, Tiktaalik was a lobe-finned fish with scales and fin rays, but also a mobile neck and a working wrist joint: a form between fishes and four-legged animals (tetrapods). It lived in shallow water. Trackways in Poland, almost 400 million years old, suggest however that the first tetrapods were already walking well before it.

events.title: The Late Devonian extinctions
events.evidenceNote: Black, oxygen-starved mud layers found around the world mark the two crises, and the fossils of reef builders and armoured fishes stop at those layers.
events.text: Two crises 13 million years apart: the Kellwasser event (about 372 million years ago), which destroyed the great reefs and perhaps 40 percent of marine species, and the Hangenberg event (about 359), which ended the armoured placoderm fishes. Both left black shales from oxygen-starved seas. The cause is disputed: nutrients washed in by the first forests (Algeo and Scheckler), volcanic eruptions, cooling and glaciers, or, for the Hangenberg, ozone damage, perhaps from a nearby supernova (Fields and colleagues, 2020).

events.title: Pangaea comes together
events.evidenceNote: Matching rocks, fossils and mountain belts on continents now far apart fit together like a jigsaw, as Alfred Wegener pointed out in 1912.
events.text: Gondwana in the south collided with Laurussia (North America and Europe) in the north, and Siberia joined them. From about 335 million years ago nearly all land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, meaning 'all lands': a C-shaped mass reaching from pole to pole and surrounded by the world ocean Panthalassa. It held together into the age of the dinosaurs.

events.title: The Variscan mountains of Europe
events.evidenceNote: Stumps of this old mountain chain, made of folded rock of the same age, crop out in upland blocks across Europe.
events.text: As Gondwana pushed into Laurussia, a great mountain range rose across what is now central and western Europe, part of a chain that ran from the Urals to the Appalachians through the heart of Pangaea. Its eroded roots survive as upland blocks: the Massif Central, Brittany, Cornwall, the Ardennes, the Black Forest and Bohemia. The collision began in the Devonian and continued through the Carboniferous.

events.title: Joggins Fossil Cliffs: the earliest reptile
events.evidenceNote: Sea cliffs expose coal-forest layers of known age, and small animals were trapped inside hollow tree stumps.
events.text: On the shore of the Bay of Fundy, sea cliffs expose a Carboniferous coal forest. Inside hollow fossil stumps of giant clubmoss trees lie the bones of Hylonomus, the earliest known reptile, described by William Dawson in 1860: small animals seem to have sheltered in the rotting stumps and become trapped. As an amniote, Hylonomus could lay its eggs on dry land. Joggins became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

events.title: Mazon Creek
events.place: Mazon Creek, near Morris, Illinois, USA
events.evidenceNote: Animals and plants buried in mud were quickly sealed inside hard ironstone lumps, which preserved even soft bodies.
events.text: Beside the coal swamps of what is now Illinois, plants and animals were buried in mud and sealed inside ironstone nodules about 309 million years ago. Split open, the nodules reveal plants and the animals of a Carboniferous shore, among them jellyfish, sea worms, snails and shrimps, and the famous 'Tully Monster' (Tullimonstrum), the state fossil of Illinois. Few sites show so fully what lived in and around a coal forest.

events.title: The Appalachians are pushed up
events.evidenceNote: Rock layers along eastern North America are folded and stacked, and minerals that grew during the squeezing can be dated.
events.text: The Appalachians were built in stages. Earlier collisions in the Ordovician and Devonian (the Taconic and Acadian mountain building) raised their northern parts. Then, between about 325 and 260 million years ago, Africa, as part of Gondwana, collided with North America in the Alleghanian mountain building, as Pangaea came together. The range then lay deep inside the supercontinent, part of a chain that ran on through Europe to the Urals.

events.title: The Late Paleozoic ice age
events.evidenceNote: Glacial deposits of this age are found across southern Africa, South America, India and Australia, which were then joined together near the South Pole.
events.text: With Gondwana lying over the South Pole and carbon dioxide low, ice sheets spread across the southern continents. The ice age proper began about 335 to 330 million years ago and had two main cold phases, in the later Carboniferous and around the start of the Permian. Global average temperature fell to about 12 degrees Celsius, cooler than today. As the ice grew and melted, sea level swung up and down, stacking coal seams between marine layers.

events.title: The Ural Mountains rise
events.evidenceNote: A long, narrow belt of folded rock marks where an ocean closed between ancient Europe and Asia.
events.text: Baltica (eastern Europe), Siberia and the smaller continent Kazakhstania converged, raising the Urals, the seam between Europe and Asia. The main collisions took place in the late Carboniferous and the Permian, with the last movements in the Triassic and early Jurassic. With them, Siberia and its neighbours were joined to Pangaea, completing the supercontinent.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Uralian orogeny
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Carboniferous Period
Wikipedia: Pangaea

events.title: The Karoo: world of the mammal ancestors
events.place: Karoo Basin near Graaff-Reinet, South Africa
events.evidenceNote: River muds that piled up for millions of years buried skeletons in order, with volcanic ash layers that can be dated.
events.text: The Beaufort Group rocks of the Karoo, up to 6 kilometres thick, are famous for their fossils of therapsids, the 'mammal-like reptiles' on the line leading to mammals. Layer by layer they record life on land before, during and after the end-Permian extinction, which the therapsid Lystrosaurus survived. Dated ash beds suggest that the turnover of land animals here began over 300,000 years before the extinction in the sea (Gastaldo and colleagues, 2020).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Beaufort Group
Wikipedia: Karoo Supergroup
Gastaldo et al. 2020, Nature Communications: The base of the Lystrosaurus Assemblage Zone, Karoo Basin, predates the end-Permian marine extinction

events.title: The Siberian Traps erupt
events.evidenceNote: Crystals in the lavas and in ash beds date the eruptions to the same narrow window as the extinction.
events.text: One of the largest volcanic outpourings of the last 500 million years flooded Siberia with lava: about 7 million square kilometres of basalt remain today, some 4 million cubic kilometres. About two-thirds of the lava erupted within roughly 300,000 years, just before and during the end-Permian extinction. Sheets of magma also spread underground through rocks rich in coal, limestone and salt, and the carbon dioxide and other gases released are the leading suspect for the extinction.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Siberian Traps

Jurikova et al. 2020, Nature Geoscience: Permian-Triassic mass extinction pulses driven by major marine carbon cycle perturbations

events.title: The end-Permian extinction (the 'Great Dying')
events.evidenceNote: At Meishan, layers of volcanic ash just below and above the level where most fossils vanish give dates only about 60,000 years apart.
events.text: The worst extinction known: about 81 percent of marine species and 70 percent of land vertebrate species died, in the sea within about 60,000 years. The Siberian Traps eruptions are the agreed trigger. Disputed: what did the killing, and how fast. Proposals include extreme warming with loss of oxygen in the sea (Penn and colleagues, 2018), acid oceans (Jurikova and colleagues, 2020, though fossil shells from Norway show little acid damage), and ozone loss and acid rain on land.

notes.dimetrodon-skeleton: Dimetrodon lived in the Early Permian, tens of millions of years before the extinction.
notes.griffinfly-fossil-arctotypus: This fossil is from the Permian and does not show the extinction itself.
notes.herrerasaurus-eoraptor-skeletons: These dinosaurs lived in the Late Triassic, more than 20 million years after the extinction.

events.title: The Carnian Pluvial Episode
events.evidenceNote: Rock layers of this age around the world switch from dry-climate to wet-climate sediments, and their chemistry points to huge eruptions.
events.text: For one to two million years the dry Triassic world turned much rainier. The trigger was probably huge volcanic eruptions off western North America (the Wrangellia lavas), which released carbon dioxide and warmed the climate. About a third of marine genera died out. Afterwards dinosaurs, conifers, modern-type corals and other groups that still shape today's world spread widely.

sources.title: Dal Corso et al. 2020, Science Advances: Extinction and dawn of the modern world in the Carnian
Wikipedia: Carnian pluvial episode

events.title: Ischigualasto: the oldest dinosaurs
events.place: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, San Juan, Argentina
events.evidenceNote: Layers of volcanic ash between the fossil beds contain radioactive minerals that give their age.
events.text: The 'Valley of the Moon' in north-west Argentina holds some of the oldest known dinosaurs, including Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus. They lived on a volcanically active river plain with strongly seasonal rain. Dinosaurs were still a minor part of the fauna: most of the bones belong to other reptiles and to cynodonts, the relatives of mammals.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: Ischigualasto Formation, Argentina
Wikipedia: Ischigualasto Formation

events.title: Ghost Ranch and Coelophysis
events.evidenceNote: The skeletons lie in Late Triassic river sediments whose age is known from their fossils and from dated rock layers in the same region.
events.text: In 1947 a quarry at Ghost Ranch yielded hundreds of skeletons, perhaps as many as a thousand, of Coelophysis, a small meat-eating dinosaur. So many complete animals buried together is very rare, and it makes Coelophysis one of the best known early dinosaurs. It lived near the end of the Triassic, when dinosaurs were spreading but did not yet dominate the land.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ghost Ranch
Wikipedia: Coelophysis

events.title: The Central Atlantic lava floods
events.place: Newark Basin, New Jersey, USA (lavas also in Morocco, Brazil and Europe)
events.evidenceNote: Tiny zircon crystals in the lavas contain uranium that decays to lead at a known rate, dating the eruptions to within tens of thousands of years.
events.text: As Pangaea began to tear apart, basalt lava flooded more than 7 million square kilometres of what are now eastern North America, north-west Africa, Brazil and south-west Europe: the largest known lava province on the continents. Dating shows it erupted in four pulses over about 600,000 years, beginning at the same time as the end-Triassic extinction.

sources.title: Marzoli et al. 1999, Science: Extensive 200-million-year-old continental flood basalts of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province

Wikipedia: Central Atlantic magmatic province

events.title: The end-Triassic mass extinction
events.evidenceNote: Fossils vanish from rocks of this age worldwide and the same layers hold chemical signs of volcanic gases, but exactly how the eruptions killed is still argued.
events.text: One of the five great mass extinctions. Up to about half of marine species diversity was lost, and on land most large reptiles other than dinosaurs disappeared. Scientists agree the Central Atlantic eruptions were the trigger but dispute how they killed: carbon dioxide causing warming and acid oceans, a burst of methane, gases from magma baking buried sediments, or short, intense volcanic winters.

events.title: The central Atlantic opens
events.place: Central Atlantic, between eastern North America and north-west Africa
events.evidenceNote: Rift valleys filled with lava and sediment line both coasts, and the age of the sea floor between them shows when the ocean began to widen.
events.text: The first ocean to split Pangaea. Rifting between North America and Africa began in the Late Triassic, about 225 to 200 million years ago, and during the Early to Middle Jurassic new sea floor started to form between them. This narrow central Atlantic separated the northern continents, Laurasia, from the southern ones, Gondwana. The South Atlantic did not open until the Cretaceous.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: Historical perspective (break-up of Pangaea)
Wikipedia: Pangaea
Wikipedia: Jurassic

events.title: The Karoo-Ferrar lava floods
events.place: Lesotho and South Africa (matching lavas in Antarctica)
events.evidenceNote: The lava flows are dated by radioactive decay in their minerals, in both southern Africa and Antarctica.
events.text: Basalt lava poured out across southern Africa and Antarctica, which were then joined together, covering about 3 million square kilometres with more than 2.5 million cubic kilometres of rock. The eruptions mark the first stage in the break-up of the southern supercontinent Gondwana, and they happened at the same time as a crisis in the oceans, the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Karoo-Ferrar
Wikipedia: Gondwana

events.title: The Toarcian ocean crisis
events.evidenceNote: Black, carbon-rich shales of this age are found around the world; they form only where the sea floor has no oxygen.
events.text: Large parts of the ocean lost their oxygen about 183 million years ago, at the same time as the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions. Temperatures rose, the seas became more acidic and many marine species died out. Black mud built up on the stagnant sea floor and preserved fossils in remarkable detail, as in Germany's Posidonia Shale.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event
Wikipedia: Jurassic
Wikipedia: Karoo-Ferrar

events.title: Gondwana begins to break up
events.place: Mozambique Channel, between Africa and Madagascar
events.evidenceNote: The oldest sea floor between Africa and Madagascar, and lavas along the old rift, date the first split.
events.text: The southern supercontinent Gondwana started to come apart in the Early Jurassic, soon after the Karoo eruptions. East Gondwana (Antarctica, Madagascar, India and Australia) began to pull away from Africa and South America, opening the first stretch of the Indian Ocean. Over the next 150 million years Gondwana's pieces became the southern continents we know today.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gondwana
Wikipedia: Madagascar plate
Wikipedia: Pangaea

events.title: The Morrison Formation
events.place: Morrison, Colorado, USA (the formation spans the western United States)
events.evidenceNote: Volcanic ash layers within the formation have been dated by radioactive decay, bracketing the dinosaur beds.
events.text: A sheet of river and floodplain sediments covering about 1.5 million square kilometres of the western United States, and North America's most famous source of Jurassic dinosaurs. Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Brachiosaurus all come from it. Only a tiny fraction of the formation is exposed at the surface where fossil hunters can reach it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Morrison Formation
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Jurassic Period

events.title: Solnhofen and Archaeopteryx
events.evidenceNote: The fine limestone formed in still lagoons of latest Jurassic age, dated by the fossils it contains.
events.text: Fine limestone laid down in warm, salty lagoons cut off from the open sea by reefs. Almost nothing could live in the bottom water, so animals that fell or drifted in were buried undisturbed in soft mud. The most famous is Archaeopteryx, a feathered, winged animal about half a metre long that still had sharp teeth and a long bony tail like a dinosaur.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: Solnhofen Limestone
Natural History Museum, London: Archaeopteryx
Wikipedia: Solnhofen Limestone
Wikipedia: Archaeopteryx

events.title: The Paraná-Etendeka lava floods
events.place: Serra Geral, southern Brazil (matching lavas at Etendeka, Namibia)
events.evidenceNote: Lavas of the same age and chemistry are found in Brazil and in Namibia, on opposite sides of the Atlantic.
events.text: Flood basalts erupted 136 to 132 million years ago over about a million square kilometres of South America, with a smaller matching patch in Namibia and Angola. The two areas were side by side when the lava flowed. They were torn apart as the South Atlantic opened, and now lie on opposite shores of the ocean.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Paraná and Etendeka traps
Wikipedia: Pangaea

events.title: The first flowering plants
events.evidenceNote: The oldest fossil flowers and flower pollen that scientists agree on come from Early Cretaceous rocks.
events.text: Flowering plants (angiosperms) first appear as fossils in the Early Cretaceous, about 130 to 125 million years ago. By about 100 million years ago they were diversifying fast, and by the end of the period they dominated most land vegetation. Today they make up about 90 percent of living plant species. Bees and other insects diversified alongside them.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: The Cretaceous Period
Wikipedia: Cretaceous
Wikipedia: Flowering plant

events.title: The South Atlantic opens
events.place: South Atlantic, between South America and Africa
events.evidenceNote: The sea floor gets steadily older from the mid-ocean ridge towards both coasts, recording how the ocean grew.
events.text: South America and Africa, joined since Gondwana formed, split apart during the Early to middle Cretaceous. The rift unzipped from south to north, so the ocean opened first in the far south and last between Brazil and West Africa. The matching coastlines that Alfred Wegener pointed to in 1912, when he proposed that continents drift, are the scar of this break.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pangaea
Wikipedia: Cretaceous
USGS This Dynamic Earth: Historical perspective (break-up of Pangaea)

events.title: The feathered dinosaurs of Liaoning
events.evidenceNote: Volcanic layers among the fossil beds contain minerals whose radioactive decay gives their age.
events.text: Lake beds and volcanic ash in north-east China preserve an Early Cretaceous community, the Jehol Biota, in remarkable detail. The fossils include dinosaurs with feathers, such as Sinosauropteryx, which showed that feathers were not unique to birds. Early birds, mammals, insects and plants are preserved alongside them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jehol Biota
Wikipedia: Yixian Formation

events.title: Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a and a volcanic puzzle
events.place: Ontong Java Plateau, western Pacific (the long-suspected cause)
events.evidenceNote: Black, carbon-rich mud marks the event in sea-floor rocks worldwide; new dating of the volcanic plateau long blamed for it no longer fits.
events.text: In the Selli Event large parts of the ocean ran short of oxygen and black, carbon-rich mud built up on the sea floor. It was long blamed on the eruption of the Ontong Java Plateau, a vast pile of undersea lava in the western Pacific. In 2023 new argon dating by Davidson and colleagues made the plateau up to 10 million years younger, too young to be the cause, so the trigger is uncertain again.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Selli Event
Davidson et al. 2023, Science: A younger and protracted emplacement of the Ontong Java Plateau
Wikipedia: Ontong Java Plateau

events.title: Oceanic Anoxic Event 2
events.evidenceNote: A layer of black shale one to two metres thick marks the event, and the metal osmium in it carries a volcanic fingerprint.
events.text: At the boundary between the Cenomanian and Turonian ages, near the hottest point of the Cretaceous, the oceans again lost much of their oxygen. A band of black shale called the Bonarelli Level records it. Osmium in the sediments shows a huge burst of volcanic activity just before the event began, the probable trigger. Many marine species died out.

sources.title: Turgeon and Creaser 2008, Nature: Cretaceous oceanic anoxic event 2 triggered by a massive magmatic episode
Wikipedia: Cenomanian–Turonian boundary event

events.title: A sea across North America
events.place: Great Plains of North America (chalk beds in Kansas)
events.evidenceNote: Chalk, shale and the bones of sea reptiles lie across the middle of the continent, far from any modern coast.
events.text: High Cretaceous seas flooded the middle of North America, joining the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean and splitting the continent into two main landmasses, Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east. At its largest the Western Interior Seaway was about 970 km wide, more than 3,200 km long and 760 metres deep. Its sea-floor chalk now lies under the Great Plains.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Western Interior Seaway
Wikipedia: Cretaceous

events.title: India leaves Madagascar
events.evidenceNote: Sea-floor ages and matching rocks on both sides show when the two landmasses parted.
events.text: India and Madagascar had broken away from the rest of Gondwana together. Between about 95 and 84 million years ago they split from each other. Madagascar stayed beside Africa, while India crossed the ocean at 9 to 20 cm a year, very fast for a continent, towards its collision with Asia. The granite islands of the Seychelles are a fragment left behind on the way.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Madagascar plate
Wikipedia: Indian plate
Wikipedia: Seychelles
USGS This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas, two continents collide

events.title: Were the dinosaurs already in decline?
events.evidenceNote: Counting species through time depends on how many fossil-bearing rocks of each age survive and have been searched, so the same bones can be read both ways.
events.text: Were dinosaurs fading before the asteroid struck? Statistical studies of the dinosaur family tree (Sakamoto and colleagues 2016; Condamine and colleagues 2021) find new species appearing more slowly than old ones died out, from about 76 million years ago or earlier. Others (Bonsor and colleagues 2020; Dean and colleagues 2025) find no real decline, only fewer rocks of the right age to search. The question is open.

events.title: The Rocky Mountains rise
events.evidenceNote: Folded and faulted rock layers, and the sand and gravel shed from the rising ranges, date the mountain building.
events.text: A long episode of mountain building, the Laramide orogeny, raised the Rocky Mountains of western North America. It began 80 to 70 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous, and ended between 55 and 35 million years ago; the exact dates are argued over. During the same time the Western Interior Seaway drained away from the middle of the continent.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Laramide orogeny
Wikipedia: Rocky Mountains
Wikipedia: Western Interior Seaway

events.title: Hell Creek: the last dinosaurs
events.place: Hell Creek, near Jordan, Montana, USA
events.evidenceNote: Volcanic ash in these rocks has been dated by radioactive argon, and a coal layer marks the boundary above which no dinosaur bones are found.
events.text: River and swamp deposits laid down in roughly the last two million years of the Cretaceous. They hold some of the last dinosaurs: Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, the duck-bill Edmontosaurus and the armoured Ankylosaurus. The dinosaurs stop at the boundary layer at the top of the formation, where argon dating ties the extinction to the Chicxulub impact to within 32,000 years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hell Creek Formation

Renne et al. 2013, Science: Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary

events.title: The Deccan Traps eruptions
events.evidenceNote: Two teams dated the lava pile with different radioactive clocks and reached different answers about when most of it erupted.
events.text: Lava flows more than 2 km thick, covering about 500,000 square kilometres of western India, erupted across the end of the Cretaceous. Uranium-lead dating by Schoene and colleagues finds a large pulse starting tens of thousands of years before the asteroid impact; argon dating by Sprain and colleagues puts about three quarters of the lava after it. How much the eruptions added to the extinction is disputed.

sources.title: Schoene et al. 2019, Science: U-Pb constraints on pulsed eruption of the Deccan Traps

events.title: The Chicxulub impact
events.evidenceNote: The buried crater has been mapped and drilled, and a thin layer of its debris is found in rocks of exactly this age all over the world.
events.text: An asteroid about 10 km across struck where the coast of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula is now, blasting a crater 180 to 200 km wide that today lies buried under about a kilometre of younger rock. Debris from the impact forms a thin layer found around the globe. Darkness and cold followed. Argon dating places the impact within 32,000 years of the mass extinction.

sources.title: Schulte et al. 2010, Science: The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Renne et al. 2013, Science: Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary

events.title: The end-Cretaceous mass extinction
events.evidenceNote: Fossils of dinosaurs, ammonites and many plankton stop at the same thin layer of impact debris worldwide; what is argued is how much volcanoes added to the damage.
events.text: About three quarters of plant and animal species died out, including every dinosaur except the birds, the pterosaurs, the great sea reptiles and the ammonites. Most researchers hold that the Chicxulub impact was the main cause (Schulte 2010; Hull 2020; Chiarenza 2020). Others argue that the Deccan eruptions also drove the crisis (Schoene 2019). Mammals, birds, crocodiles and turtles came through.

events.title: The North Atlantic lava floods
events.place: Giant's Causeway, Northern Ireland (lavas also in Scotland and Greenland)
events.evidenceNote: The lavas on both sides of the North Atlantic have been dated by radioactive argon in their minerals.
events.text: As Greenland began to tear away from Europe, lava flooded at least 1.3 million square kilometres in two main phases, about 62 to 58 and 56 to 54 million years ago. The basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway and Fingal's Cave are remnants. The second phase coincided with a sudden global warming, the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, and may have triggered it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: North Atlantic Igneous Province

events.title: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
events.place: Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, USA (a detailed record on land)
events.evidenceNote: Sea-floor mud and land sediments of this age show a sharp shift in carbon and oxygen isotopes, the chemical signature of a sudden release of carbon and a jump in temperature.
events.text: In less than 10,000 years the average global temperature rose by about 5 to 8 °C, to as high as 34 °C, and it stayed high for about 200,000 years. Thousands of billions of tonnes of carbon entered the air and the oceans. The source is debated: volcanic activity as the North Atlantic opened, or methane released from the sea floor. It is often seen as the closest ancient parallel to modern warming.

sources.title: NOAA Climate.gov: What's the hottest Earth's ever been?

events.title: The North Atlantic opens
events.place: Norwegian Sea, between Greenland and Norway
events.evidenceNote: Lavas erupted at the moment of break-up, in East Greenland and beneath the sea, have been dated by radioactive argon.
events.text: The last major split of Pangaea's northern half. Greenland, still attached to North America, separated from north-west Europe about 55.5 million years ago and sea floor began to spread between them, opening the Norwegian Sea and completing the Atlantic Ocean. Until then, land animals could cross between Europe and North America by way of Greenland.

sources.title: Storey et al. 2007, Science: Paleocene-Eocene thermal maximum and the opening of the Northeast Atlantic
Wikipedia: Pangaea

events.title: India collides with Asia
events.evidenceNote: The last sea-floor rocks caught between the continents and the slowing of India's drift each give a slightly different date for first contact.
events.text: After crossing the ocean from Gondwana, India ran into Asia and began to push up the Himalayas. Many accounts date first contact to about 55 million years ago; the US Geological Survey gives 50 to 40. Van Hinsbergen and colleagues argue that a smaller Tibetan-Himalayan fragment arrived about 50 million years ago, and that the main Indian continent collided only 25 to 20 million years ago.

events.title: The Green River lakes
events.evidenceNote: Volcanic ash layers in the lake beds have been dated by radioactive decay, and thin yearly layers of mud count off the time between them.
events.text: Large freshwater lakes lay across what is now south-west Wyoming and neighbouring states in the warm early Eocene. Their fine mud preserved fish in huge numbers, along with stingrays, palm leaves and many other plants and animals. The layers, laid down year by year, record about six million years. They show a subtropical Wyoming at the warmest time of the last 66 million years.

sources.title: US National Park Service: Fossils, Fossil Butte National Monument
Wikipedia: Green River Formation

events.title: The Azolla event
events.evidenceNote: A drill core from the Arctic sea floor contains layers packed with the remains of the freshwater fern Azolla.
events.text: For about 800,000 years the Arctic Ocean, then almost enclosed and at times capped by fresh water, was covered again and again by mats of the floating fern Azolla. As the ferns died they sank and were buried, locking away carbon. Some researchers think this helped lower carbon dioxide and begin the long cooling from the Eocene hothouse; that link is still a hypothesis.

sources.title: Brinkhuis et al. 2006, Nature: Episodic fresh surface waters in the Eocene Arctic Ocean
Wikipedia: Azolla event

events.title: The Messel Pit
events.evidenceNote: The oil shale formed on the bottom of a lake in a volcanic crater, and the volcanic rock has been dated by radioactive decay.
events.text: A lake in an old volcanic crater whose bottom mud turned to oil shale and preserved plants, insects and backboned animals in exceptional detail. Finds include bats, early horses and the primate Darwinius. Messel is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the best windows anywhere on life in the warm middle Eocene.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Messel Pit
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Eocene Epoch

events.title: The Drake Passage opens
events.place: Drake Passage, between South America and Antarctica
events.evidenceNote: Estimates come from sea-floor ages, which are hard to read here, and from chemical traces of Pacific water in Atlantic sea-bed mud.
events.text: The sea passage between South America and Antarctica completes the ring of open ocean around Antarctica. When it opened is uncertain: estimates range from 49 to 17 million years ago. Scher and Martin found chemical traces of Pacific water reaching the Atlantic about 41 million years ago, which suggests a shallow early opening, with a deeper passage developing later.

sources.title: Scher and Martin 2006, Science: Timing and climatic consequences of the opening of Drake Passage
Wikipedia: Drake Passage

events.title: Whales with legs: Wadi al-Hitan and the Fayum
events.place: Wadi al-Hitan and the Fayum, Egypt
events.evidenceNote: The bones lie in sea-floor and river sediments dated by their fossils and by flips of Earth's magnetic field recorded in the rock.
events.text: In Egypt's Western Desert, Wadi al-Hitan ('Valley of the Whales') holds hundreds of fossils of early whales such as Basilosaurus and Dorudon, about 40 million years old. They still had small hind legs, feet and toes: proof that whales descend from land mammals. Younger river deposits in the nearby Fayum contain early relatives of monkeys and apes, such as Aegyptopithecus.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Wadi al-Hitan
Wikipedia: Jebel Qatrani Formation

events.title: Australia leaves Antarctica
events.place: Southern Ocean, between Australia and Antarctica
events.evidenceNote: Sea-floor ages south of Australia record the widening gap between the two continents.
events.text: Australia was the last large piece of Gondwana to leave Antarctica. The two finally separated about 40 to 30 million years ago, and Australia then moved quickly north, as India had done before it. Cut off from the other continents, its marsupials and other animals evolved in isolation for tens of millions of years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tasmanian Passage
Wikipedia: Pangaea

events.title: Antarctica freezes over
events.evidenceNote: Oxygen isotopes in sea-floor shells shift sharply at this time, showing both colder water and a great volume of water locked up as ice.
events.text: At the boundary between the Eocene and Oligocene a continent-wide ice sheet grew on Antarctica and sea level fell by about 55 metres. The older explanation was that new sea passages let a cold current isolate the continent. Climate modelling by DeConto and Pollard points instead to falling carbon dioxide as the main cause, with the passages playing a secondary part.

sources.title: DeConto and Pollard 2003, Nature: Rapid Cenozoic glaciation of Antarctica induced by declining atmospheric CO2
Miller et al. 2020, Science Advances: Cenozoic sea-level and cryospheric evolution
Wikipedia: Eocene–Oligocene extinction event

events.title: The Tasmanian Gateway and the circumpolar current
events.place: South Tasman Rise, south of Tasmania
events.evidenceNote: The old edges of the continents show when deep water could first pass, and a chemical tracer in sea-bed mud shows when water from different oceans began to mix.
events.text: Deep water first flowed between Australia and Antarctica 33.5 million years ago, give or take 1.5 million years. By about 30 million years ago the gap had drifted into the belt of strong westerly winds, and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, today the world's mightiest ocean current, began to circle the continent. It probably helped to keep carbon dioxide low afterwards.

sources.title: Scher et al. 2015, Nature: Onset of Antarctic Circumpolar Current 30 million years ago as Tasmanian Gateway aligned with westerlies
Wikipedia: Tasmanian Passage

events.title: The Alps rise
events.dateLabel: from c. 55 million years ago; fastest c. 34–23 million years ago
events.evidenceNote: Rocks that formed on the floor of a vanished sea are now folded and stacked high in the mountains.
events.text: As Africa moved north it squeezed the Tethys Ocean shut and pressed smaller plates into the southern edge of Europe. The main phases of mountain building began in the Paleocene and Eocene, and the Alps were rising quickly during the Oligocene. The same long collision zone continues east to the Himalayas, and parts of it are still active today.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Alpine orogeny
Wikipedia: Oligocene
Wikipedia: Tethys Ocean

events.title: Riversleigh
events.evidenceNote: The fossil-bearing limestones are placed in order by the kinds of mammals they hold, compared with dated sites elsewhere.
events.text: Limestone in north-west Queensland holds Australia's most famous fossil record of mammals, running from the late Oligocene, about 28 million years ago, through the Miocene. It preserves relatives of koalas and thylacines, bats, birds and reptiles, many known from nowhere else, and shows how the wildlife of an isolated continent changed over millions of years. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1994.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Riversleigh World Heritage Area

events.title: The Himalayas and Tibet rise
events.dateLabel: from c. 50 million years ago; high by c. 23 million years ago
events.evidenceNote: Sea fossils in rocks of the high plateau show they formed under the Tethys Sea, and isotopes in ancient sediments record how high the land stood.
events.text: India's continuing push into Asia crumpled the crust into the Himalayas, 2,900 km long, and raised the Tibetan Plateau. Isotope records suggest the plateau stood about 3,000 metres high around 23 million years ago. Major phases of Himalayan mountain building in the Miocene changed Asia's monsoons. The range is still rising by more than a centimetre a year.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas, two continents collide
Wikipedia: Tibetan Plateau
Wikipedia: Miocene

events.title: The Columbia River lava floods
events.place: Columbia Plateau, Washington and Oregon, USA
events.evidenceNote: Each lava flow can be dated by radioactive argon in its minerals.
events.text: The youngest and one of the best preserved of Earth's great lava floods covered more than 210,000 square kilometres of Oregon, Washington, Idaho and Nevada. Nearly all of it erupted between 17 and 14 million years ago, most of it between 16.7 and 15.9. That matches a warm spell called the Miocene Climatic Optimum, and gases from the eruptions are thought to be its main cause.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Columbia River Basalt Group
Wikipedia: Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum

events.title: The middle Miocene cooling
events.evidenceNote: Oxygen isotopes in sea-floor shells shift again, recording colder water and more ice on land.
events.text: After the warm Miocene Climatic Optimum, about 17 to 14 million years ago, the climate cooled sharply. The East Antarctic ice sheet grew again and has been permanent since about 12.8 million years ago. The cooler, drier world favoured open country over forest, and a wave of extinctions followed among species suited to the warmth.

sources.title: Miller et al. 2020, Science Advances: Cenozoic sea-level and cryospheric evolution
Wikipedia: Middle Miocene disruption
Wikipedia: Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum

events.title: The Andes reach their height
events.dateLabel: mostly within the last 10 million years
events.evidenceNote: The ages of folded rocks and of valleys cut into the plateau's edge show when each part of the range rose.
events.text: The Andes formed where the floor of the Pacific, the Nazca Plate, slides beneath South America. Mountain building there has gone on for a very long time, but it had its greatest effect in the Miocene. The Altiplano, the high plateau around Lake Titicaca, is estimated to have risen 2,000 to 3,000 metres in the last ten million years, to more than 3,000 metres above the sea.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Andean orogeny
Wikipedia: Miocene

events.title: Tropical grasslands spread
events.evidenceNote: The chemistry of fossil teeth and ancient soils changes when animals switch from eating leaves to eating tropical grasses.
events.text: Grasses had been moving into open country since the Oligocene. Between about 7 and 6 million years ago grasses that use a more efficient kind of photosynthesis, called C4, expanded to become a major part of the world's vegetation in warm regions. Grazing mammals diversified with them. The oldest known upright-walking apes lived in Africa at about the same time.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Miocene
Wikipedia: C4 carbon fixation
Wikipedia: Oligocene
Brunet et al. 2002, Nature: A new hominid from the Upper Miocene of Chad, Central Africa

events.title: The Mediterranean dries out
events.place: Mediterranean basin (salt deposits in Sicily and beneath the sea floor)
events.evidenceNote: Drill cores from beneath the Mediterranean sea floor brought up thick layers of salt and gypsum, which form only when sea water evaporates.
events.text: Movements of the Earth's crust closed the sea passages linking the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. Cut off, the sea lost more water by evaporation than rivers could replace, and it partly or almost completely dried out, perhaps several times, leaving thick layers of salt on its floor. The episode is called the Messinian salinity crisis.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Messinian salinity crisis
Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature: Catastrophic flood of the Mediterranean after the Messinian salinity crisis

events.title: The Zanclean flood
events.evidenceNote: A channel about 200 km long and more than 250 metres deep, cut into the sea bed through the strait, is thought to be the scar left by the flood.
events.text: The Atlantic broke through at Gibraltar and refilled the Mediterranean. A model based on the channel it carved suggests that, after a slow start, 90 percent of the water poured in within a few months to two years, at about a thousand times the flow of the Amazon, raising the sea by more than ten metres a day at the peak. The flood marks the start of the Pliocene.

sources.title: Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature: Catastrophic flood of the Mediterranean after the Messinian salinity crisis
Wikipedia: Zanclean flood
ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart v2026/06 (PDF)

events.title: The Isthmus of Panama forms
events.evidenceNote: Rocks, fossils of sea creatures on either side, and DNA differences between Pacific and Caribbean species each record when the seaway closed, and they do not all agree.
events.text: Rising land finally joined North and South America and separated the Pacific from the Caribbean. A large review led by O'Dea in 2016 puts the complete land bridge at about 2.8 million years ago. Montes and colleagues, studying river sands in Colombia, argue the seaway had already closed by the middle Miocene, millions of years earlier, and Bacon and colleagues find early waves of migration. The date is still disputed.

sources.title: O'Dea et al. 2016, Science Advances: Formation of the Isthmus of Panama
Montes et al. 2015, Science: Middle Miocene closure of the Central American Seaway
Bacon et al. 2015, PNAS: Biological evidence supports an early and complex emergence of the Isthmus of Panama
Wikipedia: Isthmus of Panama

events.title: The Great American Interchange
events.evidenceNote: South American animals appear in North American fossil beds from this time on, and northern animals appear in the south.
events.text: Once land joined the Americas, animals walked across in both directions. Ground sloths, armadillos, opossums, porcupines and giant flightless 'terror birds' went north; cats, horses, tapirs and many others went south. A few had crossed earlier, probably over water, but the exchange sped up dramatically about 2.7 million years ago. Many of South America's unique native mammals later died out.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great American Interchange
Woodburne 2010, Journal of Mammalian Evolution: The Great American Biotic Interchange
Wikipedia: Pliocene

events.title: Ice sheets grow in the north
events.evidenceNote: Sea-floor cores from the far North Pacific record colder winters and more floating ice from this time on.
events.text: After millions of years of slow cooling, large ice sheets began to grow on the northern continents about 2.7 million years ago. From then on the ice advanced and retreated in step with small, regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt: about every 41,000 years at first and, after roughly a million years ago, about every 100,000 years. This is the ice age we still live in.

sources.title: Haug et al. 2005, Nature: North Pacific seasonality and the glaciation of North America 2.7 million years ago
Miller et al. 2005, Science: The Phanerozoic record of global sea-level change
Wikipedia: Quaternary glaciation

events.title: The ice-age giants die out
events.evidenceNote: Radiocarbon dates on the last bones of each species are compared with the dates of human arrival and of climate swings, and the match differs from region to region.
events.text: Mammoths, giant ground sloths, sabre-toothed cats and most other very large animals died out: about 65 percent of large species worldwide, and more than 80 percent in South America and Australia. Many researchers blame hunting and other pressure from spreading humans (Sandom 2014; Svenning 2024). Others point to rapid climate swings (Cooper 2015; Stewart 2021) or to both together.

sources.title: Sandom et al. 2014, Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Global late Quaternary megafauna extinctions linked to humans, not climate change
Svenning et al. 2024, Cambridge Prisms: Extinction: The late-Quaternary megafauna extinctions
Cooper et al. 2015, Science: Abrupt warming events drove Late Pleistocene Holarctic megafaunal turnover
Stewart et al. 2021, Nature Communications: Climate change, not human population growth, correlates with Late Quaternary megafauna declines in North America
Wikipedia: Late Pleistocene extinctions
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Pleistocene Epoch

events.title: The La Brea Tar Pits
events.place: Rancho La Brea, Los Angeles, California, USA
events.evidenceNote: The bones are young enough to be dated by radiocarbon, which measures the decay of carbon-14 in once-living tissue.
events.text: Natural asphalt seeping to the surface in what is now Los Angeles trapped animals for tens of thousands of years. The collections cover the last 50,000 years and more than 660 species; the commonest large mammals are dire wolves, sabre-toothed cats and coyotes. A 2023 study of dated bones found the big mammals there had vanished by about 13,000 years ago, at a time of warming, more people and large fires.

sources.title: La Brea Tar Pits and Museum: Mammal collections
UC Museum of Paleontology: La Brea Tar Pits
Natural History Museums of Los Angeles County: La Brea study links extinction to climate change, humans and fire (2023)
Wikipedia: La Brea Tar Pits

events.title: The Last Glacial Maximum
events.evidenceNote: Ridges of debris left by the ice are dated by radiocarbon and by how long their boulders have been exposed, and old shorelines and corals show how far the sea fell.
events.text: The most recent peak of the ice age. Ice sheets covered Canada, Scandinavia and much of Britain: about a quarter of all land. So much water was locked up as ice that the sea stood 125 to 134 metres lower, exposing land bridges such as Beringia between Siberia and Alaska. The global average temperature was about 6 °C lower than before industry.

sources.title: Clark et al. 2009, Science: The Last Glacial Maximum
Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS: Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene
Tierney et al. 2020, Nature: Glacial cooling and climate sensitivity revisited
Wikipedia: Last Glacial Maximum

events.title: The Younger Dryas cold snap
events.evidenceNote: Yearly layers in Greenland ice record the sudden cooling and warming; the markers claimed as proof of an impact were not found when independent laboratories tested for them.
events.text: As the ice age was ending, the Northern Hemisphere swung back to near-glacial cold for about 1,200 years, then warmed abruptly into the Holocene. Most researchers link it to a disruption of the Atlantic's heat-carrying currents. Firestone, Kennett and colleagues proposed instead that a comet struck or exploded about 12,900 years ago; this impact hypothesis has been widely rejected, because independent tests failed to confirm its evidence.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Younger Dryas
Firestone et al. 2007, PNAS: Evidence for an extraterrestrial impact 12,900 years ago
Kennett et al. 2009, Science: Nanodiamonds in the Younger Dryas boundary sediment layer
Holliday et al. 2016, PLoS One: A blind test of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis
Wikipedia: Younger Dryas impact hypothesis

events.title: The Anthropocene: proposed and rejected
events.evidenceNote: Mud layers in the lake record plutonium from hydrogen-bomb tests from 1952; the argument is whether so recent a marker should define a formal unit of geological time.
events.text: Is there a new epoch made by humans? The Anthropocene Working Group proposed one beginning in 1952, marked by bomb-test plutonium in the mud of Crawford Lake. In March 2024 the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted the proposal down, 12 to 4, and the ICS and IUGS confirmed the decision. Officially we still live in the Holocene; 'Anthropocene' remains an informal word for the age of human impact.

sources.title: IUGS-ICS statement on the Anthropocene, March 2024 (PDF)
ICS: Joint statement by the IUGS and ICS on the vote by the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy
Wikipedia: Anthropocene
Zalasiewicz et al. 2024, Nature: The meaning of the Anthropocene: why it matters even without a formal geological definition

origins.name: First life
origins.sci: Last universal common ancestor (LUCA) and earlier

oldest.name: Stromatolites and hot-spring microbial deposits of the Dresser Formation

origins.evidenceNote: Layered mounds built by microbes 3.48 billion years ago are widely accepted; older claims from Greenland (3.7 billion), Quebec (3.77 to 4.28 billion) and a 4.1-billion-year-old Australian crystal are argued over, because heat and pressure can make lifeless rock look alive.
origins.text: All living things share one ancestor, a single-celled microbe that scientists call LUCA. The oldest fossils everyone accepts are mats of microbes preserved in Australian rocks 3.48 billion years old. Gene studies suggest LUCA lived far earlier, about 4.2 billion years ago, soon after the oceans formed. Life then stayed microscopic for most of Earth's history.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Earliest known life forms
Nature Communications: Earliest signs of life on land preserved in ca. 3.5 Ga hot spring deposits (Djokic et al. 2017)
Nature: Rapid emergence of life shown by 3,700-million-year-old microbial structures (Nutman et al. 2016)
Nature: Reassessing evidence of life in 3,700-million-year-old rocks of Greenland (Allwood et al. 2018)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: The nature of the last universal common ancestor (Moody et al. 2024)

origins.name: Bacteria

oldest.name: Stromatolites (microbial mats) of the Dresser Formation

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest fossil mats were built by microbes that looked like bacteria, though shape alone cannot tell bacteria from archaea; gene studies put the split between the two lines at about 4.2 billion years ago.
origins.text: Bacteria are tiny single cells without a nucleus, and they were among the first living things. For over a billion years they and the archaea had the planet to themselves. Bacteria invented most of life's chemistry, including photosynthesis, and they still outnumber every other kind of organism. Every plant and animal depends on them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bacteria
Wikipedia: Earliest known life forms
Nature Communications: Earliest signs of life on land preserved in ca. 3.5 Ga hot spring deposits (Djokic et al. 2017)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: Integrated genomic and fossil evidence illuminates life's early evolution (Betts et al. 2018)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: The nature of the last universal common ancestor (Moody et al. 2024)

origins.name: Archaea

oldest.name: Methane made by microbes, trapped in tiny fluid bubbles in hydrothermal rocks

origins.evidenceNote: No archaeal body fossils can be recognised; the evidence is methane with a chemical fingerprint of microbes, sealed inside 3.5-billion-year-old Australian rock, and methane-making today is done only by archaea.
origins.text: Archaea look like bacteria but are built differently inside and form a separate branch of life. Many thrive in extreme places such as hot springs and salt lakes, and some make methane gas. They matter to our own story: the cells of animals, plants and fungi descend from an archaeon that took in a bacterium.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Archaea
Nature: Evidence from fluid inclusions for microbial methanogenesis in the early Archaean era (Ueno et al. 2006)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: Integrated genomic and fossil evidence illuminates life's early evolution (Betts et al. 2018)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: The nature of the last universal common ancestor (Moody et al. 2024)

origins.name: Cyanobacteria (oxygen-making bacteria)

oldest.name: Chemical signs of the first oxygen-rich air (Great Oxidation Event); oldest undisputed body fossil Eoentophysalis belcherensis, c. 2.0 to 1.85 billion years ago

origins.evidenceNote: Rocks show that oxygen first built up in the air about 2.4 billion years ago, which only oxygen-making bacteria could cause; the oldest fossils that are surely cyanobacteria are about 2.0 to 1.85 billion years old, and claims of 3.5-billion-year-old ones are not accepted by all.
origins.text: Cyanobacteria were the first living things to split water using sunlight and release oxygen. Over hundreds of millions of years their waste gas changed the air and the oceans, poisoning much older life but making animals possible later. The green parts of every plant cell descend from cyanobacteria swallowed by an ancient alga.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cyanobacteria
Wikipedia: Great Oxidation Event
Nature: Oldest thylakoids in fossil cells directly evidence oxygenic photosynthesis (Demoulin et al. 2024)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: Integrated genomic and fossil evidence illuminates life's early evolution (Betts et al. 2018)

origins.name: Cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes)

oldest.name: Tappania and other large, ornamented single-celled fossils

origins.evidenceNote: Large, complex cell fossils about 1.65 billion years old are accepted as eukaryotes; older finds such as the 2.1-billion-year-old Gabon shapes and the coiled Grypania (1.87 billion) may be bacterial colonies or not fossils at all.
origins.text: Eukaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleus and have tiny power stations called mitochondria. They arose when an archaeon took a bacterium inside itself and the two became partners. Every animal, plant, fungus and alga is built from such cells. The oldest sure fossils come from China and Australia; simple many-celled forms followed quickly.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Eukaryote
Science Advances: 1.63-billion-year-old multicellular eukaryotes from North China (Miao et al. 2024)
Nature: Early fossil eukaryotes were benthic aerobes (2026)
Nature: Large colonial organisms with coordinated growth in oxygenated environments 2.1 Gyr ago (El Albani et al. 2010)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: Integrated genomic and fossil evidence illuminates life's early evolution (Betts et al. 2018)

origins.name: Red algae
origins.evidenceNote: Bangiomorpha, about 1.05 billion years old, looks so like a living red seaweed that it is widely accepted; Indian fossils 1.6 billion years old may be red algae too, but that reading is not yet agreed.
origins.text: Red algae are seaweeds, and Bangiomorpha is the oldest fossil that can be placed in a living group of complex organisms. It is also the oldest known organism with two sexes. Its threads of cells show that many-celled life and sexual reproduction were under way a billion years ago.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bangiomorpha
Wikipedia: Red algae
PLOS Biology: 1.6 billion-year-old crown-group red algae (Bengtson et al. 2017)
TimeTree: divergence time of a red alga (Pyropia) and thale cress

origins.name: Green algae
origins.evidenceNote: Tiny branching seaweed fossils from Chinese rocks one billion years old match living green algae; gene studies date the first split among green plants to roughly the same time.
origins.text: Green algae use the same green pigments as land plants, because land plants are their descendants. The tiny seaweed Proterocladus, a billion years old, already had branches and specialised cells. Green algae filled seas and fresh water for half a billion years before one line moved onto land and became the plants.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Proterocladus
Wikipedia: Green algae
Nature Ecology & Evolution: A one-billion-year-old multicellular chlorophyte (Tang et al. 2020)
TimeTree: divergence time of thale cress and the green alga Chlamydomonas

origins.name: Ediacaran biota
origins.evidenceNote: Fossil beds dated by volcanic ash show large soft-bodied organisms from about 574 million years ago; they are older than the first proven animal because, for many of them, scientists still debate whether they were animals at all.
origins.text: The Ediacaran biota were the first large, complex living things: fronds, discs and quilted mats, from millimetres to metres across, lying on the sea floor with no mouths, shells or legs. Some were early animals, others remain a puzzle. Almost all vanished about 539 million years ago, as burrowing and hunting animals took over.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ediacaran biota
Wikipedia: Mistaken Point
Europe PMC record: Ancient steroids establish the Ediacaran fossil Dickinsonia as one of the earliest animals (Science 2018)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: A crown-group cnidarian from the Ediacaran of Charnwood Forest, UK (Dunn et al. 2022)

origins.name: Jellyfish, corals and relatives
origins.evidenceNote: A fossil from England, dated to 557 to 562 million years ago, shows two tentacled polyps in a stiff skeleton and is the oldest animal that can be placed in a living group; gene studies put the group's origin at least 70 million years earlier.
origins.text: Cnidarians are simple animals with stinging cells and a single body opening: jellyfish, sea anemones and corals. Auroralumina, named in 2022 after David Attenborough, may be the oldest known animal predator. Much later, reef-building corals made some of the largest structures built by any living thing.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Auroralumina
Wikipedia: Cnidaria
Nature Ecology & Evolution: A crown-group cnidarian from the Ediacaran of Charnwood Forest, UK (Dunn et al. 2022)
TimeTree: divergence time of humans and the sea anemone Nematostella

origins.name: First animals

oldest.name: Dickinsonia (with preserved animal fats) and Kimberella

origins.evidenceNote: Dickinsonia fossils 558 million years old still hold cholesterol, a fat made by animals, which settles that they were animals; older claims, such as sponge-like textures in 890-million-year-old Canadian reefs and 'sponge' chemicals in rocks over 635 million years old, are disputed because algae or non-living processes might explain them.
origins.text: Animals are many-celled creatures that eat other living things. Genes suggest the first ones lived 700 to 800 million years ago, but they were tiny and soft and left almost no trace. The oldest fossils that are certainly animals are flat, quilted creatures and a slug-like grazer from the last stretch of the Ediacaran Period.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Animal
Wikipedia: Dickinsonia
Europe PMC record: Ancient steroids establish the Ediacaran fossil Dickinsonia as one of the earliest animals (Science 2018)
Nature Ecology & Evolution: Putative sponge biomarkers in unicellular Rhizaria question an early rise of animals (Nettersheim et al. 2019)

origins.name: Animals with a head and tail (bilaterians)

oldest.name: Kimberella quadrata; also Ikaria wariootia (South Australia, 560 to 551 million years ago)

origins.evidenceNote: Kimberella, a slug-like grazer with a front and a back, is found in Russian rocks 558 to 555 million years old, and the rice-grain-sized burrower Ikaria is of similar age; gene studies place the origin of the group 100 million years or more earlier.
origins.text: Most animals, from worms to whales, have a left and a right side, a front end with a mouth and a gut running through to the back. This body plan allowed animals to move with purpose, burrow and hunt. Within about 30 million years of these first fossils, nearly every major animal group had appeared.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kimberella
Wikipedia: Ikaria
PNAS: Discovery of the oldest bilaterian from the Ediacaran of South Australia (Evans et al. 2020)

TimeTree: divergence time of humans and fruit flies

origins.name: Sponges

oldest.name: Glass-sponge spicules (tiny skeleton needles) of the early Cambrian

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest remains that are surely sponges are glassy needles about 535 million years old; a likely sponge about 545 million years old was described from China in 2024, and older claims (890-million-year-old reef textures; sponge-type chemicals older than 635 million years) are still argued over.
origins.text: Sponges are the simplest animals: bags of cells with no nerves or gut, filtering food from sea water. Genes suggest they were among the first animal branches, perhaps 700 to 800 million years ago, yet clear fossils are much younger, probably because early sponges had no hard parts. That gap is one of the big puzzles of early animal life.

origins.name: Arthropods (jointed-legged animals)

oldest.name: Rusophycus resting traces, dug by animals with jointed legs
oldest.place: Earliest Cambrian sea-floor sediments on several continents

origins.evidenceNote: Scratch marks and resting hollows made by jointed legs appear in the earliest Cambrian rocks, somewhat before the first arthropod bodies (trilobites, about 521 million years ago) are preserved.
origins.text: Arthropods have a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs: insects, spiders, crabs, millipedes and the extinct trilobites. They appear early in the Cambrian explosion and quickly became the most varied animals in the sea. Today four out of five known animal species are arthropods.
