origins.name: Molluscs (snails, clams and relatives)

oldest.name: Helcionellids: tiny cap-shaped shells among the 'small shelly fossils'

origins.evidenceNote: Tiny shells about 535 million years old are the first fossils that can be placed on the mollusc line; the older, shell-less Kimberella (558 million years) grazed like a mollusc and may be an early relative, but scientists do not agree that it was one.
origins.text: Molluscs are soft-bodied animals that usually build a shell: snails, clams, and the squid and octopus. Their first shells were only a millimetre or two across. Molluscs became one of the most successful animal groups in the sea, and their shells make up a large share of the fossil record.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mollusca
Wikipedia: Small shelly fauna
Wikipedia: Kimberella
TimeTree: divergence time of octopus and the lamp shell Lingula

origins.name: Lamp shells (brachiopods)
origins.evidenceNote: Shells of simple lamp shells appear in early Cambrian rocks about 530 million years old; gene studies date their split from the mollusc line to 550 to 610 million years ago.
origins.text: Brachiopods look like clams but are built differently, with an upper and a lower shell and a feathery feeding organ. For 250 million years they carpeted sea floors and are among the commonest fossils of that time. Most were wiped out in the great extinction 252 million years ago; a few hundred species survive.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Brachiopod
TimeTree: divergence time of octopus and the lamp shell Lingula

origins.name: Trilobites
origins.evidenceNote: Hard-shelled trilobites appear suddenly in rocks about 521 million years old in Siberia, North America, Morocco and Spain; the last ones died in the mass extinction 252 million years ago.
origins.text: Trilobites were armoured sea animals with many legs and, in most kinds, eyes built from crystal lenses. They were the first arthropods with hard shells, so they fossilised well: over 22,000 species have been described. They thrived for almost 270 million years before the largest of all extinctions finished them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Trilobite
Wikipedia: Profallotaspis
UC Museum of Paleontology: Fossil record of the Trilobita

origins.name: Chordates (animals with a backbone or its forerunner)

oldest.name: Chengjiang chordates such as Yunnanozoon and the first fish-like animals

origins.evidenceNote: Soft-bodied animals with a stiffening rod along the back and blocks of muscle are preserved in Chinese mudstones 518 million years old; gene studies suggest the line began in the Ediacaran, 590 to 660 million years ago.
origins.text: Chordates have a flexible rod along the back, with a nerve cord above it and muscles in blocks on either side. In most, the rod is replaced by a backbone. The group includes every fish, amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal, as well as sea squirts and lancelets. The first were small, soft-bodied swimmers.

origins.name: Jawless fish (first vertebrates)
origins.sci: Vertebrata (early jawless forms; living lampreys and hagfish)
origins.evidenceNote: Small fish-shaped fossils with gills, a distinct head and fins are preserved in Chinese rocks 518 million years old; they are the oldest known animals on the vertebrate line.
origins.text: The first vertebrates were small jawless fish that sucked or filtered food. For a hundred million years all fish were jawless, many of them armoured with bony plates. Their invention of a skull, eyes and a brain set the pattern for every later backboned animal. Lampreys and hagfish are the only jawless fish alive today.

origins.name: Starfish, sea urchins and relatives

oldest.name: Helicoplacus and other early Cambrian echinoderms

origins.evidenceNote: The first fossils with the special chalky skeleton plates of echinoderms appear in early Cambrian rocks about 516 million years old; gene studies put their split from our own branch well before that.
origins.text: Echinoderms are the starfish, sea urchins, sea lilies and sea cucumbers: sea animals with a skeleton of chalky plates and, in living forms, a five-rayed body. Surprisingly, they are among the closest relatives of animals with backbones. Sea lilies formed vast underwater meadows in later ages.

origins.name: Cephalopods (squid, octopus, nautilus)
origins.evidenceNote: Small chambered shells from the late Cambrian of China are the oldest agreed cephalopods; cone-shaped fossils 522 million years old from Newfoundland were proposed as cephalopods in 2021, but other specialists argue they are mixed-up remains of different animals.
origins.text: Cephalopods are molluscs that turned their shell into a float with gas-filled chambers and their foot into arms. That let them rise off the sea floor and become the first large swimming hunters. Squid and octopus later lost the outer shell and evolved the biggest brains of any animals without a backbone.

origins.name: Land plants

oldest.name: Cryptospores (tough-walled spores of the first land plants)

origins.evidenceNote: The first sign of land plants is their spores, about 470 million years old; plant bodies are not found until about 430 million years ago. Spore-like fossils 480 million years old and older are argued over, some saying they come from algae on the way to becoming plants.
origins.text: Plants came ashore from freshwater green algae. The first were small and moss-like, with no roots or leaves, and clung to damp ground. By breaking down rock, making soil and adding oxygen to the air, they prepared the land for animals. Genes suggest plants reached land tens of millions of years before their first known spores.

origins.name: Sea scorpions
origins.evidenceNote: The oldest named sea scorpion comes from rocks in Iowa about 467 million years old; undescribed finds may push the group back to about 480 million years, and the last ones died out by the end of the Permian.
origins.text: Sea scorpions were armoured hunters related to spiders and horseshoe crabs. The largest grew to about 2.5 metres, the biggest arthropods ever known. They were top predators of Silurian seas and later moved into rivers and lakes. Despite the name, they were not true scorpions.

origins.name: Jawed fish

oldest.name: Qianodus duplicis (tooth whorls) and Fanjingshania renovata

origins.evidenceNote: Teeth and spiny fish remains from China, 439 million years old, are the oldest sure jawed vertebrates, with whole fish from 436 million years ago; loose scales from the Late Ordovician (about 458 to 443 million years ago) may be older jawed fish but cannot be identified for certain.
origins.text: Jaws, probably made from the front gill supports, let fish bite, grasp and chew. It was one of the great turning points for animals with backbones: almost every vertebrate alive today, including people, descends from the first jawed fish. Finds from China reported in 2022 pushed their record back by about 14 million years.

origins.name: Sharks, rays and relatives
origins.evidenceNote: Spines, scales and plates of a shark relative lie in Chinese rocks 439 million years old; shark-like scales from the Late Ordovician could be older still, but nobody has found the fish they came from.
origins.text: Sharks, rays and chimaeras have skeletons of cartilage, the bendy material in your nose, in place of bone. The earliest relatives were small, spiny fish. Cartilage seldom fossilises, so most of their history is read from teeth and scales. Sharks have survived every mass extinction since.

origins.name: Armoured fish (placoderms)
origins.evidenceNote: A 3-centimetre armoured fish from Chongqing, 436 million years old, is the oldest complete placoderm; the group disappears from the rocks at the end of the Devonian, about 359 million years ago.
origins.text: Placoderms were fish with heads and shoulders cased in bony plates, and they are the earliest branch of jawed fish. In the Devonian, the 'Age of Fishes', they reached their greatest variety, and some became large hunters. All died out at the end of that period.

origins.name: Bony fish
origins.evidenceNote: A nearly complete bony fish under 3 centimetres long, described in 2026 from Chinese rocks about 436 million years old, is the oldest known; before it, the record began with Guiyu at about 425 million years.
origins.text: Bony fish have skeletons of true bone. They split early into two lines: ray-finned fish, which became nearly all the fish in today's seas and rivers, and lobe-finned fish, which gave rise to every land animal with a backbone. Counting those land descendants, bony fish make up about 98 per cent of vertebrate species.

origins.name: Arachnids (scorpions, spiders, mites)
origins.evidenceNote: A scorpion from Scottish rocks between 436 and 428 million years old is the oldest known arachnid; an older American fossil called a scorpion in 2020 was shown in 2021 to be a different kind of arthropod.
origins.text: Arachnids have eight legs and no antennae. Scorpions are the oldest known, and the first may still have lived in or near water. Arachnids were among the earliest animals to breathe air and hunt on land. True spiders, with silk-spinning organs, appear in the coal forests over 100 million years later.

origins.name: Vascular plants (plants with water pipes)
origins.evidenceNote: Leafless forked stems a few centimetres tall, tipped with spore capsules, come from Irish and Welsh rocks of the mid-Silurian; a 2024 study dated the oldest beds to at most 426 million years.
origins.text: Vascular plants have tubes that carry water from the ground to their tips and stiffen the stem. This plumbing let plants stand upright and grow tall, away from damp ground. Cooksonia, the earliest, was only a few centimetres high. Ferns, conifers and flowering plants are all vascular plants.

origins.name: Lobe-finned fish
origins.evidenceNote: Guiyu, a well-preserved fish from Yunnan about 425 million years old, already shows features of the lobe-finned line; gene studies date the split from ray-finned fish slightly earlier.
origins.text: Lobe-finned fish have fleshy fins with bones inside, arranged like the bones of an arm or leg. Only coelacanths and lungfish survive, but in the Devonian the group was large and varied. One branch used its sturdy fins to push through shallow water and became the four-legged animals.

origins.name: Clubmosses and scale trees
origins.evidenceNote: Leafy stems of Baragwanathia from Australian rocks of the late Silurian, about 425 million years old, are among the oldest fossils of this group.
origins.text: Clubmosses are today small creeping plants, but they are one of the oldest plant lines with true leaves. In the Carboniferous their relatives the scale trees grew over 40 metres tall in vast swamp forests. The buried remains of those forests became much of the coal that powered the Industrial Revolution.

origins.name: Millipedes and centipedes (first land animals)
origins.evidenceNote: Millipede-like fossils from Scotland about 425 million years old are among the oldest land animals; the famous millipede Pneumodesmus, once dated to 428 million years, was re-dated in 2017 to about 414 million.
origins.text: Millipedes were among the first animals to live on land and breathe air, feeding on rotting plants. Their walking tracks are older than their bodies. Genes say the group itself began in the sea far earlier. Centipedes, which are hunters, belong to the same group, as did the giant Arthropleura of the coal forests.

origins.name: Ray-finned fish (including teleosts)
origins.evidenceNote: Meemannia from the Early Devonian of China is the oldest fish placed on the ray-finned line by a 2016 restudy; scales of Andreolepis, about 420 million years old, were long called the oldest ray-fin but may belong to an earlier side branch.
origins.text: Ray-finned fish have fins that are webs of skin spread over thin bony rods. They began as a minor group but now make up the great majority of fish in seas, rivers and lakes. Nearly all belong to the teleosts, a branch whose first fossils appear in the Triassic and which includes cod, salmon, eels and seahorses.

origins.name: Ammonites

oldest.name: Earliest ammonoids, descended from straight-shelled bactritids

origins.evidenceNote: Coiled ammonoid shells first appear about 410 to 408 million years ago, and the last ones vanish at or just after the extinction 66 million years ago that also killed the dinosaurs.
origins.text: Ammonites were squid-like animals living in coiled, chambered shells. They evolved so fast, and are so common, that geologists use them to tell the age of rocks, especially from the Jurassic and Cretaceous. They survived three mass extinctions by a whisker before the fourth ended them. The living nautilus is only a distant cousin.

origins.name: Fungi

oldest.name: Fungi preserved in the Rhynie chert

origins.evidenceNote: Fungi that nobody doubts are preserved in Scottish rock about 407 million years old; microscopic fossils from Arctic Canada (about 1 billion years), Congo (810 to 715 million) and China (635 million) are claimed as fungi, but simple threads are hard to tell from other microbes.
origins.text: Fungi are neither plants nor animals: they feed by soaking up food from their surroundings. Genes show they are close relatives of animals and split from them over a billion years ago, but their soft bodies rarely fossilise. Fungi helped the first plants take root on land and still feed most plants through their roots.

origins.name: First trees and forests

oldest.name: Calamophyton forest
oldest.place: Hangman Sandstone, near Minehead, Somerset, England

origins.evidenceNote: Fossil trunks and fallen branches in sea cliffs in Somerset, about 390 million years old, are the oldest known forest; the forests at Cairo and Gilboa in New York State are about 385 million years old.
origins.text: The first trees were not related to modern ones. Calamophyton and Wattieza looked like palms or tree ferns, from under 1 to about 8 metres tall; Archaeopteris, soon after, had wood and deep roots like a modern tree. Forests drew carbon dioxide from the air, cooled the climate and held river banks together.

origins.name: Ferns and fern-like plants
origins.evidenceNote: Fern-like plants first appear in the middle Devonian, and the best known is the tree Wattieza from New York, about 385 million years old; gene studies date the fern line a little earlier.
origins.text: Ferns reproduce by spores, not seeds, and uncurl their fronds from coiled tips. Their early relatives were among the first trees, and tree ferns shaded the coal swamps. Four in five ferns alive today belong to one much younger branch, the Polypodiales.

origins.name: Four-legged animals (tetrapods)

notes.ai-tetrapod-devonian-trackway: These traces predate the 375-million-year event; their interpretation is debated.
notes.ai-tetrapod-jaekelopterus: This sea scorpion lived earlier in the Devonian and is shown for wider context.

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest bones of four-legged animals are about 375 million years old; footprints in a Polish quarry, about 390 million years old, would be 18 million years older, but some specialists think the marks were not made by walking animals.
origins.text: Tetrapods are the animals with four limbs: amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. They arose from lobe-finned fish whose fins became legs with fingers and toes, at first for moving through weedy shallows. The fish Tiktaalik, 375 million years old, shows the change half-way, with a neck and wrist-like fins.

origins.name: Seed plants
origins.evidenceNote: Small seed-bearing shoots from the Late Devonian of West Virginia are the oldest known seed plant; a 385-million-year-old plant from Belgium, Runcaria, was a forerunner with a seed that was not yet fully wrapped.
origins.text: A seed is a baby plant packed with food inside a protective coat. Seeds freed plants from needing wet ground to reproduce, so they could spread into dry country and uplands. The first seed plants looked like ferns. Their descendants are the conifers, cycads, ginkgos and all flowering plants.

origins.name: Giant early amphibians (temnospondyls)
origins.evidenceNote: The first temnospondyl bones are about 330 million years old, from Scotland and Germany; the last, Koolasuchus, lived in Australia about 125 to 120 million years ago.
origins.text: Before reptiles ruled, the largest land and river animals were temnospondyls, flat-headed relatives of amphibians. Some looked like salamanders, others like crocodiles several metres long. They lived for 200 million years, and many scientists think frogs and salamanders descend from small members of the group.

origins.name: Insects

oldest.name: Delitzschala bitterfeldensis, one of the oldest undoubted insects

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest fossils that are certainly insects are winged ones about 328 to 324 million years old; a 407-million-year-old jaw from Scotland, Rhyniognatha, was called the first insect, but a 2017 study argued it is more likely a centipede. Gene studies put the origin of insects near 479 million years ago.
origins.text: Insects have six legs and a body in three parts. Genes say they arose from crustacean-like ancestors soon after plants reached land, but for 150 million years they left almost no fossils. They became the most varied animals on Earth: more than a million species have been described, over half of all known animal species.

origins.name: Flying insects

oldest.name: Delitzschala bitterfeldensis and other mid-Carboniferous winged insects

origins.evidenceNote: Winged insects appear in the rocks about 328 to 324 million years ago, already varied, which suggests flight began earlier; one gene study estimates about 406 million years ago.
origins.text: Insects were the first animals to fly, some 100 million years before any reptile, bird or bat. Wings let them escape hunters, find mates and reach new food. In the oxygen-rich air of the coal forests, dragonfly-like griffinflies reached wingspans of about 70 centimetres, the largest insects ever.

origins.name: Amniotes (reptiles and their relatives)
origins.evidenceNote: Hylonomus, found inside fossil tree stumps 318 million years old, is the classic oldest reptile, though some recent studies place it just outside the group; clawed footprints from Australia about 355 million years old were reported in 2025 as reptile tracks, which others question because some non-reptiles may have had claws.
origins.text: Amniotes lay eggs with a waterproof inner membrane, or carry their young inside the body, so they can breed away from water. This freed backboned animals to live anywhere on land. Early on they split into two great lines: one led to reptiles and birds, the other to mammals.

origins.name: Conifers

oldest.name: Earliest conifer remains (Late Carboniferous)
oldest.place: Late Carboniferous rocks of Europe and North America

origins.evidenceNote: Conifers first appear in the fossil record in the Late Carboniferous, a little over 300 million years ago.
origins.text: Conifers carry their seeds in cones and most have needle or scale leaves: pines, firs, cedars, redwoods. Their tough leaves cope with drought and cold, which helped them spread as the coal swamps dried. They were the main trees of the dinosaur age, and the tallest and oldest living trees are conifers.

origins.name: Synapsids (the mammal line)
origins.evidenceNote: Archaeothyris and Melanedaphodon, about 307 million years old, are the oldest confidently identified members; a skull from Joggins, Asaphestera, about 318 million years old, was reinterpreted in 2020 as an even older one, but it is fragmentary.
origins.text: Synapsids are the branch of amniotes that leads to mammals, marked by a single opening in the skull behind each eye. Early ones, such as the sail-backed Dimetrodon, are often called mammal-like reptiles, though they were never reptiles. Before the dinosaurs, synapsids were the dominant land animals.

origins.name: Beetles
origins.evidenceNote: A single small fossil from the early Permian of Germany, about 297 million years old, is the oldest known beetle; gene studies place the split of the beetle line from wasps and bees somewhat earlier.
origins.text: Beetles turned their front wings into hard cases that protect the flying wings beneath. That armour let them squeeze under bark, into soil and through water. They are the most species-rich order of animals: roughly one in every four named animal species is a beetle.

origins.name: Ginkgos
origins.evidenceNote: The earliest probable ginkgo relative, Trichopitys, comes from French rocks of the earliest Permian, between 299 and 293 million years old.
origins.text: Ginkgos are seed plants with fan-shaped leaves. They were common across the world in the age of dinosaurs, then dwindled until a single species, Ginkgo biloba, survived in China. It is often called a living fossil: plants with seeds like those of the living tree are known from the Middle Jurassic, over 160 million years ago.

origins.name: Cycads

oldest.name: Early cycad leaves (probable examples such as Crossozamia are older)

origins.evidenceNote: Leaves that are probably cycads are known from China and South Korea about 300 million years ago, but they cannot be identified for certain; fossils that are clearly cycads appear in the early to middle Permian, around 280 to 270 million years ago.
origins.text: Cycads look like stubby palms with a crown of stiff leaves and large cones, but they are not related to palms. They were a common part of the vegetation in the age of dinosaurs. Two families survive today, in warm regions.

origins.name: Therapsids (advanced mammal relatives)
origins.evidenceNote: Raranimus, a partial skull from China about 272 million years old, is the most primitive therapsid known; a sabre-toothed gorgonopsian from Mallorca, reported in 2024, may be as old or slightly older.
origins.text: Therapsids were synapsids with legs held more upright beneath the body and teeth of different kinds for biting and chewing. Many were probably warm-blooded and some may have had hair. They ruled the land in the late Permian, were almost wiped out 252 million years ago, and one small branch became the mammals.

origins.name: Modern amphibians (frogs, salamanders, caecilians)
origins.evidenceNote: A frog-like fossil from Madagascar about 250 million years old is the oldest sure member of the modern amphibians; Gerobatrachus, 290 million years old from Texas, may be an earlier relative of frogs and salamanders, but its place is debated. Gene studies suggest the group is older than both.
origins.text: Frogs, salamanders and the legless caecilians have thin, moist skin and most lay eggs in water. They are the survivors of the first four-legged animals, though they have changed greatly. Triadobatrachus still had a short tail and many more backbones than a modern frog.

origins.name: Ichthyosaurs

oldest.name: Ichthyosaur tail bones from Spitsbergen; oldest good skeletons: Cartorhynchus and Chaohusaurus, Chaohu, China, c. 248 million years ago

origins.evidenceNote: Bones from Arctic Spitsbergen, reported in 2023, show ichthyosaurs already at sea about 250 million years ago, within 2 million years of the great Permian extinction; the group died out about 94 million years ago.
origins.text: Ichthyosaurs were reptiles that returned to the sea and evolved the shape of dolphins, with flippers, a tail fin and huge eyes. They breathed air and gave birth to live young. They ranged from 1 metre to about 26 metres long. They vanished about 28 million years before the dinosaurs.

origins.name: Archosaurs (ruling reptiles)

oldest.name: Ctenosauriscus koeneni (a sail-backed crocodile relative); also Xilousuchus from China

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest true archosaurs are sail-backed reptiles from Germany and China, about 247 to 248 million years old, only a few million years after the Permian extinction.
origins.text: Archosaurs are the group that contains crocodiles, pterosaurs, dinosaurs and birds. They rose from the ruins of the greatest mass extinction and dominated the land for the next 180 million years. Birds and crocodiles, the only survivors, are each other's closest living relatives.

origins.name: Lizards and snakes
origins.evidenceNote: A small reptile from the Italian Alps, about 240 million years old, was shown in 2018 to be the oldest known member of the lizard line; fossils of the modern lizard groups begin about 168 million years ago, and a claimed 202-million-year-old one from England is disputed.
origins.text: Lizards and snakes shed their scaly skin and have very flexible skulls. With nearly 12,000 species they are the most varied reptiles alive. Their early fossils are scarce because small, light bones rarely survive, leaving a gap of about 70 million years between the first lizard relative and the next good fossils.

origins.name: Dinosaurs

oldest.name: Staurikosaurus, Buriolestes and other Santa Maria Formation dinosaurs
oldest.place: Santa Maria, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest sure dinosaurs come from Brazil and Argentina, about 233 to 231 million years old; Nyasasaurus from Tanzania, about 243 million years old, is known from an arm bone and a few backbones and is either the earliest dinosaur or a very close cousin.
origins.text: Dinosaurs were reptiles that walked with their legs straight under the body. They began small and two-legged, as minor players in a world of crocodile relatives, and took over after an extinction 201 million years ago. All died out 66 million years ago, except one branch that is still with us: the birds.

origins.name: Long-necked dinosaurs (sauropods and their relatives)
origins.evidenceNote: Buriolestes, a small two-legged meat-eater from Brazil about 233 million years old, is the earliest known member of the long-necked line; true giant sauropods on four legs are certain from the Early Jurassic, about 200 million years ago.
origins.text: The ancestors of the long-necked giants were dog-sized runners. Their descendants walked on four pillar-like legs, grew long necks to reach high leaves and became the largest animals ever to live on land. Sauropods such as Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus belong here, and the group lasted until the end of the dinosaur age.

origins.name: Meat-eating dinosaurs (theropods)
origins.evidenceNote: Eodromaeus, a slim hunter about 1.2 metres long from Argentine rocks about 231 million years old, is among the earliest theropods.
origins.text: Theropods were two-legged dinosaurs with hollow bones and, in most, sharp teeth and claws. They include Allosaurus, Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus. Many had feathers. One branch of small feathered theropods took to the air and became the birds, so theropods are the only dinosaurs still alive.

origins.name: Crocodiles and their relatives
origins.evidenceNote: The first crocodile relatives are small, slender land-runners from Late Triassic rocks, roughly 235 to 225 million years old; gene studies date the split of the crocodile line from the bird line to about 245 million years ago.
origins.text: The first crocodile relatives were not river ambushers but lightly built animals that ran on long legs. Over time the group produced sea-going forms with flippers, plant-eaters and giants. The modern crocodiles, alligators and gharials belong to a branch that appeared in the Cretaceous and survived the extinction that killed the dinosaurs.

origins.name: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles)

oldest.name: Preondactylus buffarinii and other Late Triassic pterosaurs of the Alps

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest pterosaur skeletons come from Late Triassic rocks of the Italian Alps and nearby, up to about 228 million years old; they were already fully able to fly, so their beginnings are still unknown.
origins.text: Pterosaurs were the first animals with backbones to fly under their own power, on wings of skin stretched from one enormously long finger. They were close cousins of dinosaurs, not dinosaurs. Early kinds had wingspans of up to 2 metres; later ones included the largest flying animals known. They died out with the dinosaurs.

origins.name: Turtles and tortoises
origins.evidenceNote: Odontochelys, 220 million years old, had teeth and only the lower half of a shell; Pappochelys from Germany (240 million years) is a shell-less forerunner, and Eunotosaurus from South Africa (about 260 million years) has turtle-like broad ribs, but whether it is a true turtle ancestor is debated.
origins.text: Turtles are reptiles whose ribs and backbone grew into a bony shell. Where they fit among reptiles was argued over for a century; DNA now places them nearest the crocodiles and birds. Fossils show the shell was built in stages, the belly plate first. The body plan has barely changed in 200 million years.

origins.name: Mammals
origins.evidenceNote: Shrew-sized Morganucodon, about 205 million years old, is usually called the first mammal; Brasilodon from Brazil, 225 million years old, changed its teeth only once as mammals do and was called the oldest mammal in 2022, but others say that makes it a very close relative, not a mammal.
origins.text: Mammals have hair, feed their young on milk and hear with three tiny bones in the middle ear. They appeared at almost the same time as the dinosaurs and stayed small, mostly active at night, for 140 million years. The last shared ancestor of today's mammals lived about 180 million years ago.

origins.name: Plesiosaurs
origins.evidenceNote: The only plesiosaur skeleton known from the Triassic, about 205 million years old, was described from Germany in 2017; the group lasted until the extinction 66 million years ago.
origins.text: Plesiosaurs were sea reptiles that swam with four large flippers, as if flying under water. Some had small heads on very long necks; others, the pliosaurs, had short necks and huge jaws. They breathed air, and they shared the seas of the Jurassic and Cretaceous with ichthyosaurs and later mosasaurs.

origins.name: Moths and butterflies

oldest.name: Fossil wing scales (oldest body fossil: Archaeolepis mane, Dorset, England, c. 190 million years ago)

origins.evidenceNote: Wing scales from a German drill core, about 201 million years old, are the oldest sure trace of moths; scales in 236-million-year-old dung from Argentina are probably from moths too, but that is less certain.
origins.text: Moths and butterflies are insects whose wings are covered in tiny coloured scales. Surprisingly, the first moths with sucking mouthparts lived tens of millions of years before flowers existed, so they must have drunk something else. When flowering plants spread, moths became some of their most important pollinators.

origins.name: Bird-hipped dinosaurs (armoured, horned and duck-billed)

oldest.name: Lesothosaurus and other Early Jurassic forms

origins.evidenceNote: Sure members of this group appear at the start of the Jurassic, about 200 million years ago; Pisanosaurus from Argentina, about 229 million years old, was long counted as the oldest, but since 2017 many researchers place it outside the dinosaurs.
origins.text: This great branch of plant-eating dinosaurs includes Stegosaurus, Triceratops, Ankylosaurus and the duck-bills. They had a beak at the front of the mouth and rows of grinding teeth behind. Despite the name bird-hipped, birds did not come from them. Their near absence from the Triassic is an unsolved puzzle.

origins.name: Tyrannosaurs
origins.evidenceNote: A crested skull found in England in rocks about 166 million years old belongs to the earliest known tyrannosaur relative, an animal about 3 metres long.
origins.text: For their first 80 million years tyrannosaurs were small or middle-sized hunters living in the shadow of bigger meat-eaters, and some had feathers. Only near the end of the dinosaur age did they become giants. Tyrannosaurus, which grew over 12 metres long, was among the very last dinosaurs.

origins.name: Birds
origins.evidenceNote: Archaeopteryx, 150 million years old, has long been called the first bird; feathered Chinese animals about 160 million years old, such as Anchiornis and Aurornis, are birds in some family trees and bird-like dinosaurs in others, because there is no sharp line between the two.
origins.text: Birds are living dinosaurs, descended from small feathered meat-eaters. Archaeopteryx had wings and flight feathers but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. Baminornis, a bird of the same age described from China in 2025, already had a short tail, showing that birds were varied by the Late Jurassic.

origins.name: Flowering plants

oldest.name: Montsechia vidalii (older flowering-plant pollen is known from about 135 million years ago)

origins.evidenceNote: Pollen and water plants such as Montsechia show flowering plants by about 135 to 125 million years ago; Nanjinganthus, a 174-million-year-old Chinese fossil described as a flower in 2018, is read by critics as a conifer cone, while gene studies point to an origin tens of millions of years before any sure fossil.
origins.text: Flowering plants enclose their seeds in fruit and use flowers to recruit insects and other animals as pollen carriers. They appear late and then spread with astonishing speed, which Darwin called an abominable mystery. With about 300,000 known species they are by far the most varied land plants, and they provide nearly all our food.

origins.name: Egg-laying mammals (monotremes)
origins.evidenceNote: Tiny jawbones from Australian rocks about 125 million years old belong to the earliest known monotreme; gene studies show the line split from other mammals about 180 million years ago, so some 55 million years of its history are missing.
origins.text: The platypus and the echidnas are the only mammals that lay eggs. They feed their young on milk, but it oozes from the skin because they have no teats. Monotremes are the last survivors of the oldest branch of living mammals and have always been known only from the southern continents.

origins.name: Ants
origins.evidenceNote: A winged 'hell ant' with scythe-like jaws, found in Brazilian limestone and described in 2025, is 113 million years old, about 13 million years older than the previous record; gene studies suggest ants began a little before that.
origins.text: Ants evolved from wasps and live in colonies where most members are workers that never breed. The earliest known ants already lived alongside the dinosaurs. They later became some of the most numerous animals on land, turning over soil, spreading seeds and farming fungi and aphids.

origins.name: Marsupials and their relatives
origins.evidenceNote: The oldest fossils on the marsupial line are from the mid-Cretaceous, about 110 million years ago; Sinodelphys from China, 125 million years old, was hailed as the first, but a 2018 study moved it to the placental side. Gene studies date the split between the two lines to about 160 million years ago.
origins.text: Marsupials give birth to tiny young that finish growing while attached to a teat, often inside a pouch. Their line began in the northern continents, reached South America and crossed Antarctica to Australia, where it produced kangaroos, koalas and wombats. Opossums are their best-known representatives in the Americas.

origins.name: Grasses

oldest.name: Grass skin cells and silica bodies stuck to the teeth of the dinosaur Equijubus

origins.evidenceNote: Microscopic grass remains were found in 2018 on the teeth of a plant-eating dinosaur from China that lived 113 to 100 million years ago; grass fragments also occur in dinosaur dung from India about 66 million years old.
origins.text: Grasses grow from the base, so they survive being grazed or burned. They were a minor part of the dinosaurs' world and only formed open grasslands tens of millions of years later. Grazing mammals such as horses evolved with them, and wheat, rice and maize are grasses.

origins.name: Snakes

oldest.name: Haasiophis, Pachyrhachis and other sea snakes with small hind legs

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest snakes known from good skeletons are about 100 to 95 million years old and still had small back legs; jaw fragments from England about 167 million years old were described in 2015 as the oldest snakes, but not everyone accepts scraps of jaw as proof.
origins.text: Snakes are lizards that lost their legs and evolved long bodies with hundreds of backbones and jaws that open extremely wide. Fossils with small hind legs show the change under way. Whether the first snakes burrowed underground or swam in the sea is still debated. Today there are about 4,000 species.

origins.name: Mosasaurs

oldest.name: Dallasaurus turneri, one of the earliest and smallest

origins.evidenceNote: Mosasaurs appear in sea rocks about 94 million years old (possibly 98); Dallasaurus, under a metre long, still had limbs that could walk. All died out 66 million years ago.
origins.text: Mosasaurs were lizards, relatives of monitor lizards and snakes, that took to the sea just as the ichthyosaurs disappeared. They soon evolved flippers and became the dominant hunters of the seas for the last 20 million years of the dinosaur age.

origins.name: Bees

oldest.name: Cretotrigona prisca (a stingless bee in amber)

origins.evidenceNote: The oldest bee body fossil is in New Jersey amber about 70 million years old; fossil nests from Patagonia were reported in 2020 as bee nests 100 million years old, and an insect in 100-million-year-old amber has been called a bee, but both are debated.
origins.text: Bees are wasps that switched from hunting insects to feeding their young on pollen. They rose alongside the flowering plants, each shaping the other: flowers evolved colours, scents and nectar to attract bees, and bees evolved hairy bodies to carry pollen. Much of our fruit depends on them.

origins.name: Modern birds
origins.evidenceNote: A skull from Belgium, 66.7 million years old, is the oldest fossil that is beyond doubt a modern-type bird; Vegavis from Antarctica, 69 million years old, is argued by some to be a relative of ducks and by others to lie outside modern birds. Gene studies place the first modern birds about 95 to 110 million years ago.
origins.text: All of today's 11,000 and more bird species descend from a few lineages that were already alive just before the asteroid struck 66 million years ago. All other dinosaurs died; the survivors then spread rapidly into forests, seas and skies. Asteriornis may be close to the ancestry of chickens and ducks.

origins.name: Placental mammals

oldest.name: Earliest Paleocene placentals such as Purgatorius

origins.evidenceNote: No fossil older than 66 million years is accepted by all as a placental, yet gene studies say the group began in the Late Cretaceous, some 90 to 100 million years ago; Juramaia from China, about 160 million years old, is the oldest claimed animal on the placental side of the family tree, and its age and position are both questioned.
origins.text: Placental mammals nourish their young inside the womb through a placenta until they are well developed. They include the great majority of living mammals, from bats to blue whales. Their early history is hidden: they seem to have lived unnoticed beside the dinosaurs, then spread explosively once the dinosaurs were gone.

origins.name: Carnivorans (cats, dogs, bears and relatives)
origins.evidenceNote: A fossil from Canada about 64.5 million years old belongs to one of the earliest known relatives of the carnivorans; members of the living group appear about 42 million years ago, while gene studies date the split between the cat and dog branches to about 54 million years ago.
origins.text: Carnivorans are the mammals with a pair of blade-like cheek teeth for slicing meat. Their first relatives were small, weasel-like tree climbers. The group later split into a cat branch, with hyenas and mongooses, and a dog branch, with bears, weasels and seals. Not all eat meat: the giant panda lives on bamboo.

origins.name: Elephants and their relatives
origins.evidenceNote: Jaw and tooth fossils from Morocco about 60 million years old belong to a rabbit-sized animal that is the oldest and most primitive known elephant relative.
origins.text: The elephant line began in Africa with an animal that weighed only a few kilograms and had no trunk. Over 60 million years it produced many kinds of trunked giants, including mastodons and mammoths. The family of modern elephants appeared in Africa about 10 million years ago, and only three species remain.

origins.name: Butterflies
origins.evidenceNote: Butterfly fossils are rare and the oldest are only about 56 million years old, so their origin is worked out mainly from DNA: a 2023 study of 2,300 species puts it at about 100 million years ago.
origins.text: Butterflies are a branch of moths that took to flying by day. A study of the DNA of thousands of species concluded that the first butterflies lived about 100 million years ago in what is now the Americas, while dinosaurs were still alive, and that their caterpillars fed on plants of the bean family.

origins.name: Primates

oldest.name: Teilhardina and other early true primates (Altiatlasius from Morocco, c. 57 million years old, may be older)
oldest.place: Asia (Teilhardina asiatica, China); also Europe and North America

origins.evidenceNote: Animals that all agree are primates appear about 56 million years ago; Purgatorius, known from teeth and ankle bones in Montana within about 100,000 to 140,000 years after the dinosaur extinction (65.9 million years ago), is the oldest claimed primate relative, but some researchers do not count its group as true primates.
origins.text: Primates are tree-living mammals with grasping hands, nails in place of claws, and forward-facing eyes. Purgatorius, their likely forerunner, was a mouse-sized animal that scampered through the branches right after the dinosaurs died. Genes suggest the primate line began even earlier, while the dinosaurs were still alive.

oldest.name: Paramys and other late Paleocene rodents

origins.evidenceNote: The first mammals with the rodent pattern of ever-growing gnawing teeth appear in rocks from the end of the Paleocene, about 56 million years ago; gene studies place their split from rabbits 15 to 20 million years earlier.
origins.text: Rodents have a single pair of chisel-like front teeth, top and bottom, that never stop growing. Mice, rats, squirrels, beavers and porcupines are all rodents. They are the most successful mammals: about four in every ten mammal species is a rodent.

origins.name: Horses
origins.evidenceNote: The oldest known member of the horse family, a forest animal the size of a small dog, comes from Wyoming rocks about 56 million years old.
origins.text: The first horses were small woodland browsers with four toes on the front feet. As grasslands spread, their descendants grew larger, ran on a single hoofed toe and evolved tall teeth for grinding gritty grass. The many fossils of this change made horses a classic example of evolution. Most of it happened in North America.

origins.name: Bats

oldest.name: Isolated bat teeth (Archaeonycteris praecursor, Altaynycteris aurora); oldest skeletons: Icaronycteris gunnelli, c. 52 million years ago
oldest.place: Fossil Lake, near Kemmerer, Wyoming, USA (oldest skeletons)

origins.evidenceNote: A few bat teeth are 55 to 56 million years old, and the oldest whole skeletons, from Wyoming, are about 52 million years old; those bats could already fly, and no fossil of a half-way stage has been found.
origins.text: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly, on wings of skin stretched between very long fingers. The earliest skeletons look much like modern bats, so how flight began is unknown. Most bats find their way and catch insects in the dark by echolocation. One in five mammal species is a bat.

origins.name: Whales and dolphins
origins.evidenceNote: Pakicetus, a wolf-sized animal with four legs and the ear bones of a whale, lived about 49 million years ago; a jaw from India, Himalayacetus, was reported in 1998 as 53.5 million years old, but later work dates it to about 47 million.
origins.text: Whales descend from hoofed land mammals that began feeding in rivers and shallow seas. In about 10 million years their front legs became flippers, their back legs shrank away and their nostrils moved to the top of the head. Their closest living relatives are hippos.

origins.evidenceNote: Jaws and foot bones of thumb-sized primates from Chinese rocks about 45 million years old are widely accepted as the oldest members of the monkey and ape line.
origins.text: Anthropoids are the monkeys, apes and humans: primates with larger brains, forward-facing eyes shielded by bone and a liking for daylight. The earliest known ones were tiny tree-dwellers in Asia. Their descendants spread to Africa and, about 40 million years ago, to South America.

origins.evidenceNote: A piece of jaw with four teeth from Tanzania, dated precisely to 25.2 million years ago, is the oldest known ape; it agrees with gene studies that place the split between apes and Old World monkeys 25 to 30 million years ago.
origins.text: Apes are primates without tails, with broad chests and very flexible shoulders for hanging and swinging beneath branches. Gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and humans are all apes. Rukwapithecus was found beside the oldest known Old World monkey, showing that the two groups had already parted.

oldest.name: Pierolapithecus catalaunicus (Sivapithecus from South Asia is nearly as old)
oldest.place: Els Hostalets de Pierola, Catalonia, Spain

origins.evidenceNote: Fossil apes about 13 to 12 million years old from Spain and South Asia are among the oldest generally placed with the great apes; gene studies date the split of the orangutan line from our own to about 15 to 16 million years ago.
origins.text: The great apes are the orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans: large-bodied, big-brained apes that grow up slowly and learn much from one another. Sivapithecus, from the foothills of the Himalayas, had a face like an orangutan's and may be near that animal's ancestry.

origins.name: The human line (hominins)

oldest.name: Australopithecus anamensis, the oldest hominin whose upright walking is not disputed

origins.evidenceNote: Sahelanthropus from Chad, about 7 million years old, is claimed as the first member of the human line because it may have walked upright: studies of its thigh bone in 2022 and 2026 say it did, studies in 2020 and 2024 say it did not. A shin bone 4.2 million years old from Kenya is the oldest proof of upright walking that nobody disputes.
origins.text: Hominins are humans and all our extinct relatives since our line parted from that of chimpanzees. DNA estimates of that split range from about 5 to 13 million years ago; the average of 90 studies collected by TimeTree is about 6.4 million. The first sign of the human line is walking on two legs, long before large brains or stone tools.

origins.evidenceNote: Jaws, teeth and a shin bone from northern Kenya, dated between 4.2 and 3.9 million years ago using volcanic ash layers, are the oldest Australopithecus fossils; the last species lived about 1.9 million years ago.
origins.text: Australopiths walked upright on two legs but had brains little bigger than a chimpanzee's and were still good climbers. The best known is Lucy, a partial skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis from Ethiopia. One of the australopiths, or a close relative, gave rise to our own genus, Homo.

origins.name: The genus Homo

oldest.name: LD 350-1, a lower jaw with teeth

origins.evidenceNote: Half a lower jaw found in Ethiopia in 2013, dated to between 2.80 and 2.75 million years ago by volcanic ash, mixes features of Australopithecus and Homo and is the oldest fossil assigned to our genus.
origins.text: Homo is the group of humans: species with smaller teeth, larger brains and a growing dependence on stone tools and meat. It appeared in eastern Africa as the climate became drier and more changeable. About 2 million years ago Homo erectus appeared and spread through Africa and into Europe and Asia.

origins.name: Neanderthals

oldest.name: Sima de los Huesos fossils, early members of the Neanderthal line

origins.evidenceNote: Bones about 430,000 years old from a cave pit in Spain have DNA showing they were early relatives of Neanderthals; classic Neanderthals disappeared across Europe and most of Asia by about 40,000 years ago.
origins.text: Neanderthals were stocky, big-brained humans of Europe and western Asia, adapted to Ice Age cold. They made tools, used fire and buried their dead. They are our closest extinct relatives, and they met and had children with our own species, so most people today carry a little Neanderthal DNA.

origins.name: Our species, Homo sapiens

oldest.name: Jebel Irhoud skulls, jaws and teeth

origins.evidenceNote: Fossils from a Moroccan cave are dated to about 315,000 years ago (give or take 34,000) by heat-altered flint tools found with them; their faces are modern but their skulls are longer and lower, and the oldest fossils with fully modern skulls, from Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, are at least 233,000 years old.
origins.text: Our own species arose in Africa. The Moroccan fossils have faces like ours but a braincase of an older shape, showing that the modern human form came together gradually and across the whole continent, not in one spot. From Africa our species later spread to every continent.

curves.title: Global average temperature
curves.note: Worked out by combining more than 150,000 chemical temperature readings from fossil shells and ancient sea-floor mud with climate-model runs, one value per geological stage; the broad ups and downs are well supported, but any single value is uncertain by several degrees (the band is the 5th to 95th percentile).

source.title: PhanDA: files with the GMST, CO2 and LTG values of Judd et al. (2024), A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature, Science 385, eadk3705
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (repository LICENSE file: 'Attribution 4.0 International'; README badge 'License: CC BY 4.0')

curves.how: File 5_Outputs/PhanDA_GMSTandCO2_percentiles.csv, all 85 stage rows (Tremadocian, base 486.85 Ma, to Holocene). x = AverageAge (midpoint of the stage, Ma), y = GMST_50 (median), band = GMST_05 to GMST_95. Rounded to 0.1 °C; no resampling or smoothing. Each value is a stage average, so events shorter than a stage (for example the 200,000-year warm spike 56 million years ago) do not show.

curves.title: Carbon dioxide in the air
curves.note: Estimated from chemical and fossil clues such as the pores on fossil leaves, ancient soils and boron in sea shells, averaged over each geological stage; values for the last 66 million years are fairly firm, older ones are rough and the Mesozoic is the least certain (the band is the 5th to 95th percentile).

source.title: PhanDA: files with the GMST, CO2 and LTG values of Judd et al. (2024), A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature, Science 385, eadk3705. Its CO2 series is 'largely based on the data from Foster et al. (2017) in the Paleozoic and Mesozoic, and the data from Rae et al. (2021) in the Cenozoic' (Judd et al. 2024, Fig. 4 caption)
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (repository LICENSE file: 'Attribution 4.0 International'; README badge 'License: CC BY 4.0')

curves.how: Same file and rows as the temperature curve. x = AverageAge, y = CO2_50 (median), band = CO2_05 to CO2_95, rounded to 1 ppm; no resampling. The youngest row (Holocene, 276 ppm) is the pre-industrial level, not today's (over 420 ppm).

curves.title: Carbon dioxide in the air (finer curve, older study)
curves.note: A smooth line fitted through more than 1,200 separate CO2 estimates made by five different methods (fossil leaves, ancient soils, sea-shell chemistry and others); it shows the long swings in CO2 well, but newer work puts CO2 around 55 to 45 million years ago clearly higher than this line does.

source.title: Foster, G. L., Royer, D. L. & Lunt, D. J. (2017) Future climate forcing potentially without precedent in the last 420 million years. Nature Communications 8, 14845. Supplementary Data 2 (LOESS fit)
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (article page: 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License')

curves.how: Supplementary Data 2 (file 41467_2017_BFncomms14845_MOESM2875_ESM.xlsx, sheet 'LOESS Fit', 840 rows at 0.5 Myr steps). x = 'Age (Ma)', y = 'pCO2 probability maximum', band = 'lw68%' to 'up68%'. Thinned, not smoothed: every row from 0 to 66 Ma, every fourth row (2 Myr steps) before that. Do not join this line to the 'co2' curve: they are two different reconstructions.

curves.title: Oxygen in the air
curves.note: A consensus curve: the authors weighed the different ways of estimating ancient oxygen against each other and drew the most likely path between them; it is a best judgement, not a measurement, and the band shows how far the methods disagree (often by ten percentage points or more).

source.title: Mills, B. J. W., Krause, A. J., Jarvis, I. & Cramer, B. D. (2023) Evolution of Atmospheric O2 Through the Phanerozoic, Revisited. Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 51, 253-276. Data of Figure 6
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 for the article (Crossref licence record for the DOI: http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The author's GitHub data repository ('Data from Figure 6 in Mills et al. (2023)') carries no separate licence file.

curves.how: File Mills_etal_2023_AREPS_O2.xlsx, Sheet1, 542 rows at 1 Myr steps (columns Time, Mid, Min, Max; Time is negative Ma). x = -Time, y = Mid, band = Min to Max, in percent of the atmosphere. Thinned to every second row (odd ages 541 to 1 Ma, plus 0); rounded to 0.1; no smoothing.

curves.title: Oxygen in the air before animals (rough limits)
curves.note: Only upper and lower limits are known, from chemical traces in very old rocks: almost no free oxygen before about 2.4 billion years ago, then somewhere between a ten-thousandth and a tenth of today's level for more than a billion years, rising towards modern levels after about 800 million years ago; the limits span factors of a thousand or more and are still argued over.

source.title: Ranges as stated in Chen, G. et al. (2022) Reconstructing Earth's atmospheric oxygenation history using machine learning, Nature Communications 13, 5862 (introduction and methods, summarising the two-step model of Lyons et al. 2014); checked against Kasting & Ji (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, doi 10.1098/rstb.2024.0093, and Lyons et al. (2021), Astrobiology 21, 906, doi 10.1089/ast.2020.2418 (both CC BY 4.0)
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (article page: 'licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License')

curves.how: Not a data file: six range points built from numbers stated in the text of the paper. 'from 10^-9 to 10^-5 PAL pre-GOE' (4000 to 2500 Ma); the Great Oxidation Event 'around 2.5 to 2.0 billion years ago'; '10^-4 to 10^-1 PAL during the boring billion interval from ~2.0 to 1.0 Ga' (held to 800 Ma, where Lyons et al. 2021 put the start of the second rise, 'between 800 and 600 million years ago'); '10^-1 to ~1 PAL from ~0.5 Ga to present' (placed at 541 Ma, the start of the Phanerozoic curve). PAL (present atmospheric level) converted to percent of the air by multiplying by 20.95. The straight lines between the points are schematic; use a logarithmic axis. Points are [Ma, low, high].

curves.title: Global sea level
curves.note: Worked out by measuring, on maps of ancient coastlines drawn every 10 million years, how much of today's land was under the sea, then converting flooded area into a height; it shows the big long swings but the heights are uncertain by many tens of metres and other methods give lower values, especially before 250 million years ago.

source.title: Marcilly, C. M., Torsvik, T. H. & Conrad, C. P. (2022) Global Phanerozoic sea levels from paleogeographic flooding maps. Gondwana Research 110, 128-142. Table 1
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (first page of the article: 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)')

curves.how: Table 1 of the article PDF (open copy from the Norwegian research archive), all 53 rows, 520 to 0 Ma at 10 Myr steps. x = 'Age (Ma)', y = column 'Modern land sea level (C = 0.0057 km/10^6 km2), relative m', rounded to 1 m; no resampling. Text extracted with pdftotext; the PDF's minus glyph was restored by hand-checked rule (this column is negative only at 30 Ma, -2.88 m, and 10 Ma, -3.62 m). Ten-million-year steps cannot show ice-age swings of about 120 m.

curves.title: Variety of sea animals (number of genera)
curves.note: A count of the kinds (genera) of sea animals known as fossils from each geological stage, from the Paleobiology Database; the sharp drops are the mass extinctions, but the count depends on how much rock of each age has been searched, and the fall over the last 12 million years or so is not real: the database holds fossils only, so living genera with no recent fossils drop out.

source.title: The Paleobiology Database, data service 1.2, diversity of marine Metazoa by stage (downloaded 21 November 2026)
source.licence: CC0 (response header: 'Data License: Creative Commons CC0', https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)

curves.how: One API call (occs/diversity, base_name=Metazoa, envtype=marine, count=genera, time_reso=stage; 1,092,300 occurrences, 98 stages). y = X_Ft + X_bL + X_FL + X_bt, i.e. every genus known or implied to have lived during the stage (range-through count, raw, not corrected for sampling); x = midpoint of the stage. No resampling. The Pridoli (423 to 420 Ma) has no stage in the database and is missing. Stage dates are the database's own.

curves.title: Length of the day
curves.note: Read from regular layers in ancient sediments that record the wobble of the Earth's axis, whose pace depends on how fast the Earth spins and how far away the Moon is; ten rock sections give ten points, each good to about a quarter to half an hour, and the day may not have lengthened as smoothly between them as a joined-up line suggests.

source.title: Zhou, M., Wu, H., Hinnov, L. A., Fang, Q., Zhang, S., Yang, T. & Shi, M. (2022) Empirical reconstruction of Earth-Moon and Solar System dynamical parameters for the past 2.5 billion years from cyclostratigraphy. Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL098304. Supporting Information, Table S4
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (figshare record of the Supporting Information: licence 'CC BY 4.0')

curves.how: Table S4 of 'Supporting Informtion S1.docx' (figshare file 36699174), column 'Length of Day [h]', one point per rock section: Dales Gorge (~2465 Ma), Xiamaling (~1400), Datangpo (~655), Luoyixi (~500), Alum Shale (~493), Pingliang (~455), Wanhe (~445), Lucaogou (~269), Wujiaping (~259), Walvis Ridge (~55). Band = the table's plus-or-minus (two standard deviations for the TimeOpt MCMC rows). Lucaogou has two rows; the TimeOpt MCMC one (22.41 h) is used, the other method gives 22.78 h. The present day (0 Ma, 24.0 h) is added by hand and is not in the table. Ages are approximate ('~' in the table).

curves.title: Deep-sea climate record (oxygen isotopes)
curves.note: Measured directly in the shells of tiny sea-floor animals from drill cores, dated by counting the Earth's orbital cycles; it is the most detailed climate record of the last 66 million years, but it is a chemical signal that mixes deep-sea temperature and the amount of ice on land, not a temperature in degrees.

source.title: Westerhold, T. (2020) S34. Binned and LOESS smoothed Cenozoic deep-sea benthic foraminifer stable carbon and oxygen isotope reference splice (CENOGRID). PANGAEA. Data of Westerhold et al. (2020), Science 369, 1383-1387
source.licence: CC BY 4.0 (file header: 'License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY-4.0)')

curves.how: Tab-delimited file of PANGAEA dataset 917717 (23,629 rows). x = 'Tuned time [Ma]', y = column 'ISOBENd18oLOESSsmooth' (the authors' short LOESS smooth of benthic δ18O). Thinned, not re-smoothed, by taking the nearest row to a target grid: every 0.02 Myr from 0 to 2.6 Ma, every 0.1 Myr to 10 Ma, every 0.3 Myr to 67.1 Ma. Draw with the axis upside down (warm at the top). Extra curve, not a temperature: no conversion to degrees was applied.

images.subject: Moon-forming impact
images.caption: A Moon-sized body smashes into a rocky planet in a NASA artist's concept, the kind of giant collision thought to have made our Moon.
images.note: Painted to show a collision seen around the star HD 172555, not the Earth itself. It is a stand-in for the Theia impact, whose details are still debated.

images.subject: Early molten Earth
images.caption: An artist's view of the young Earth's surface, with lava flows, falling meteors and a huge Moon hanging close overhead.
images.note: Artistic impression. The Moon really was much closer then, but nobody knows what the surface looked like, and newer work suggests oceans may have formed early in the Hadean.

images.subject: Archean banded chert, Pilbara
images.caption: Red and white banded chert at Marble Bar in Western Australia, sea-floor rock laid down about 3.4 billion years ago.
images.note: A sandal is in the corner of the photo for scale.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 3.4 billion years ago

images.subject: Stromatolite, about 3.4 billion years old
images.caption: A cut slice of layered rock from the Pilbara of Western Australia, about 3.4 billion years old, with wavy layers thought to have been built by mats of microbes.
images.note: Most researchers accept the Strelley Pool stromatolites as made by life, but for rocks this old a non-living origin is still argued by some.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 3.4 billion years ago

images.subject: Acasta Gneiss, the oldest known rock
images.caption: A piece of the Acasta Gneiss from northern Canada, about 4.03 billion years old and the oldest known rock that is still part of the Earth's crust.
images.note: Its age marks the boundary between the Hadean and the Archean, so it could sit under either unit.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 4.03 billion years ago

images.subject: Banded iron formation
images.caption: Red and grey striped banded iron formation at Dales Gorge in Western Australia, iron that rusted out of the sea about 2.5 billion years ago as oxygen first built up.
images.note: These Hamersley rocks are about 2.5 billion years old, right at the Archean to Proterozoic boundary.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 2.5 billion years ago

images.subject: Stromatolites
images.caption: Living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool, Shark Bay, Western Australia: rocky mounds built layer by layer by microbes, just as they were billions of years ago.
images.note: A photo of modern stromatolites, a few thousand years old, used to show what the Precambrian shallows looked like.

images.subject: Proterozoic stromatolite
images.caption: A polished slice through fossil stromatolites about 1.4 billion years old from Montana, showing the fine layers laid down by microbial mats.

images.subject: Stromatolites
images.caption: A wide view of living stromatolites along the shore of Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, Western Australia.
images.note: Modern stromatolites, shown as a living example of the microbe-built mounds that dominated Precambrian coasts.

images.subject: Snowball Earth
images.caption: An artist's view of the Earth from space almost wholly covered in ice during an ancient global glaciation.
images.note: Drawn for the Huronian glaciation of about 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago. How completely the Earth froze, then and in the later Cryogenian snowballs, is still debated.

images.subject: Dickinsonia
images.caption: A fossil of Dickinsonia costata, a flat, ribbed oval that is one of the oldest known animals, pressed into sandstone about 555 million years ago.

images.subject: Ediacaran sea floor
images.caption: A museum model of the Ediacaran sea floor with tall frond-like Charnia and flat, ribbed Dickinsonia lying on the sand.
images.note: Colours are invented, and what kind of creatures the fronds were is still uncertain.

images.subject: Fractofusus, Mistaken Point
images.caption: A digital reconstruction of Fractofusus, a spindle-shaped Ediacaran organism, lying on a dark sea floor about 570 million years ago with smaller young around it.
images.note: The threads linking the individuals follow a published idea about how it reproduced; colour and texture are guesses.

images.subject: Anomalocaris
images.caption: A nearly complete Anomalocaris canadensis fossil from the Burgess Shale of Canada, about 505 million years old, showing the body flaps and tail fan.
images.note: Portrait format.

images.subject: Hallucigenia
images.caption: A detailed digital reconstruction of Hallucigenia, a tiny spiny worm with legs, climbing on a sponge in the dark Cambrian sea.
images.note: Shown the right way up and the right way round, following the 2015 study that found its head. Portrait format, with a small artist signature.

images.subject: Anomalocaris
images.caption: A clean modern reconstruction of Anomalocaris canadensis on a white background, with its two spiny grasping arms, stalked eyes and swimming flaps.
images.note: Has a small artist signature in the corner.

images.subject: Anomalocaris
images.caption: Anomalocaris, the top hunter of the Cambrian seas, chases shelled Isoxys through sunlit blue water.
images.note: Colours are invented. Recent studies suggest Anomalocaris chased soft, fast prey in open water, as shown here, instead of crushing trilobites.

images.subject: Cambrian sea life
images.caption: A busy Cambrian sea floor in what is now North China about 504 million years ago, with swimming radiodonts, trilobites, sponges and jellyfish.
images.note: Based on the Linyi fossil site and published in a scientific paper; drawing by Dinghua Yang. The original is 1269 px wide.

images.subject: Trilobite (Olenoides)
images.caption: A Burgess Shale trilobite, Olenoides serratus, preserved with its legs and antennae as well as its hard shell.
images.note: Portrait format.

images.subject: Opabinia
images.caption: A reconstruction of Opabinia regalis on a white background, with five eyes on stalks and a long trunk ending in a claw.
images.note: Has a small artist signature in the corner.

images.subject: Opabinia
images.caption: Two Opabinia search the Cambrian sea floor among sponges, using their clawed trunks to grab food.
images.note: Colours are invented.

images.subject: Ordovician sea (Fezouata)
images.caption: The Early Ordovician sea of Morocco, with the two-metre filter-feeding giant Aegirocassis gliding over a sea floor crowded with trilobites and other arthropods.
images.note: Based on the Fezouata fossil beds, about 478 million years old. Colours are invented.

images.subject: Sea scorpion (Pentecopterus)
images.caption: Pentecopterus, a sea scorpion nearly as long as a person, hunts over rippled sand 467 million years ago.
images.note: The oldest known sea scorpion. Colours are invented.

images.subject: Ordovician sea floor
images.caption: A museum model of a Late Ordovician sea floor with a straight-shelled nautiloid, a large trilobite, sea lilies, corals and shells.
images.note: An older style museum diorama; the bright colours are guesses and the seaweeds are stand-ins.

images.subject: Silurian sea floor (Herefordshire)
images.caption: A dark Silurian sea floor about 430 million years ago, crowded with small arthropods, worms and a shelled brachiopod, all known from fossils found in Herefordshire, England.
images.note: The animals are only a few millimetres to centimetres long in life. Colours are invented.

images.subject: Cooksonia, an early land plant
images.caption: A museum model of Cooksonia, an early land plant with leafless forked stems and spore capsules at their tips.
images.note: Shown ten times life size.

images.subject: Sea scorpion (Eurypterus)
images.caption: A complete fossil of the sea scorpion Eurypterus remipes from New York State, with its swimming paddles and tail spine.

images.subject: Sea scorpion (Eurypterus)
images.caption: Three Eurypterus sea scorpions swim over a sandy bottom in clear blue water, paddling with their broad back legs.
images.note: A digital model placed on a modern underwater photograph.

images.subject: Dunkleosteus
images.caption: The armoured skull of Dunkleosteus terrelli, with self-sharpening bony blades in place of teeth.
images.note: A museum cast of the original fossil.

images.subject: Dunkleosteus
images.caption: Three species of the armoured fish Dunkleosteus drawn to scale, with the bladed jaws and bony head shield of the largest, D. terrelli, at the top.
images.note: Follows the 2023 rethink that made Dunkleosteus shorter and deeper bodied (about 4 m) than older 6 to 9 m pictures. Species labels and a scale bar are part of the image.

images.subject: Devonian river life (Hyneria)
images.caption: Hyneria, a lobe-finned fish up to three metres long, swims through a weedy Late Devonian river past smaller fish.
images.note: Painted in 2015; the body shape is partly guessed, as Hyneria is known from incomplete remains.

images.subject: Tiktaalik
images.caption: The front half of a Tiktaalik fossil from Arctic Canada, showing the flat, crocodile-like skull, the neck and the scaly body.
images.credit: Matt Mechtley from Tempe, Arizona, USA

images.subject: Tiktaalik
images.caption: Tiktaalik, a fish with a flat head, a neck and sturdy front fins, props itself up at the water's edge about 375 million years ago.
images.note: Made in 2006. Later finds showed Tiktaalik also had a large pelvis and strong hind fins.

images.subject: Trilobite (Walliserops)
images.caption: A Devonian trilobite from Morocco, Walliserops trifurcatus, with a long three-pronged fork on its head and rows of spines.

images.subject: Arthropleura
images.caption: Arthropleura, a millipede relative more than two metres long, walks along a sandy shore, leaving a trackway behind it.
images.note: Has a small artist signature in the corner. Colour is a guess.

images.subject: Carboniferous coal forest
images.caption: A large early four-legged animal lies among ferns at the foot of giant scale trees in a museum reconstruction of a coal swamp.
images.note: Photograph of a museum diorama.

images.subject: Carboniferous coal forest
images.caption: A museum reconstruction of a coal swamp 310 million years ago, with giant horsetails and scale trees standing over misty water.
images.note: Photograph of a museum diorama.

images.subject: Meganeura
images.caption: A life-size model of Meganeura, a dragonfly-like insect with a wingspan of about 70 cm, resting on the trunk of a scale tree.
images.note: Photograph of a museum model.

images.subject: Dimetrodon
images.caption: A detailed 3D model of Dimetrodon, the sail-backed hunter of the early Permian, standing with its legs held fairly upright.
images.note: Dimetrodon was not a dinosaur but an early relative of mammals. Skin and colour are informed guesses.

images.subject: Dimetrodon
images.caption: A mounted Dimetrodon skeleton from Texas against a black background, showing the tall spines that held up its sail.

images.subject: Dimetrodon
images.caption: Dimetrodon grandis in side view on a white background, walking with its belly off the ground and the tips of its sail spines bare.
images.note: The name and dates are written on the image.

images.subject: Giant griffinfly fossil (Arctotypus)
images.caption: The imprint of a giant griffinfly with a 68 cm wingspan, a close relative of Meganeura, preserved in dark Permian slate from France.
images.note: The file name says Meganeura monyi, but the Commons description identifies the specimen as Arctotypus intermedius, a Permian relative.

images.subject: Helicoprion
images.caption: Helicoprion, a Permian relative of ratfish with a spiral saw of teeth set in its lower jaw.
images.note: Only the tooth spirals and some jaw cartilage are known, so the body is modelled on relatives.

images.subject: Gorgonopsian (Inostrancevia)
images.caption: Inostrancevia, a sabre-toothed gorgonopsian and top predator at the very end of the Permian, drawn on a white background.
images.note: Colour is a guess; whether gorgonopsians had hair is not known.

images.subject: Permian lakeshore, South Africa
images.caption: A middle Permian lakeshore in South Africa, with Glossopteris trees, horsetails and early mammal relatives at the water's edge.
images.note: From a 2022 scientific paper; three round inset panels with letters are part of the image.

images.subject: Scutosaurus
images.caption: Scutosaurus, a bulky, armour-skinned plant eater of the late Permian of Russia, shown on a white background.
images.credit: Marco Romano, Fabio Manucci, Bruce Rubidge and Marc J. Van den Brandt
images.note: From a 2021 scientific paper that built the body around a real skeleton.

images.subject: Herrerasaurus
images.caption: Herrerasaurus, one of the earliest known meat-eating dinosaurs, from Argentina about 231 million years ago, on a plain white background.
images.note: Colour and pattern are guesses.

images.subject: Morganucodon
images.caption: Morganucodon, a shrew-sized early relative of mammals that lived alongside the first dinosaurs.
images.note: Lived about 205 million years ago, across the Triassic to Jurassic boundary. Fur colour is a guess.

images.subject: Early Triassic river landscape
images.caption: A river plain in Australia a few million years after the end-Permian extinction, with spiky Pleuromeia plants, seed ferns, a reptile on the bank and an amphibian in the shallows.
images.note: Portrait format (taller than wide).

images.subject: Early dinosaurs (coelophysids)
images.caption: Slender early meat-eating dinosaurs walk through a Late Triassic landscape of conifers and ferns while small pterosaurs fly overhead.
images.note: Photograph of a traditional painting. The dinosaurs are generic coelophysids shown with the Italian pterosaur Peteinosaurus.

images.subject: Triassic riverbank with Prestosuchus
images.caption: A giant crocodile-line predator, Prestosuchus, feeds on a dicynodont beside a river in Brazil about 237 million years ago, while small Parvosuchus scavenge.
images.note: Shows a bloody carcass. Based on the Santa Maria Formation of Brazil (Middle to Late Triassic), a world still ruled by crocodile relatives rather than dinosaurs.

images.subject: Coelophysis
images.caption: Coelophysis, a light, fast early dinosaur from the Late Triassic of North America, drawn for the US National Park Service.
images.note: The thin fuzzy coat and the bright colours are speculative; no skin or feathers are known for Coelophysis.

images.subject: Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor skeletons
images.caption: Museum skeletons of two of the earliest dinosaurs, large Herrerasaurus and small Eoraptor, with a Plateosaurus skull, in a display on dinosaur origins.
images.note: Casts behind glass with a light reflection on the case. No good openly licensed life reconstruction of Eoraptor was found.

images.subject: Lystrosaurus
images.caption: Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized tusked plant-eater that survived the end-Permian extinction and spread across the Early Triassic world.
images.note: Coloured-pencil drawing. Skin covering and colour are not known from fossils.

images.subject: Lystrosaurus and its predator Moschorhinus
images.caption: The predator Moschorhinus stands over a Lystrosaurus it has killed in South Africa around the time of the end-Permian extinction.
images.note: Fur and whiskers on the predator are speculative. Shows a wound on the prey.

images.subject: Archaeopteryx (Berlin specimen)
images.caption: The Berlin specimen of Archaeopteryx, found in Bavarian limestone, with clear feather impressions around its wings and tail.
images.note: Portrait format (taller than wide).

images.subject: Sauropods (Europasaurus) on a Jurassic island
images.caption: Europasaurus sauropods cross a beach beside tall conifer forest on a Late Jurassic island in what is now Germany, with iguanodont dinosaurs and pterosaurs around them.
images.note: Europasaurus was a dwarf island sauropod only about 6 metres long, not a giant like Brachiosaurus.

images.subject: Sauropod herds of the Morrison Formation
images.caption: Herds of several kinds of long-necked diplodocid sauropods gather at a Late Jurassic waterhole at sunset.
images.credit: Pedro Salas and Sergey Krasovskiy, with others

images.subject: Ammonite (Dactylioceras)
images.caption: Dactylioceras commune, a ribbed ammonite from the Early Jurassic of England, photographed on a white background.

images.subject: Archaeopteryx
images.caption: A black-feathered Archaeopteryx chases a young Compsognathus through a Late Jurassic forest in what is now Germany.
images.note: The black wing colour follows a pigment study of a single fossil feather; whole-body colour and this hunting behaviour are guesses.

images.subject: Brachiosaurus
images.caption: Brachiosaurus, a giant sauropod with a giraffe-like upright neck and long front legs, on a plain white background.
images.note: Colours and skin pattern are guesses.

images.subject: Diplodocus
images.caption: Diplodocus, a 25-metre long-necked sauropod with a whip-like tail, on a plain white background.
images.note: The row of small spines along the back is based on skin fossils of a related diplodocid. Colours are guesses.

images.subject: Ichthyosaur fossil (Stenopterygius)
images.caption: Fossil of the ichthyosaur Stenopterygius from Holzmaden, Germany, preserved with the dark outline of its skin, back fin and tail, with a young one beside it.
images.note: On some Holzmaden specimens the body outline was touched up by preparators. A museum label is visible in the lower left corner.

images.subject: Ichthyosaur (Temnodontosaurus)
images.caption: The giant ichthyosaur Temnodontosaurus seizes a smaller ichthyosaur, Stenopterygius, in an Early Jurassic sea.

images.subject: Early Jurassic forest scene
images.caption: A large meat-eating dinosaur, early sauropods and small theropods in an Early Jurassic forest of conifers, cycads and ferns in what is now Poland.
images.note: Many of the animals are known there only from footprints or fragments. The artist's signature and date are painted into the lower left corner.

images.subject: Morrison Formation panorama
images.caption: A panoramic mural of the Late Jurassic Morrison floodplain of western North America, with Allosaurus, long-necked sauropods and Stegosaurus along a river.
images.credit: National Park Service / Bob Walters and Tess Kissinger
images.note: Extremely wide panorama (about 4.3 to 1); the original is 23,847 px wide.

images.subject: Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus
images.caption: Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus squabble over dried-out carcasses during a drought in the Late Jurassic of Colorado.
images.note: Dark and gory. A small artist credit line with a web address sits in the lower right corner. Illustrates a 2020 study of bite marks, including possible cannibalism.

images.subject: Pliosaur (Liopleurodon)
images.caption: Liopleurodon, a short-necked pliosaur and top predator of Middle to Late Jurassic seas, swims just under the surface.

images.subject: Plesiosaur (Plesiosaurus)
images.caption: Two long-necked Plesiosaurus hunt fish in a sunlit Early Jurassic sea.
images.note: Drawn in 2007. Newer research suggests plesiosaurs had a small tail fin and a stiffer neck than shown.

images.subject: Pterosaur (Rhamphorhynchus)
