images.caption: A flock of long-tailed Rhamphorhynchus pterosaurs skims over a Late Jurassic sea.
images.note: 3D render in a very wide banner format (3 to 1).

images.subject: Stegosaurus
images.caption: Stegosaurus, with two rows of large plates along its back and four spikes on its tail, on a plain white background.
images.note: Plate colours are guesses.

images.subject: Late Cretaceous Alberta panorama
images.caption: Horned dinosaurs, armoured dinosaurs and duck-bills in a sunlit forest clearing in Late Cretaceous Alberta, about 75 million years ago.
images.note: Very wide panorama (3.4 to 1); the original is 2758 px wide.

images.subject: Pterosaurs of Late Cretaceous Mongolia
images.caption: Giant azhdarchid pterosaurs fly, squabble and catch small prey beside a lake in Late Cretaceous Mongolia while duck-billed dinosaurs drink.
images.note: From a 2025 paper naming new pterosaur species from fragmentary bones; crest shapes and colours are guesses.

images.subject: Arctic dinosaurs of Alaska
images.caption: Feathered dromaeosaurs, horned Pachyrhinosaurus and tiny mammals under the northern lights in the polar forest of Late Cretaceous Alaska.
images.credit: Andrey Atuchin from Chiarenza et al. 2020
images.note: The dromaeosaur is known there only from a jaw fragment and teeth, so its appearance is based on relatives.

images.subject: Mosasaur (Tylosaurus)
images.caption: The mosasaur Tylosaurus lunges at a short-necked plesiosaur in the Late Cretaceous inland sea of North America.
images.credit: Andrey Atuchin in Zietlow et al.
images.note: Commons marks this file as awaiting licence review; it is credited to a CC BY 4.0 paper (Zietlow et al.).

images.subject: Pterosaur (Pteranodon) seized by a shark
images.caption: The shark Cretoxyrhina leaps from the Late Cretaceous inland sea of North America with a Pteranodon in its jaws.
images.note: Based on a Pteranodon neck bone with a shark tooth stuck in it; whether the shark hunted or scavenged is not known.

images.subject: Tyrannosaurus rex (Sue)
images.caption: Sue, one of the largest and most complete Tyrannosaurus rex skeletons, on display at the Field Museum in Chicago.
images.note: The skull on the mount is a cast; the real skull is displayed separately.

images.subject: Ammonite with iridescent shell
images.caption: A fossil ammonite whose mother-of-pearl shell still shimmers with rainbow colours, on display at the American Museum of Natural History.
images.note: The species and age are not given on the file page; ammonites preserved like this usually come from the Late Cretaceous of North America.

images.subject: Chicxulub impact
images.caption: A NASA painting of the asteroid striking the shallow sea at Chicxulub, Mexico, 66 million years ago.
images.note: Commons tags this as inaccurate paleoart: the pterosaurs look like Pteranodon, which had died out millions of years earlier, and are drawn in an outdated style. The impact itself is an artist's impression.

images.subject: Mid-Cretaceous river scene
images.caption: Plant-eating dinosaurs, an armoured nodosaur, a small raptor and a crocodile relative at a forest river in mid-Cretaceous Colorado, with fresh footprints in the mud.
images.note: Painted for the US National Park Service from footprints and bones found in the area.

images.subject: Feathered dinosaur (Deinonychus)
images.caption: Deinonychus, a wolf-sized raptor with a large sickle claw on each foot, shown fully feathered on a plain white background.
images.note: Feathers are inferred from close relatives; none are preserved with Deinonychus itself.

images.subject: Feathered dinosaur (Microraptor)
images.caption: Microraptor, a crow-sized dinosaur with flight feathers on both its arms and its legs, gliding on a plain white background.
images.note: The glossy black colour follows a 2012 pigment study. How it held its hind wings in the air is debated.

images.subject: Pterosaur (Quetzalcoatlus)
images.caption: Giraffe-sized Quetzalcoatlus pterosaurs walk on all fours across a fern prairie and one snatches a baby sauropod.
images.note: Painted in 2008; later studies have revised the head and crest shape.

images.subject: Sinosauropteryx fossil
images.caption: Fossil of Sinosauropteryx from China, the first dinosaur found with a coat of simple feathers, seen as a dark fringe along its back and tail.
images.credit: Sam / Olai Ose / Skjaervoy from Zhangjiagang, China

images.subject: Triceratops skeleton
images.caption: Mounted Triceratops skeleton from the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, cut out on a white background.
images.note: The museum background has been removed digitally.

images.subject: Feathered dinosaur (Zhenyuanlong)
images.caption: Zhenyuanlong, a relative of Velociraptor from China whose fossil preserves large bird-like wing and tail feathers.
images.note: Feather shapes come from the fossil; colours are guesses.

images.subject: Chicxulub crater today
images.caption: Radar and satellite views of the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico, where a faint curved trough marks the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater.
images.note: Two stacked images in portrait format. The crater is buried under younger rock and shows only faintly.

images.subject: Tyrannosaurus rex in the Hell Creek swamp
images.caption: Tyrannosaurus rex wades through a swamp forest with duck-billed Edmontosaurus, dome-headed Pachycephalosaurus and a feathered dromaeosaur.
images.note: Photograph of a traditional painting. Dakotaraptor, the feathered animal, is based on disputed fossil material.

images.subject: Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary clay
images.caption: The thin grey clay layer at Stevns Klint, Denmark, that marks the asteroid impact, lying between white Cretaceous chalk below and younger limestone above.

images.subject: Mosasaur (Mosasaurus)
images.caption: Mosasaurus hoffmannii, one of the largest mosasaurs, carries prey in its jaws over a shallow Late Cretaceous sea floor, with ammonites and a shark nearby.
images.note: Simple digital style in a wide banner format.

images.subject: Early mammal (Repenomamus) attacking a dinosaur
images.caption: Pencil drawing of the badger-sized mammal Repenomamus biting the dinosaur Psittacosaurus, as the two were found locked together in a fossil from China.
images.note: Black and white drawing. Whether the fossil records a real attack was questioned when it was published in 2023.

images.subject: Triceratops
images.caption: Triceratops, the three-horned plant-eater with a bony neck frill, in side view on a plain white background.
images.note: Colours are guesses.

images.subject: Tyrannosaurus rex
images.caption: A heavily built Tyrannosaurus rex seen from the front and side, painted by palaeontologist and artist Mark Witton.
images.note: Loose painterly style. Colours are guesses.

images.subject: Feathered dinosaur (Yutyrannus)
images.caption: Yutyrannus, a 9-metre early relative of T. rex from China that was covered in long, simple feathers.
images.note: Filament feathers are preserved in the fossils; the colour is a guess.

images.subject: Paleocene rocks
images.caption: Badlands in North Dakota cut into mud and sand laid down by rivers and swamps in the Paleocene, soon after the dinosaurs died out.
images.note: A modern landscape photograph: the rocks are Paleocene (Fort Union Group), the scenery is today's.

images.subject: Pantolambda
images.caption: Pantolambda, a sheep-sized plant eater and one of the first large mammals to appear after the dinosaurs.
images.note: Fur colour and pattern are guesses.

images.subject: Eocene rainforest
images.caption: A hot, wet Eocene forest in what is now Oregon, with palms, banana plants, a crocodile and early hoofed mammals.
images.note: Based on the plant and animal fossils of the Clarno Nut Beds (about 44 million years old). Very wide panorama.

images.subject: Darwinius ('Ida')
images.caption: 'Ida', a 47-million-year-old early primate from the Messel Pit in Germany, preserved with the outline of her fur.
images.note: Once promoted as a human ancestor; most researchers now place Darwinius closer to lemurs than to monkeys and apes.

images.subject: Early whale (Basilosaurus / Dorudon)
images.caption: The backbone and ribs of an early whale lie in the Egyptian desert at Wadi al-Hitan, once the floor of a shallow sea.
images.note: The file does not say which whale this is; Basilosaurus and Dorudon skeletons are both found here, about 37 to 40 million years old.

images.subject: Early whale (Basilosaurus)
images.caption: Basilosaurus, an early whale about 15 to 18 metres long with a long eel-like body, swimming under the surface.
images.note: Skin colour and the exact body outline are guesses; the tail fluke is inferred from the tail bones.

images.subject: Early horse (Propalaeotherium)
images.caption: The complete skeleton of a fox-sized early horse relative from the Messel Pit in Germany, about 47 million years old.
images.note: Propalaeotherium is a close European relative of the first horses (Eohippus), not Eohippus itself.

images.subject: Early whale (Pakicetus)
images.caption: Pakicetus, a wolf-sized four-legged animal from about 50 million years ago and one of the earliest known relatives of whales.
images.note: Fur and colour are guesses; how much time it spent in water is still discussed.

images.subject: Early horse (Orohippus) and Uintatherium
images.caption: Small early horses run from the water's edge as two horned Uintatherium come to drink in a warm Eocene forest.
images.note: Painted in 1931 by Charles R. Knight. Still broadly reasonable, but the animals' build and the plants follow the knowledge of that time.

images.subject: Early whale (Ambulocetus)
images.caption: A cast skeleton and a life model of Ambulocetus, the 'walking whale' that could move on land and swim.
images.note: Museum display in Pisa: the skeleton is a restored cast and the model is an older, rather crocodile-like interpretation.

images.subject: Early horse (Sifrhippus / Eohippus)
images.caption: Sifrhippus, one of the very first horses, was about the size of a small dog and had several toes on each foot.
images.note: The spotted coat is a guess, modelled on small forest animals of today. The artist's signature is on the picture.

images.subject: Oligocene rocks (Badlands)
images.caption: The striped hills of Badlands National Park, South Dakota, built from mud and ash that buried Eocene and Oligocene animals.
images.note: A modern landscape photograph: the rock layers are about 37 to 28 million years old.

images.subject: Paraceratherium
images.caption: Two Paraceratherium, hornless rhinoceros relatives and among the largest land mammals ever, tower over a pair of Hyaenodon.
images.note: Known from incomplete skeletons, so the exact size, neck length and skin are estimates.

images.subject: Oligocene woodland
images.caption: Three-toed horses, early dogs, a tortoise and a cat-like nimravid in an open Oligocene woodland in Oregon, about 30 million years ago.
images.credit: Bureau of Land Management Oregon and Washington
images.note: Mural by Roger Witter for the John Day Fossil Beds, based on the fossils of the Turtle Cove beds. Commons marks it public domain as a US government work.

images.subject: Arsinoitherium
images.caption: Arsinoitherium, a rhinoceros-sized plant eater from Egypt with a pair of huge bony horns.
images.note: Pencil drawing by Mauricio Antón. It looks like a rhinoceros but was more closely related to elephants.

images.subject: Megalodon
images.caption: A megalodon, the largest shark known, bursts from the sea among small whales and seabirds.
images.note: Megalodon is known almost only from teeth and a few backbones, so its body shape is an estimate; this picture models it on a great white shark, which newer studies suggest may be too stocky. The artist's signature is in the corner.

images.subject: Ashfall Fossil Beds rhinoceroses
images.caption: Skeletons of barrel-bodied rhinoceroses lie where they died at a waterhole in Nebraska, buried by volcanic ash about 12 million years ago.
images.note: The red numbered discs are excavation markers.

images.subject: Megalodon
images.caption: Rebuilt jaws of megalodon set with real fossil teeth, hanging in the American Museum of Natural History.
images.note: Only the teeth are fossils. The jaw is a model, because shark skeletons are made of cartilage and rarely fossilise.

images.subject: Miocene landscape
images.caption: A warm late Miocene landscape in central Europe, with an elephant relative, a hornless rhinoceros and clawed chalicotheres.
images.note: A 2026 reconstruction published in a scientific paper; it combines animals and plants known from fossils into one imagined view.

images.subject: Miocene grassland
images.caption: Giant pig-like Daeodon, clawed Moropus, small rhinoceroses, camels and three-toed horses on the Miocene plains of North America.
images.note: Painted by Charles R. Knight about 1929 for the Field Museum. Still broadly reasonable, though details of the animals follow the knowledge of that time.

images.subject: Terror bird (Phorusrhacos)
images.caption: Phorusrhacos, a flightless hunting 'terror bird' about 2.5 metres tall that lived in South America.
images.note: Feather colours and the bare red face are guesses.

images.subject: Australopithecus afarensis ('Lucy')
images.caption: A digital reconstruction of the face of Lucy's species, Australopithecus afarensis.
images.note: Lucy's own skull is very incomplete, so a face like this leans on other skulls of her species. Skin, hair and eye colour cannot be known from fossils.

images.subject: Australopithecus afarensis ('Lucy')
images.caption: The bones of 'Lucy', a 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus afarensis from Ethiopia who walked upright.
images.note: This is a cast in the Paris natural history museum; the original bones are kept in Addis Ababa. Tall, narrow picture.

images.subject: Pliocene landscape
images.caption: A Pliocene river landscape in central Europe, with mastodon-like elephants, a rhinoceros, tapirs and deer.
images.note: A 2026 reconstruction published in a scientific paper; it combines animals and plants known from fossils into one imagined view.

images.subject: Laetoli footprints
images.caption: Footprints left in wet volcanic ash at Laetoli, Tanzania, about 3.66 million years ago by upright-walking human relatives.
images.note: A museum cast in Vienna, not the original trackway, which is reburied in Tanzania to protect it.

images.subject: Ice Age animals
images.caption: Woolly mammoths, wild horses, a woolly rhinoceros and cave lions on a snowy plain in northern Spain during the last Ice Age.
images.note: Painting by Mauricio Antón, published in the open-access journal PLoS Biology.

images.subject: Neanderthal
images.caption: A life-size reconstruction of an older Neanderthal man holding a wooden spear, from the Neanderthal Museum in Germany.
images.note: Model by the Kennis brothers. The bone structure follows real skulls; skin tone, hair and expression are informed guesses. Tall picture.

images.subject: Woolly mammoth
images.caption: A life-size model of a woolly mammoth at the Royal British Columbia Museum.
images.note: A museum model; hair length and colour are based on frozen mammoths found in Siberia.

images.subject: Diprotodon
images.caption: A Diprotodon skeleton built from bones found at Lake Callabonna, South Australia.
images.note: A composite: the bones come from several animals.

images.subject: Glyptodon
images.caption: Glyptodon, a car-sized relative of armadillos with a domed shell made of hundreds of bony plates.
images.note: Colour is a guess.

images.subject: Glyptodon and relatives
images.caption: Three kinds of giant armoured glyptodonts on the grasslands of Ice Age South America, one with a spiked club on its tail.
images.note: Shows Glyptodon, Doedicurus and Panochthus together; colours are guesses.

images.subject: Sabre-toothed cat (Smilodon) at La Brea
images.caption: Sabre-toothed cats and giant vultures gather round animals trapped in the sticky tar pools of La Brea, California.
images.note: Mural by Charles R. Knight, about 1931. The cats look rather lion-like by today's standards, but the scene is still broadly reasonable.

images.subject: Ice Age steppe
images.caption: Central Europe in the last Ice Age: a cold open grassland with mammoths, woolly rhinoceros, bison and saiga antelope.
images.note: A 2026 reconstruction published in a scientific paper; it combines animals and plants known from fossils into one imagined view.

images.subject: Giant ground sloth (Megatherium)
images.caption: The skeleton of Megatherium, a giant ground sloth, rearing up against a tree trunk in the Natural History Museum, London.
images.note: The London skeleton is a plaster cast, not original bone.

images.subject: Neanderthal
images.caption: The face of a Neanderthal man, reconstructed for the Natural History Museum in London.
images.note: Model by the Kennis brothers. Skin, hair and the headband are informed guesses. Tall picture.

images.subject: Neanderthal
images.caption: The skull of the 'Old Man' of La Chapelle-aux-Saints, a Neanderthal who lived in France about 50,000 to 60,000 years ago.
images.note: The background has been replaced with a grey fade.

images.subject: Sabre-toothed cat (Smilodon)
images.caption: Smilodon fatalis, the sabre-toothed cat of Ice Age North America, with a heavy body and a short tail.
images.note: The spotted coat is a guess; fossils do not preserve fur colour.

images.subject: Woolly mammoth
images.caption: A herd of woolly mammoths crosses a snowy valley, with woolly rhinoceroses in the distance.
images.note: Mural by Charles R. Knight, about 1929. It still looks reasonable, though mammoths probably lived more on dry grassland than in deep snow.

images.subject: Diprotodon
images.caption: Diprotodon, a wombat relative the size of a rhinoceros and the largest marsupial that ever lived, grazing in Ice Age Australia.
images.note: Illustration by palaeontologist Nellie Pease. Fur and nose shape are guesses. Square picture with a soft white edge.

images.subject: Glacier ice
images.caption: The front of the Perito Moreno Glacier in Patagonia: a living reminder of the ice that covered far more of the world until about 12,000 years ago.
images.note: A modern photograph standing in for the Ice Age world; this glacier is not a leftover of the great ice sheets.

images.subject: Giant deer (Irish elk)
images.caption: The skull and antlers of a giant deer, whose antlers spanned up to 3.6 metres.
images.note: Mainly an Ice Age animal, placed here because it outlived the ice: the last giant deer lived in Siberia about 7,700 years ago.

images.subject: Moa and Haast's eagle
images.caption: A giant Haast's eagle attacks moa in New Zealand, where huge birds lived until people arrived about 700 years ago.
images.note: Painting by John Megahan (2004), published in the open-access journal PLoS Biology. Feather colours are guesses.

images.subject: Muskox
images.caption: Muskoxen in Alaska: shaggy survivors of the Ice Age that once lived alongside woolly mammoths.
images.note: A modern wildlife photograph.

images.subject: Tundra (Wrangel Island)
images.caption: Tundra on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean, where the last woolly mammoths survived until about 4,000 years ago.
images.note: A modern photograph (2006), fittingly taken on the Mamontovaya, or Mammoth, River.

images.subject: Young planets colliding
images.caption: Two young rocky planets about to collide in a dusty disc around a young star, in a NASA artist's concept of the violent era when Earth was built.
images.note: Painted for a planetary system around a pair of distant stars, not the early Solar System; a stand-in for Earth's era of giant impacts.

images.subject: Late Heavy Bombardment
images.caption: Comets and asteroids pound the young Moon, scarring it with the craters still seen on its face today.
images.note: Whether a sharp 'late heavy bombardment' spike happened about 3.9 billion years ago is now debated; many scientists favour a slower decline in impacts. Portrait format, with a small artist's credit in a corner.

images.subject: Lava erupting under the sea
images.caption: Glowing lava breaks out on the deep sea floor at the West Mata volcano near Tonga today, a modern analogue for the volcanic sea floors of the young Earth.
images.note: Present-day photo from a deep-sea vehicle, whose basket shows at the bottom edge.

images.subject: Jack Hills, Western Australia
images.caption: The Jack Hills of Western Australia seen from orbit today; zircon crystals in their rocks are the oldest known pieces of Earth, about 4.4 billion years old.
images.note: The rocks of the hills are Archean; only tiny zircon grains inside them date from the Hadean. Satellite view, square.

images.subject: Acasta Gneiss
images.caption: A banded piece of the Acasta Gneiss from northern Canada, at about 4 billion years one of the oldest rocks on Earth.
images.note: Small file (1024 px). The oldest parts are about 4.03 billion years old, right at the Hadean-Archean boundary.

images.subject: Living stromatolites, Lake Thetis
images.caption: Stromatolites on the shore of Lake Thetis in Western Australia today, a modern analogue of the microbial mounds that were among Earth's first signs of life.
images.note: Present-day photo standing in for the Archean.

images.subject: Stromatolites under water, Shark Bay
images.caption: A snorkeller glides over living stromatolites in Shark Bay, Western Australia, a modern analogue of the shallow Archean sea floor.
images.credit: Ed Landing and Markes E. Johnson
images.note: Present-day photo; the swimmer gives scale.

images.subject: Banded iron formation, Barberton
images.caption: Red and grey layers of a banded iron formation from the Barberton Greenstone Belt of South Africa, laid down in Archean seas over 3 billion years ago.
images.note: Hand specimen with a ruler at the edge.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed over 3 billion years ago

images.subject: Archean pillow lava
images.caption: Rounded pillows of Archean lava, about 2.7 billion years old, in Michigan; they formed when lava erupted under water.
images.imageDateLabel: Lava erupted about 2.7 billion years ago

images.subject: Banded iron gorge, Karijini
images.caption: Kalmina Gorge in Karijini National Park, Western Australia, cut through layered banded iron rock laid down around 2.5 billion years ago, when oxygen first built up.
images.note: Present-day photo; the rocks belong to the Hamersley Group, at the Archean-Proterozoic boundary.
images.imageDateLabel: Present day · rocks about 2.5 billion years old

images.subject: Grypania
images.caption: Coiled ribbons of Grypania, one of the oldest fossils visible to the naked eye and possibly an early alga.
images.note: Grypania fossils range from about 1.9 to 1.4 billion years old; the age of this slab is not stated, and what Grypania was is still debated.

images.subject: Belt Supergroup stromatolites
images.caption: Columns of fossil stromatolites in limestone beside the Going-to-the-Sun Road in Glacier National Park, built by microbes about 1.4 billion years ago.

images.subject: Bass Limestone stromatolites, Grand Canyon
images.caption: Wavy layers of fossil stromatolites in the Bass Limestone deep in the Grand Canyon, about 1.25 billion years old.

images.subject: Kimberella on a microbial mat
images.caption: A museum model of the Ediacaran sea floor, with slug-like Kimberella grazing a green microbial mat and leaving scratch trails behind.
images.note: Museum case seen from above; the frame edge shows.

images.subject: Frond fossil, Mistaken Point
images.caption: A feathery Ediacaran frond pressed into the rock at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, about 565 million years old; a coin gives the scale.

images.subject: Burgess Shale quarry slope
images.caption: The scree slope below Walcott's quarry high in the Canadian Rockies today, where the Burgess Shale fossils of the Cambrian sea were found.
images.note: Present-day photo of the fossil site.

images.subject: End-Ordovician sea retreat
images.caption: Long-shelled nautiloids lie stranded on a drained sea floor as ice ages lowered the oceans at the end of the Ordovician.
images.note: An artist's interpretation of the end-Ordovician extinction; the scene is imagined, not based on one fossil site.

images.subject: Sacabambaspis
images.caption: Sacabambaspis, an armoured jawless fish of Ordovician seas, swims head-on toward the viewer.

images.subject: Waukesha biota
images.caption: Life on a Silurian sea floor in what is now Wisconsin: a horseshoe-crab-like arthropod, worms, small crustaceans and a looming nautiloid.
images.note: Small artist's name in the lower right corner.

images.subject: Guiyu
images.caption: Guiyu, one of the earliest bony fish, swims over a reef in a Silurian sea in what is now China.
images.note: Portrait format.

images.subject: Pterygotus
images.caption: Pterygotus, a giant sea scorpion with long grasping claws that hunted in Silurian and Devonian seas.
images.note: Drawn on a white background.

images.subject: Cooksonia
images.caption: Cooksonia, one of the first land plants, a few centimetres tall, rising from bare Silurian mud.
images.note: Small file (900 px). Simple 3D render.

images.subject: Silurian shore
images.caption: A calm Silurian sea with colourful reefs of corals and sea lilies, painted by Charles R. Knight.
images.note: Early 20th-century painting; the reef colours are imagined.

images.subject: Gooloogongia
images.caption: Gooloogongia, a large predatory lobe-finned fish of Devonian rivers in Australia.

images.subject: Jaekelopterus
images.caption: Jaekelopterus, the largest sea scorpion ever found, about 2.5 metres long, from Devonian waters in Germany.

images.subject: Devonian sea floor with Terataspis
images.caption: A museum diorama of a Devonian reef with the large spiny trilobite Terataspis among corals and sea lilies.

images.subject: Acanthostega
images.caption: Acanthostega, an early four-legged animal with gills and a fish-like tail that still lived in water.
images.note: Very wide cut-out on a white background.

images.subject: Arthropleura
images.caption: Arthropleura, a millipede relative over two metres long that crawled through Carboniferous forests.
images.note: Cut-out on a white background.

images.subject: Meganeura
images.caption: A model of Meganeura, a dragonfly-like insect with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres from the Carboniferous.
images.note: Museum model photographed on white.

images.subject: Carboniferous sea lilies
images.caption: Orange sea lilies sway in a museum diorama of a Carboniferous sea floor, with a fish painted in the background.
images.note: Colours in the diorama are imagined.

images.subject: Moschops
images.caption: Two Moschops, heavily built plant-eating relatives of mammals, from the Permian of South Africa.

images.subject: Sinophoneus
images.caption: A family of Sinophoneus, a big Permian relative of mammals from China, with a young one at the bottom.
images.credit: He who needs to be silenced
images.note: Dark background.

images.subject: Siberian Traps, Putorana Plateau
images.caption: The stepped lava cliffs of the Putorana Plateau in Siberia today, part of the Siberian Traps whose eruptions are blamed for the end-Permian mass extinction.
images.note: Present-day aerial photo; the lavas erupted about 252 million years ago.

images.subject: Saurosuchus and Hyperodapedon
images.caption: Saurosuchus, a large Triassic predator related to crocodiles, faces a herd of beaked Hyperodapedon in Argentina.

images.subject: Fallen conifers, Chinle Formation
images.caption: A painting of a Late Triassic river plain in Arizona strewn with fallen conifer logs, the trees that became the Petrified Forest.
images.note: Photo of a museum painting.

images.subject: Whale skeleton in the desert, Wadi Al-Hitan
images.caption: The skeleton of an Eocene whale weathering out of the desert floor at Wadi Al-Hitan, Egypt, where a sea lay 40 million years ago.

images.subject: Andrewsarchus
images.caption: Andrewsarchus, a large Eocene meat-eating mammal from Mongolia known mainly from a huge skull.
images.note: Only the skull is known, so the body is a guess.

images.subject: Paraceratherium herd
images.caption: A herd of Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever, browsing on an open plain in an early 20th-century painting.
images.note: Painted in the 1920s; the animals' proportions are dated.

images.subject: Hoplophoneus
images.caption: Hoplophoneus, a sabre-toothed cat-like hunter of Oligocene North America.
images.note: Cut-out on a white background.

images.subject: Batallones fauna
images.caption: Animals of the late Miocene Batallones fossil pits near Madrid, including sabre-toothed cats, a bear-dog and a mastodon.
images.note: Line-up on a white background.

images.subject: Paratethys sea
images.caption: A whale and a giant elephant relative meet on the shore of the Paratethys, a huge inland sea that covered eastern Europe in the Miocene.
images.note: Smaller file (1403 px).

images.subject: Kelenken
images.caption: Kelenken, a terror bird with the biggest skull of any known bird, feeds in Miocene Patagonia.

images.subject: Livyatan
images.caption: Livyatan, a sperm-whale relative with teeth up to 36 centimetres long that hunted in Miocene seas.
images.note: Cut-out on a white background.

images.subject: The young Earth under bombardment
images.caption: Meteors streak through a dark sky over glowing lava fields on the young Earth, in a NASA artist's view of the planet's violent first age.
images.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab
images.note: An artist's impression; how much of the Hadean surface was molten, and when oceans first formed, is still debated (zircons hint at liquid water by 4.4 billion years ago). Very wide banner.

images.subject: Birth of the planets
images.caption: A young star wrapped in a glowing disc of gas and dust, the kind of disc in which Earth and the other planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
images.note: Shows another young star, not the Sun; a stand-in for the birth of the Solar System.

images.subject: Cratered lunar highlands
images.caption: Crater upon crater on the Moon's highlands, photographed from Apollo 17 in 1972; the Moon still keeps the scars of the bombardment that also struck the young Earth.
images.note: Present-day photo of the Moon, standing in for the battered surface of the Hadean Earth.

images.subject: Lava lake at dusk, Kīlauea
images.caption: A crusted lake of molten lava glows at dusk in Kīlauea's summit crater in Hawaii in 2021, a modern glimpse of the molten surfaces of the young Earth.
images.note: Present-day photo used as an analogue.

images.subject: Allende meteorite
images.caption: A slice of the Allende meteorite, whose pale grains are about 4.567 billion years old, among the first solids to form in the Solar System.
images.note: Museum photo with reflections; older than the Earth itself.

images.subject: Microbial mats, Grand Prismatic Spring
images.caption: Orange carpets of microbes spread from the steaming Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone today, a modern analogue of the microbial world of the Archean.
images.note: Present-day photo; the colours come from bacteria and other microbes living in the hot water.

images.subject: Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains
images.caption: Misty green hills of the Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains in South Africa today, built of some of the best-preserved rocks on Earth, 3.2 to 3.6 billion years old.
images.note: Present-day panorama (very wide).
images.imageDateLabel: Present day · rocks 3.2–3.6 billion years old

images.subject: Strelley Pool stromatolite
images.caption: Wavy layers in a slab from the Strelley Pool rocks of Western Australia, among the oldest widely accepted traces of life, about 3.4 billion years old.
images.note: Most scientists read these layers as microbial, but a non-living origin has been argued for some very old stromatolites.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 3.4 billion years ago

images.subject: Isua banded iron, Greenland
images.caption: Banded iron rock about 3.8 billion years old from the Isua belt of Greenland, one of the oldest sedimentary rocks on Earth.
images.note: A small museum label shows on the specimen.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 3.8 billion years ago

images.subject: Komatiite lava
images.caption: Needle-like 'spinifex' crystals in komatiite, an extremely hot lava that erupted often in the Archean but almost never since; Ontario, about 2.7 billion years old.
images.imageDateLabel: Lava erupted about 2.7 billion years ago

images.subject: Banded iron, Hamersley Range
images.caption: Red jasper, grey iron oxide and golden tiger-eye bands in a banded iron formation from the Hamersley Range, Western Australia, about 2.5 billion years old.
images.note: Close-up of a polished rock surface; the age straddles the Archean-Proterozoic boundary.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 2.5 billion years ago

images.subject: Microbial mats, Yellowstone
images.caption: Cracked, orange microbial mats around the Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone today, a modern analogue of the mats that carpeted shallow water through the long Proterozoic.
images.note: Present-day photo used as an analogue.

images.subject: Vishnu Schist, Grand Canyon
images.caption: Rafts drift beneath cliffs of Vishnu Schist in the inner Grand Canyon today, rock formed about 1.75 billion years ago when island arcs crashed into early North America.
images.note: Present-day photo.
images.imageDateLabel: Present day · rocks about 1.75 billion years old

images.subject: The Great Unconformity
images.caption: In the Grand Canyon, flat Cambrian sandstone sits directly on dark Proterozoic schist; over a billion years of Earth's record is missing at the join.
images.note: Present-day photo; deep shadows.

images.subject: Charnia
images.caption: Charnia, a frond-shaped Ediacaran organism that grew anchored to the deep sea floor about 570 to 555 million years ago.
images.note: Cut-out on a white background; the colours are imagined.

images.subject: Marjum biota, Utah
images.caption: A Cambrian sea floor in what is now Utah, with radiodont predators overhead, trilobites, sponges and sea lilies, about 500 million years ago.
images.note: Figure from a paper: small key numbers sit beside each animal.

images.subject: Astraspis
images.caption: Astraspis, one of the earliest armoured jawless fish, stirs up sand on an Ordovician sea floor.
images.note: Close to square, on a pale background.

images.subject: Anji glass-sponge reef
images.caption: A large trilobite-like arthropod crawls through a dark forest of glass sponges on an Ordovician sea floor in what is now China.
images.note: Small artist's mark in the lower left corner.

images.subject: Cabrières biota
images.caption: A crowded Early Ordovician sea floor in southern France, with algae, sponges, a large nautiloid and dozens of small animals, about 470 million years ago.
images.note: Wide format (1950 px).

images.subject: Nautiloids over a Late Ordovician sea floor
images.caption: Long straight-shelled nautiloids hunt among sea lilies and seaweed in a museum diorama of the Late Ordovician sea that covered Ohio.
images.note: Diorama colours are imagined.

images.subject: Isotelus trilobite
images.caption: The large trilobite Isotelus crawls past orange bryozoans in a museum diorama of the Late Ordovician sea floor of Ohio.

images.subject: Late Ordovician reef life
images.caption: Yellow sea lilies, corals, clams and a nautiloid's tentacles in a museum diorama of the Late Ordovician sea floor of Ohio.

images.subject: Rugose corals
images.caption: Horn-shaped rugose corals with their tentacles out, a coral group that first appeared in the Ordovician and died out at the end of the Permian.
images.note: 3D render on a black background; the colours are imagined.

images.subject: Endoceras
images.caption: Endoceras, a nautiloid with a straight shell that could reach several metres, one of the largest animals of Ordovician seas.
images.note: Cut-out on a white background.

images.subject: Nesonektris
images.caption: Nesonektris, a strange swimming vetulicolian, glides through shallow Cambrian water.
images.credit: He who needs to be silenced
images.note: What group vetulicolians belong to is still debated.

images.subject: Silurian reef
images.caption: A busy Silurian reef in a museum diorama: corals, sea lilies, snails, trilobites, a nautiloid and an early fish.
images.note: Diorama colours are imagined.

images.subject: Trilobite on a Silurian reef
images.caption: A trilobite rests on a coral head among sea lilies and bryozoans in a museum diorama of a Silurian reef.

images.subject: Sea scorpions in a Silurian lagoon
images.caption: Sea scorpions stalk through seaweed in a museum diorama of a shallow Silurian lagoon.

images.subject: Sea stacks of Gotland
images.caption: Limestone sea stacks on the coast of Gotland, Sweden, today; they are the remains of reefs that grew in a warm Silurian sea about 425 million years ago.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Niagara Falls
images.caption: Niagara Falls today; the hard ledge the water pours over is dolostone laid down on the floor of a shallow tropical Silurian sea.
images.note: Present-day photo; the falls themselves were cut after the last ice age.

images.subject: Dickinsonia
images.caption: A ribbed oval impression of Dickinsonia from South Australia; traces of cholesterol in such fossils suggest it was one of the earliest animals.

images.subject: Spriggina
images.caption: The small segmented Ediacaran fossil Spriggina, about 3 centimetres long, on a slab from the Ediacara Hills of South Australia.
images.note: What kind of animal Spriggina was is still uncertain.

images.subject: Devonian reef with trilobites
images.caption: Corals, sea lilies and spiny trilobites crowd a museum diorama of a Devonian reef in New York.

images.subject: Joggins Fossil Cliffs
images.caption: The Joggins Fossil Cliffs on the Bay of Fundy, Nova Scotia, today; their layers hold upright fossil trees and early reptiles of the Carboniferous coal forests.
images.note: Present-day photo; a very wide panorama.

images.subject: Gastornis
images.caption: Gastornis, a giant flightless bird, walks across open woodland in a 1917 drawing.
images.note: Gastornis lived from the late Paleocene into the Eocene. Black-and-white drawing; the bird's feathering is a guess.

images.subject: Paleocene badlands, Painted Canyon
images.caption: Badlands of Painted Canyon in North Dakota today, carved from river and swamp deposits laid down in the Paleocene, soon after the dinosaurs died out.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Paraceratherium skull
images.caption: The skull of Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal known, in the American Museum of Natural History.
images.note: Museum photo with reflections in the glass.

images.subject: Hyaenodon gigas
images.caption: Hyaenodon gigas, a large meat-eating mammal of the late Eocene in Asia, from a group unrelated to modern cats and dogs.
images.note: Cut-out on white with a 50 cm scale bar.

images.subject: Inostrancevia attacking Scutosaurus
images.caption: The sabre-toothed Inostrancevia brings down a Scutosaurus on a late Permian plain in Russia.
images.note: Shows a kill, with some blood.

images.subject: Barylambda
images.caption: Barylambda, a heavy, slow plant-eating mammal the size of a pony from the late Paleocene of North America.
images.note: Cut-out on a white background.

images.subject: Painted Canyon, Theodore Roosevelt National Park
images.caption: Badlands under towering clouds in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, today; the layers are Paleocene muds and sands from rivers and swamp forests.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Paleocene petrified logs
images.caption: Petrified tree trunks weathering out of the badlands in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, remains of Paleocene swamp forests of redwood-like trees.

images.subject: Painted Canyon in spring
images.caption: Green grass and striped Paleocene layers in Painted Canyon, North Dakota, today.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Painted Hills, Oregon
images.caption: The banded Painted Hills of Oregon today, made of volcanic ash soils that weathered under a warm, wet climate around the Eocene-Oligocene boundary.
images.note: Present-day panorama (very wide). The layers span roughly 39 to 30 million years ago.

images.subject: Painted Hills with wildflowers
images.caption: Wildflowers in front of the red and gold Painted Hills of the John Day Fossil Beds, Oregon, today.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Hagerman horse
images.caption: A skeleton of the Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens, one of the earliest members of the horse genus, from about 3.5 million years ago in Idaho.
images.note: Museum photo.

images.subject: Late Miocene Oregon
images.caption: Horses, camels and other grazers cross a grassland in late Miocene Oregon as a volcanic ash cloud rolls in, in a mural for the John Day Fossil Beds.
images.note: Public-domain mural painted for a US federal agency; very wide.

images.subject: Ischigualasto, Valley of the Moon
images.caption: The grey badlands of Ischigualasto in Argentina today, Late Triassic rocks that hold some of the oldest dinosaurs, such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus.
images.note: Present-day panorama.

images.subject: Eryops
images.caption: Eryops, a big early Permian amphibian, lies among ferns and horsetails in a museum diorama of a swampy forest floor.

images.subject: Dimetrodon in a forest diorama
images.caption: A model Dimetrodon, a sail-backed early Permian predator related to mammals, in a museum diorama of a fern forest.

images.subject: Mississippian sea lilies
images.caption: Sea lilies with arms like lace in a museum diorama of an early Carboniferous sea floor, when crinoids formed vast meadows.

images.subject: Late Carboniferous sea
images.caption: Fish, sponges, a coiled nautiloid and shells on a late Carboniferous sea floor, in a museum diorama.
images.note: Diorama colours are imagined.

images.subject: Fossil tree standing in the cliff, Joggins
images.caption: A fossil scale-tree trunk still standing upright where it grew, buried in the Carboniferous cliffs of Joggins, Nova Scotia; a hammer gives scale.

images.subject: Postosuchus, Coelophysis and Placerias
images.caption: The big predator Postosuchus, small Coelophysis dinosaurs and a herd of tusked Placerias share a Late Triassic river plain in what is now the American Southwest.

images.subject: Burgess Shale sea floor
images.caption: Worms, the lobopodian Aysheaia, a trilobite and the lace crab Marrella on the sea floor in a museum diorama of the Burgess Shale.
images.note: Older museum diorama; some animals are shown as they were understood in past decades.

images.subject: Fortiforceps and Sklerolibyon
images.caption: Two early Cambrian arthropods with grasping head claws, Fortiforceps and Sklerolibyon, in a sea in what is now southern China.

images.subject: Dinictis and Protoceras
images.caption: The cat-like hunter Dinictis watches a group of horned Protoceras in an Oligocene landscape painted by Charles R. Knight in 1904.
images.note: Painted in 1904; details are dated.

images.subject: Flysch cliffs near Zumaia
images.caption: Tilted layers of deep-sea rock in the cliffs near Zumaia, Spain, today; this coast holds the world reference points for two of the Paleocene's ages.
images.note: Present-day photo. The Zumaia flysch spans the Late Cretaceous to the Eocene; not every layer in view is Paleocene.

images.subject: Ankalagon
images.caption: Ankalagon, a wolf-sized meat-eating mammal from the early Paleocene of New Mexico, shown as a female and a larger male.
images.note: Cut-out with labels and a scale bar.

images.subject: Alcidedorbignya
images.caption: Alcidedorbignya, a small early Paleocene mammal from Bolivia, one of the first of the plant-eating pantodonts.
images.note: Cut-out on white with a 5 cm scale bar.

images.subject: Wilpena Pound
images.caption: Sunset lights the quartzite walls of Wilpena Pound in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia today; rock layers in these ranges hold the Ediacaran fossils and gave the period its name.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Ounianga lakes from space
images.caption: The blue Ounianga lakes in the Sahara of Chad seen from the International Space Station, leftovers of the much larger lakes of the 'Green Sahara' in the early Holocene.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Lake Yoa
images.caption: Lake Yoa in the Chad desert today; its layered mud records how the green Sahara of the early Holocene dried into desert over thousands of years.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Göbekli Tepe
images.caption: Stone pillars at Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, raised about 11,000 years ago, at the very start of the Holocene, by people who had not yet begun farming.
images.note: Excavation photo; scaffolding and fences are visible.

images.subject: Rock engraving of an extinct buffalo
images.caption: A rock engraving of a giant buffalo from Tin Taghirt in the Algerian Sahara, carved when the region was green grassland in the early Holocene.
images.note: The age of Saharan rock engravings is hard to pin down; estimates for this style range widely.

images.subject: Cattle herders in Saharan rock art
images.caption: People and cattle painted on a rock shelter in the Sahara, a record of the herders who lived there when it was greener, several thousand years ago.
images.note: Exact site and date of the painting are not given on the file page.

images.subject: Dodo
images.caption: A dodo skeleton; this flightless pigeon of Mauritius was wiped out by the late 1600s, within a century of people arriving.
images.note: Museum photo.

images.subject: Pliocene grazers of East Africa
images.caption: Giraffes, antelopes, pigs, a three-toed horse and a rhino from the Pliocene of East Africa, drawn by Mauricio Antón.
images.note: Black-and-white line-up on a grid.

images.subject: Pliocene North America
images.caption: Rhinos wallow and mastodons graze by a lake in Charles R. Knight's mural of Pliocene North America.
images.note: Early 20th-century painting; animals and dating are old interpretations. Very wide.

images.subject: Thalassocnus
images.caption: Thalassocnus, a ground sloth that waded into the sea to graze on seagrass along the desert coast of Peru.
images.note: Cut-out on white. Thalassocnus species lived from the late Miocene into the Pliocene.

images.subject: Deinotherium
images.caption: Deinotherium, a huge elephant relative with tusks curving down from its lower jaw, beside a human silhouette for scale.
images.note: Cut-out on white. Deinotherium lived from the Miocene into the Pleistocene.

images.subject: Blue Mesa, Petrified Forest
images.caption: Striped badlands and fallen stone logs at Blue Mesa in Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, today; the logs are conifers that grew about 220 million years ago.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: El Capitan, a Permian reef
images.caption: Snow on El Capitan in the Guadalupe Mountains of Texas today; the cliff is part of a reef that ringed a Permian sea about 260 million years ago.
images.note: Present-day photo.

images.subject: Lemurosaurus
images.caption: Lemurosaurus, a small late Permian relative of mammals from South Africa.
images.note: Cut-out on white with a 10 cm scale bar.

images.subject: Old Red Sandstone
images.caption: Red sandstone and pebble beds in the sea cliffs at Auchmithie, Scotland, today, laid down by rivers on a dry Devonian continent.
images.note: A person at the far right gives scale.

images.subject: Archaeotherium
images.caption: Two Archaeotherium, big pig-like 'hell pigs' of Oligocene North America, root at a carcass in a drawing by R. Bruce Horsfall.
images.note: Early 20th-century black-and-white drawing; entelodonts were not true pigs.

images.subject: Kimberella fossil
images.caption: A fossil of Kimberella from the White Sea coast of Russia, about 555 million years old; many scientists think it was an early mollusc-like animal.
images.note: Kimberella's place among animals is still debated.

images.subject: Gilboa tree stump
images.caption: The fossil base of an Eospermatopteris tree from Gilboa, New York, one of the trees of the first forests on Earth, about 385 million years ago.
images.note: Museum photo of a rock stump; portrait format.

images.subject: Ediacaran sea floor
images.caption: Pink and orange fronds, quilted discs and other soft Ediacaran organisms cover the sea floor in a diorama at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History.
images.note: Colours are imagined; how these organisms lived is still debated.

images.subject: Kimberella
images.caption: Kimberella, a soft-bodied Ediacaran animal, creeps across a green microbial mat that it may have grazed.
images.note: 3D render; the body shape follows one interpretation of the fossils.

images.subject: Camp dels Ninots crater lake
images.caption: Deer, tapirs and birds around a volcanic crater lake in a Pliocene forest in Catalonia, Spain, about 3 million years ago, painted by Mauricio Antón.
images.note: Wide format.

images.subject: Ardi
images.caption: A cast of 'Ardi', the 4.4-million-year-old skeleton of Ardipithecus ramidus from Ethiopia, an early member of the human line who walked upright but also climbed trees.
images.note: Museum photo of a cast; how Ardipithecus is related to later hominins is debated.

images.subject: Scale-tree stump
images.caption: The scaly stump of a Lepidodendron tree and a large mayfly-like insect in a museum diorama of a late Carboniferous coal-swamp floor.

images.subject: Thylacine
images.caption: A thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, photographed at Hobart Zoo in 1928; the last known one died there in 1936.
images.note: Historical black-and-white photo with a dark border.

images.subject: Hyracodon
images.caption: Two Hyracodon, slender, long-legged hornless rhinos of the Oligocene plains, squabble in a 1912 drawing by R. Bruce Horsfall.
images.note: Early 20th-century black-and-white drawing; the artist's signature shows in the corner.

images.subject: Mesohippus
images.caption: A small herd of Mesohippus, three-toed horses the size of a large dog, in an Oligocene woodland drawn by R. Bruce Horsfall in 1913.
images.note: Early 20th-century drawing; the spotted coat is the artist's guess.

images.subject: Isthmus of Panama
images.caption: The Isthmus of Panama from space today; when this land bridge closed in the Pliocene, animals crossed between the Americas and ocean currents changed.
images.credit: Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Rapid Response Team, NASA
images.note: Present-day satellite image. Most scientists date the full closure to about 3 million years ago, but some argue for a much earlier link.

images.subject: Kanapoi, Kenya
images.caption: Dry country near Lake Turkana in northern Kenya seen from space; Kanapoi's 4.2-million-year-old rocks yielded Australopithecus anamensis, the earliest known Australopithecus.
images.note: Present-day astronaut photo; the fossil site itself is too small to pick out.

images.subject: Painted Canyon under cloud
images.caption: Grassy slopes and banded buttes of Paleocene rock stretch to the horizon in Painted Canyon, North Dakota, today.
images.note: Present-day photo; flat light.

images.subject: Taeniolabis
images.caption: The head of Taeniolabis, a beaver-sized multituberculate, one of the largest mammals of the early Paleocene, drawn by R. Bruce Horsfall.
images.note: Early 20th-century drawing of the head only.

images.subject: Snowball Earth
images.caption: An artist's view of the Earth almost entirely frozen over, as it was during the great Cryogenian glaciations.
images.note: Painted for the earlier Huronian glaciation about 2.4 billion years ago; the outlines of the land are not a reconstruction.

images.subject: The end of a Snowball Earth
images.caption: At Enorama Creek in South Australia, pale limestone laid down as the last Snowball Earth melted sits on top of the glacial rocks; this layer marks the start of the Ediacaran, about 635 million years ago.
images.imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 635 million years ago

images.subject: An acritarch
images.caption: A spiny acritarch, a microscopic fossil less than a millimetre across, from the Weng'an rocks of southern China; acritarchs are the walls of single cells, many probably algae, whose true nature is unknown.
images.credit: Cunningham, Vargas, Yin, Bengtson and Donoghue
images.note: Scanning electron microscope image of Mengeosphaera.

images.subject: Grypania
images.caption: Coiled ribbons of Grypania in iron-rich rock from Michigan, among the oldest fossils big enough to see with the naked eye and probably early algae.
images.note: The rock is dated to either about 1.87 or 2.1 billion years ago; scientists disagree.

images.subject: Early Earth Lava
images.caption: Ancient zircon crystals suggest that solid crust and liquid water existed by about 4.4 billion years ago.

images.subject: Moon Forming Impact
images.caption: A possible Moon-forming impact. One leading explanation is that a large body struck the young Earth and debris gathered to form the Moon; the details remain uncertain.

images.subject: Early Earth Dusk
images.caption: Ancient crystals point to liquid water on the Hadean Earth; the shape of its coastlines and appearance of the sky are unknown.

images.subject: Planets Before Impact
images.caption: In the giant-impact hypothesis, a body often called Theia struck the early Earth; its exact appearance and orbit are unknown.

images.subject: Young Solar Disc
images.caption: The planets formed from a disc of gas and dust around the young Sun; the detailed appearance of the disc is unknown.

images.subject: Young Moon Highlands
images.caption: Lunar samples show that an early molten Moon cooled to form a light-coloured crust.

images.subject: Hadean Crater Lava
images.caption: Volcanism shaped the early Earth, but its particular landscapes are not known.

images.subject: Young Moon Impact
images.caption: The Moon’s ancient cratered surface preserves evidence of collisions early in solar system history.

images.subject: Early Earth Seafloor
images.caption: Ancient zircon chemistry suggests liquid water existed on the young Earth; the location and appearance of its earliest seafloor are unknown.
During the Cryogenian glaciations ice spread across much of Earth. Its extent remains uncertain.
images.subject: Snowball Earth Globe

images.caption: Fossil impressions preserve the branching, spindle-shaped body of Fractofusus; its colour and surroundings are uncertain.
images.subject: Fractofusus Seafloor

images.caption: Fossils of Anomalocaris preserve large eyes and grasping appendages; its prey and hunting behaviour are uncertain.
images.subject: Anomalocaris Hunting

images.caption: Hallucigenia sparsa had seven pairs of defensive spines and soft legs. Burgess Shale fossils show an animal only a few centimetres long.
images.subject: Hallucigenia On Sponge

images.caption: Opabinia was a small animal with five eyes, a long grasping trunk and swimming flaps.
images.subject: Opabinia Seafloor

images.caption: Early Ordovician Fezouata fossils record a diverse marine fauna, including filter-feeding radiodonts.
images.subject: Fezouata Biota Scene
Devonian Shallows
images.caption: Lobe-finned fish lived in watery habitats during the Late Devonian, about 375 million years ago.

images.subject: Tiktaalik Shallows
images.caption: Tiktaalik, a fossil fish from about 375 million years ago, had a broad head, a neck and sturdy fins with rays.

images.subject: Acanthostega Water
images.caption: Acanthostega was a largely aquatic early tetrapod. Fossils show limbs with digits and a fish-like tail.

images.subject: Ichthyostega Water
images.caption: The robust skeleton and limbs of Ichthyostega are known from fossils; exactly how it moved on land is still debated.

images.subject: Fin Limb Comparison
images.caption: An illustrative comparison of a Tiktaalik-like fin and an Acanthostega-like limb. The generated skeletons are schematic, not anatomically exact or to scale; Acanthostega fossils show eight digits on the forelimb.

images.subject: Acanthostega
images.caption: A slab with Acanthostega skeletons from the Late Devonian rocks of East Greenland, about 365 million years old, on display in Brussels. Acanthostega had eight digits on its front limbs, yet kept gills: legs evolved in animals that still lived in water.
images.imageDateLabel: Late Devonian, about 365 million years ago
images.note: Its limbs were described by Coates and Clack in 1990 (Nature 347:66), its gills in 1991 (Nature 352:234).

images.subject: Devonian Trackway
images.caption: Devonian traces in Poland record early trackways, although the makers of some tracks are debated.

images.subject: Dunkleosteus terrelli
images.caption: Dunkleosteus terrelli was an armoured fish of the Late Devonian. Fossils preserve the bony head armour and cutting jaw plates; its colour, fins, body shape and the surrounding sea are an artist’s interpretation. Its full size remains debated.

images.subject: Hyneria in a Devonian river
images.caption: Hyneria lindae was a large predatory lobe-finned fish that lived in Late Devonian waters of what is now Pennsylvania.

images.subject: Gooloogongia
images.caption: Gooloogongia loomesi was a lobe-finned fish known from Late Devonian fossils at Canowindra in Australia.

images.subject: Jaekelopterus
images.caption: Jaekelopterus rhenaniae was a large aquatic arthropod from the Early Devonian of what is now Germany. Fossils preserve parts including its claws.

images.subject: An early tetrapod at the water’s edge
images.caption: An Ichthyostega-like tetrapod at a shoreline around 365 million years ago. How it moved on land and how often it left the water are uncertain; the transition happened over many generations.

size.name: Ichthyostega-like tetrapod
size.note: The scene is a reconstruction; fossil individuals varied in size.

images.subject: A shallow Archean lagoon
images.caption: Layered rocks in the Pilbara preserve evidence of microbial mats and stromatolites about 3.4 billion years ago.

images.subject: An Archean volcanic coast
images.caption: Ancient volcanic rocks record eruptions beside Archean oceans.

images.subject: Microbial mats along a river
images.caption: Fossil evidence indicates microbial mats grew on river sediments about 3.22 billion years ago in what is now South Africa.

images.subject: The Archean Earth from space
images.caption: The Archean Earth had oceans and land; their arrangement and the presence of atmospheric haze are uncertain.

images.subject: Underwater volcanic eruption
images.caption: Rounded pillow lavas in Archean rocks record eruptions beneath water.

images.subject: A seafloor hydrothermal vent
images.caption: Hydrothermal vents release hot, mineral-rich fluids into the ocean. Whether microbes inhabited a particular ancient vent is uncertain.

images.subject: Archean hot springs
images.caption: Rocks in the Pilbara preserve evidence interpreted as hot-spring deposits about 3.48 billion years old, with possible microbial traces.

images.subject: An Archean glacial shore
images.caption: Deposits in southern Africa suggest glaciation about 2.9 billion years ago; the evidence does not show that the whole planet froze.

images.subject: An impact in an Archean ocean
images.caption: Layers of impact debris record ancient impacts during the Archean.

images.subject: A storm over an Archean river
images.caption: Fossil evidence indicates microbial mats grew on river sediments about 3.22 billion years ago in what is now South Africa.

images.subject: An iron-rich sea
images.caption: Ancient banded iron formations record the deposition of iron-rich minerals in early seas.

images.subject: A microbial shore during the Great Oxidation
images.caption: Microbial communities lived in shallow water as oxygen began to accumulate in the atmosphere over a long, uneven interval.

images.subject: Ice at an ancient coast
images.caption: Glacial deposits record ice ages in the early Paleoproterozoic; the extent of ice remains uncertain.

images.subject: A possible Francevillian seafloor
images.caption: Lobed structures in rocks from Gabon have been interpreted as large early life, but their origin and biological identity remain debated.

images.subject: The Vredefort impact
images.caption: Shocked and melted rocks record a giant impact at Vredefort in what is now South Africa about 2.02 billion years ago.

images.subject: The Gunflint microbial shallows
images.caption: Gunflint rocks preserve microbial fossils and iron-rich stromatolitic structures from an ancient sea.

images.subject: Continents collide
images.caption: Ancient mountain belts record continental collisions during the assembly of landmasses sometimes grouped as Columbia or Nuna.

images.subject: A microscopic view of early life
images.caption: The magnified circle shows simple filaments inspired by microscopic fossils from North China, interpreted as early multicellular eukaryotes.

images.subject: Microscopic life in the Roper sea
images.caption: A magnified view of microscopic life inspired by fossils from the Roper Group of Australia. Living colours, internal features and relative sizes are not known.

images.subject: A dry Belt Basin shore
images.caption: Mud cracks and other sedimentary features in Belt rocks record ancient shallow-water environments.

images.subject: The Moon over an ancient shore
images.caption: Rhythmic layers in ancient rocks provide estimates of the Earth–Moon system at this time. The Moon was closer than today.

images.subject: Lava in the Midcontinent Rift
images.caption: Basalt flows record volcanism during the formation of North America’s Midcontinent Rift.

images.subject: A lake in the rift
images.caption: Sediments of the Nonesuch Formation record an ancient lake within the rift.

images.subject: Bangiomorpha under magnification
images.caption: A magnified view of Bangiomorpha, a microscopic filamentous red alga. Its living colour and exact appearance are uncertain.

images.subject: Rodinia coming together
images.caption: Continental blocks were assembling into Rodinia; their arrangement and coastlines remain uncertain.

images.subject: A conceptual early eukaryotic cell
images.caption: A magnified conceptual cutaway showing a nucleus and mitochondrion-like structures in a eukaryotic cell. Internal details are inferred from cell biology, not observed in a particular Mesoproterozoic fossil.

images.subject: A tiny green alga
images.caption: Proterocladus fossils preserve tiny branched, multicellular forms measured in millimetres. This view is magnified; exact proportions and living colours are uncertain.

images.subject: Inside a microbial reef
images.caption: Textures in microbial reefs about 890 million years old have been proposed as sponge fossils, but that interpretation is disputed.

images.subject: A world of microscopic scales
images.caption: Fossil mineral scales show that some Tonian microorganisms made intricate coverings. This view is magnified; their whole living forms remain uncertain.

images.subject: A sheltered Tonian lagoon
images.caption: Fossils record microscopic life in late Tonian waters, including sheltered coastal environments.

images.subject: Vase-shaped microscopic life
images.caption: Vase-shaped microfossils are interpreted as the tiny outer coverings of amoeba-like cells. Their living soft parts are uncertain; this view is magnified.

images.subject: Rodinia begins to pull apart
images.caption: Geological evidence records the stretching and breakup of Rodinia. The arrangement of its landmasses remains uncertain.

images.subject: A late Tonian volcanic coast
images.caption: Volcanic rocks record major eruptions near the end of the Tonian. The Sturtian glaciation followed near the beginning of the Cryogenian.

images.subject: A coast before the great freeze
images.caption: The Sturtian glaciation began near the start of the Cryogenian, after the Tonian Period.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Ancient zircon crystals suggest liquid water and a solid crust existed by about 4.3 billion years ago. The extent and arrangement of early land are unknown.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Early continental blocks grew and collided during the Paleoproterozoic. Their arrangement and coastlines remain uncertain.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Continental blocks began to separate during Rodinia’s breakup. Their exact positions and coastlines remain uncertain.

images.subject: A view from the mountains
images.caption: Ancient zircon crystals suggest that Earth had a solid crust and liquid water by about 4.3 billion years ago. The extent and position of early land are unknown.

images.subject: A view from the mountains
images.caption: Rivers crossed Archean land, and fossil evidence shows microbial mats on river sediments about 3.22 billion years ago.

images.subject: A view from the mountains
images.caption: Glacial deposits record ice ages in the early Paleoproterozoic. The total extent of ice remains uncertain.

images.subject: A view from the mountains
images.caption: The Nonesuch Formation preserves sediments from an ancient lake within North America’s Midcontinent Rift.

images.subject: A view from the mountains
images.caption: Geological records show continental stretching and rifting during the breakup of Rodinia. The positions of its landmasses remain uncertain.

images.subject: Earth during the Sturtian
images.caption: Glacial deposits show ice reached low latitudes during the Sturtian. Whether sea ice covered the entire ocean remains debated.

images.subject: Above the Sturtian ice
images.caption: Glaciers reached low-latitude coasts during the Sturtian glaciation; the extent of sea ice remains uncertain.

images.subject: Ice reaches the coast
images.caption: Dated glacial deposits show that ice reached sea level near the tropics during the Sturtian glaciation.

images.subject: A possible refuge beneath the ice
images.caption: Microbes and algae survived the glaciations. Water beneath ice is one possible refuge, although the habitats and amount of light are uncertain.

images.subject: The Sturtian thaw
images.caption: The Sturtian glaciation ended around 660 million years ago, leaving evidence of a major transition from glacial conditions.

images.subject: The interval between glaciations
images.caption: A nonglacial interval separated the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations. Microbial life persisted through this period.

images.subject: The Marinoan glaciation
images.caption: The Marinoan was the second major Cryogenian glaciation. Its onset remains less securely dated than its end.

images.subject: The final thaw
images.caption: Carbonate layers above glacial deposits mark a major environmental transition at the end of the Marinoan glaciation.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Continental blocks were coming together to form Gondwana. Their exact positions and coastlines remain uncertain.

images.subject: Above the Gaskiers coast
images.caption: Glacial deposits in what is now Newfoundland record the Gaskiers ice age. The extent of ice beyond the regions with known deposits is uncertain.

images.subject: The microscopic world of Weng’an
images.caption: The Weng’an rocks of South China preserve tiny spheres with clusters of cells. Some resemble embryos, but their biological identity is disputed. This is a magnified view.

images.subject: A deep seafloor at Mistaken Point
images.caption: Frond-shaped rangeomorphs stood above the deep seafloor, while spindle-shaped Fractofusus lay along it. Beds of volcanic ash helped preserve these communities.

images.subject: Dickinsonia on a microbial mat
images.caption: Fossils preserve Dickinsonia’s flat, ribbed body. Lipids preserved with some specimens support its identification as one of the earliest known animals.

images.subject: Kimberella and its feeding traces
images.caption: Fan-shaped scratches found near Kimberella fossils suggest it scraped food from the seafloor. Chemical evidence also points to a diet that included algae and bacteria.

images.subject: A threefold body plan
images.caption: Three curving ridges distinguish Tribrachidium. Simulations of water flowing over its body suggest it may have captured suspended food.

images.subject: Small skeletons build a reef
images.caption: Reefs in Namibia’s Nama Group preserve small Cloudina tubes and cup-shaped Namacalathus. Many small skeletons helped build much larger reef structures.

images.subject: The last Ediacaran seas
images.caption: Fossils from Jiangchuan in what is now Yunnan preserve Ediacaran forms alongside bilaterian body fossils and traces of movement, shortly before the Cambrian.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Gondwana covered much of the Southern Hemisphere while Laurentia lay near the equator. The positions and coastlines of ancient continents are approximate.

images.subject: Above the Chengjiang delta
images.caption: Sediments in what is now Yunnan suggest the Chengjiang community lived in a delta where rivers delivered sediment to the sea.
Treptichnus pedum consists of linked probing burrows. Fossil traces preserve patterns of activity, but the identity of the animal that made them is uncertain.
Halkieria had a covering of small scales and a shell at each end.

size.name: Halkieria
size.note: Approximate; individuals varied.

images.subject: An archaeocyath reef
images.caption: Cup-shaped archaeocyath sponges and calcifying microbes built some of the earliest animal reefs. Their skeletons created shelter for other seafloor life.
Fish-like animals, trilobites and sponges are known from early Cambrian Chengjiang fossils.
Fossils of Kerygmachela from the early Cambrian Sirius Passet preserve lateral flaps, frontal appendages and a tail spine; colours and behaviour are uncertain.

size.name: Kerygmachela
size.note: Fossils preserve the body; total length is uncertain.

images.caption: Haikouichthys was a tiny early vertebrate from Chengjiang. A 2026 study interpreted two lateral eyes and two smaller eyes on top of the head; their appearance and soft tissues are uncertain.

size.name: Haikouichthys
size.note: Approximate; fossil individuals vary.

images.caption: Opabinia, Wiwaxia and Pikaia are known from Burgess Shale fossils. Pikaia has no known fossil evidence of eyes.

size.name: Opabinia
size.note: Fossil body lengths, excluding the proboscis.

images.caption: Burgess Shale fossils of Anomalocaris canadensis preserve its large eyes, grasping appendages and swimming flaps.

size.name: Anomalocaris canadensis
size.note: Isolated fragments suggest larger individuals, perhaps up to 1 m; that maximum is an estimate.

images.caption: Hallucigenia sparsa had seven pairs of defensive spines and soft legs. Burgess Shale fossils show an animal only a few centimetres long.
images.subject: Hallucigenia On Sponge

images.caption: Opabinia was a small animal with five eyes, a long grasping trunk and swimming flaps.
images.subject: Opabinia Seafloor

images.caption: Pikaia was a small, segmented early chordate known from the Burgess Shale; its anatomy remains debated.

images.subject: A late Cambrian shelf
images.caption: Trilobite fossils help date the early Furongian. Carbon isotope changes in marine rocks record a disruption to the carbon cycle around this time.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Gondwana extended toward the south pole while the Iapetus Ocean separated other continents. The positions and coastlines are approximate.

images.subject: Above the Taconic coast
images.caption: Collisions along Laurentia’s eastern margin raised mountains during the Taconic orogeny, an early chapter in Appalachian mountain building.
Early Ordovician Fezouata fossils record a diverse marine fauna, including filter-feeding radiodonts.
images.subject: Fezouata Biota Scene

images.caption: Aegirocassis was an Early Ordovician filter-feeding radiodont that grew more than two metres long, after the Cambrian.

size.name: Aegirocassis
size.note: Approximate body length reconstructed from fossil material.

images.subject: Early plants on land
images.caption: Microscopic spores provide evidence for small early land plants. Their exact appearance is uncertain. The inset shows a magnified cluster of four spores.

images.subject: Life on a shallow Ordovician shelf
images.caption: Diversification in Ordovician seas produced communities rich in brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids and corals. Straight-shelled cephalopods also lived in these seas.

images.subject: Ice reaches Gondwana’s coast
images.caption: Glacial deposits record ice reaching the margins of Gondwana during the Hirnantian. The advance and retreat of ice also affected sea levels far from the ice sheets.

images.subject: Survivors on the late Ordovician shelf
images.caption: The end-Ordovician extinction unfolded in two pulses. The organisms that survived and the severity of losses varied by habitat. The causes of each pulse remain debated.
Geologists in hard hats on the tilted rock layers at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, the world reference point for the start of the Cambrian.
Small shelly fossils from the earliest Cambrian of Shaanxi, China, seen under an electron microscope: tiny tubes and plates less than a millimetre long.
A fossil Anomalocaris eye preserved in pyrite, showing its honeycomb of tiny lenses.
Olenellus, an early Cambrian trilobite from Vermont, on display in the National Museum of Natural History, Paris.
images.note: Olenellus lived somewhat after the very first trilobites.

images.caption: The Maotianshan Shale near Chengjiang, Yunnan, where the Chengjiang fossils were found, now protected inside a museum building.
Retifacies, an arthropod from Chengjiang with a net-patterned armour, preserved in yellow mudstone.
A slab with Haikouichthys fossils, outlined and labelled in ink, at the Paleozoological Museum of China in Beijing.
A Burgess Shale fossil of Wiwaxia corrugata, an oval animal covered in overlapping scales with two rows of spines.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Gondwana covered much of the south while the Iapetus Ocean narrowed between Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia. The positions and coastlines are approximate.

images.subject: From a Caledonian mountaintop
images.caption: Continental collisions raised the Caledonian mountains as the Iapetus Ocean closed. Parts of the range survive in Scotland, Norway and Greenland.

images.subject: Early jawed fish in Chongqing
images.caption: The small armoured Xiushanosteus and the early shark relative Shenacanthus are known from unusually complete fossils in the same fossil beds in Chongqing, China.

size.name: Xiushanosteus
size.note: Shenacanthus measures about 2.2 cm from snout to anal fin in the fossil

images.subject: Cooksonia on wet ground
images.caption: Cooksonia stood only a few centimetres tall. Fossils preserve simple forked stems and spore capsules at their tips.

images.subject: Sollasina on the Herefordshire seabed
images.caption: Sollasina was a small relative of sea cucumbers. Its Herefordshire fossil preserves fleshy tube feet, which probably helped it move and feed.

size.name: Sollasina
size.note: About 3 cm across the fossil, including tube feet

images.subject: Gotland’s living reef
images.caption: Stromatoporoid sponges and ancient corals built reefs in the Silurian sea. Reef limestone survives in the cliffs and sea stacks of Gotland, Sweden.

images.subject: A bony fish in the Yunnan sea
images.caption: Guiyu was an early bony fish from what is now Yunnan, China. Its closely packed, diamond-shaped scales and parts of its bony armour are preserved in the fossil.

size.name: Guiyu
size.note: Estimated from a fossil missing the tail fin

images.subject: Sea scorpions in the shallows
images.caption: Eurypterus swam with broad paddles on its rear pair of limbs. Fossils from New York preserve the paddles, segmented body and straight tail spine.

size.name: Eurypterus remipes
size.note: Measured specimen PRI 70770

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Laurussia lay near the equator and Gondwana stretched far to the south. Shallow seas covered parts of the continental margins.

images.subject: Above the Old Red Sandstone rivers
images.caption: Rivers in what is now eastern Scotland deposited red sand and gravel. Those deposits are visible today in cliffs around Arbroath and Auchmithie.

images.subject: Rhynie hot-spring wetland
images.caption: Small plants such as Rhynia and Asteroxylon grew in a wetland around hot springs. Silica from the spring water preserved parts of this ecosystem in the Rhynie chert.

images.subject: Inside the Gilboa forest
images.caption: Fossil stumps and an attached crown show how Wattieza grew. Tall trunks carried crowns of forked branches above the damp forest floor.

images.subject: Along the Gogo barrier reef
images.caption: Fossils from the Gogo reef complex in Western Australia include armoured fish such as Mcnamaraspis and lobe-finned fish such as Gogonasus.

size.name: Mcnamaraspis
size.note: Measured fossil head

images.subject: A fish carrying young
images.caption: A Materpiscis fossil from Gogo preserves an embryo and its umbilical cord. It is direct evidence that some Devonian armoured fish gave birth to live young.
images.credit: AI-generated illustration. Anatomy reference by Kym Haines and Jon Augier, Museums Victoria (CC BY 4.0)

size.name: Materpiscis
size.note: Based on the fossil specimen

images.subject: A reef before the Kellwasser crisis
images.caption: Reef-building sponges and corals supported diverse seafloor communities before the Kellwasser extinction. This coastal reef sets the scene for the next picture.

images.subject: A reef after the Kellwasser crisis
images.caption: A reduced reef community after the Kellwasser extinction pulse. Trace fossils and sediment chemistry indicate low and variable oxygen in some seas.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Gondwana and Laurussia were joining to form Pangaea. Shallow seas covered parts of the continental margins, and ice reached parts of southern Gondwana.

images.subject: From a Variscan mountaintop
images.caption: The collision that brought Pangaea together raised the Variscan mountains. At low latitudes, river basins between uplands supported wetlands where peat accumulated.

images.subject: A sea-lily meadow
images.caption: Stalked sea lilies and blastoids filtered food from currents above the seafloor. Their fossils are abundant in the Burlington Limestone in what is now Iowa.

images.subject: Arthropleura on a sandy riverbank
images.caption: A fossil from Howick in northern England preserves part of the broad, segmented armour of an unusually large Arthropleura. The sediments and plant remains indicate a relatively open coastal environment.

size.name: Arthropleura
size.note: Estimated from the partial Howick fossil

images.subject: At the edge of Gondwana’s ice
images.caption: Sediments in western Argentina record repeated Carboniferous advances and retreats of ice. Rock fragments dropped from floating ice are one clue that glaciers reached this region.

images.subject: Inside the Joggins coal forest
