images.caption: The small early reptile Hylonomus lived among tall scale trees. At Joggins, Nova Scotia, bones of Hylonomus were found inside the remains of upright trees.

size.name: Hylonomus
size.note: Approximate size of the Joggins reptile

images.subject: The Tully monster in Mazon Creek waters
images.caption: Tullimonstrum had eyes on a crossbar and a long proboscis tipped with a small grasping mouth. Fossils from Illinois preserve both features. Its place on the animal family tree remains debated.

size.name: Tullimonstrum
size.note: Range estimated from fossil specimens

images.subject: Meganeura over a forest pool
images.caption: Meganeura was a giant griffinfly with four veined wings. Fossils from the coal basin at Commentry, France, preserve its wing shapes.

size.name: Meganeura
size.note: Estimate from the Commentry fossil

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Pangaea stretched from north to south around an arm of the Tethys Ocean. Panthalassa covered much of the rest of Earth.

images.subject: From a young Ural ridge
images.caption: Continental collision raised the Urals and folded rocks along the edge of Baltica. Erosion carried sediment from the growing mountains into the basin below.

images.subject: Two sail-backed animals at a Texas pool
images.caption: Dimetrodon, a predator, and Edaphosaurus, a plant eater, were early relatives of mammals. Fossils from the Texas red beds preserve the tall spines that supported their sails.

size.name: Dimetrodon
size.note: Approximate adult size. Length varies by species.

images.subject: Mesosaurs in the Mangrullo basin
images.caption: Long-snouted mesosaurs lived in a basin in what is now Uruguay. The basin gradually became more isolated from the open sea, and the salinity varied as water evaporated.

size.name: Mesosaurus
size.note: Typical length estimated from fossil specimens

images.subject: Tracks across the Coconino dunes
images.caption: Footprints crossed windblown sand in what is now Arizona. Layers of that sand became the Coconino Sandstone. The tracks preserve toe marks, but the animal that made them is uncertain.

images.subject: Helicoprion in the Phosphoria Sea
images.caption: CT scans of a fossil from Idaho show how the tooth spiral sat inside the lower jaw. Most of the animal’s body is unknown from fossils.
images.credit: AI-generated illustration. Jaw reference: Troll and Ramsay, figure 1(l) in Tapanila et al.

size.name: Helicoprion
size.note: Measured tooth whorl, specimen IMNH 37899

images.subject: Moschops on a Karoo floodplain
images.caption: Moschops was a broad-bodied plant eater with a thick skull roof. It lived in South Africa’s Karoo several million years before the sabre-toothed animals in the late Permian scenes.

size.name: Moschops
size.note: Measured adult skulls

images.subject: Scutosaurus and Inostrancevia at Sokolki
images.caption: The bulky, armoured plant eater Scutosaurus and the sabre-toothed predator Inostrancevia are known from the same Late Permian fossil assemblage in northern Russia.

size.name: Scutosaurus
size.note: Mass estimated from a large Scutosaurus skeleton. A nearly complete Inostrancevia skeleton is about 3 m long.

images.caption: The living Capitan Reef in what is now Texas, about 262 million years ago. Sponges, brachiopods and microbial communities contributed to a reef unlike most modern coral reefs. The reef stopped growing millions of years before the end-Permian extinction.
images.subject: The living Capitan Reef

images.caption: A view of Emeishan flood-basalt eruptions in what is now China, around 260 million years ago. These eruptions and the associated crisis came before the Siberian Traps and the end-Permian extinction.
images.subject: Lava floods the Emeishan region

images.caption: Diictodon, a small tusked plant-eating relative of mammals, beside a burrow in the Late Permian Karoo. Fossils found inside burrow casts show that these animals used underground shelters.

size.name: Diictodon
size.note: Body masses are estimates; individuals vary.

images.subject: Diictodon beside its burrow

images.caption: Rubidgea, a sabre-toothed predator from the Late Permian Karoo. Its heavily built fossil skull had few teeth behind the upper canines and none behind the lower canines; body form, covering and colour are uncertain.

size.name: Rubidgea
size.length: Body uncertain; skull up to 45 cm
size.note: Skull measurement; body size is reconstructed.

images.subject: Rubidgea in the late Permian Karoo

images.caption: A southern Permian forest of Glossopteris seed ferns beside a river. Fossil leaves and coal beds record these forests before their collapse around the end-Permian crisis.
images.subject: A Glossopteris forest beside a river

images.caption: Successive lava flows of the Siberian Traps, interpreted as a landscape around 252 million years ago. The appearance and timing of individual eruptions are not known; the flows accumulated over time.
images.subject: The Siberian Traps erupt

images.caption: Brachiopods and other marine animals lived on the Permian seafloor before the end-Permian extinction.
images.imageDateLabel: Just before the extinction, about 252 million years ago
images.subject: The Meishan seafloor before the extinction

images.caption: An ironstone nodule from Mazon Creek split in two to show both halves of a Tully monster, Tullimonstrum, in the Natural History Museum of Milan.
Fronds of the seed fern Neuropteris from a coal-mine spoil heap near Essex, Illinois, part of the Mazon Creek fossil beds.
images.note: On show at the Field Museum, Chicago.

images.caption: Fossil skeletons of two Diictodon that curled up together in an underground burrow, on show at the Iziko South African Museum.
images.note: Museum display; part of a label shows behind the block.

images.caption: Tongue-shaped Glossopteris leaves from the late Permian of Australia, from the trees whose forests collapsed at the end of the Permian.
images.note: Shown at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, Canada.

images.caption: A spiny productid brachiopod from Permian Texas; nearly all productid species vanished in the Great Dying.
images.note: From the Glass Mountains of Texas, about 270 million years old, not from Meishan.

images.caption: A cut slab of Siberian Traps basalt from Putorana glittering with metallic iron, formed when magma reacted with coal underground.
images.note: The link between the iron and coal is the usual explanation for such rocks, not stated on the file page.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Pangaea was still joined, with a vast interior and the Tethys Ocean at its eastern margin.

images.subject: Above a Chinle river plain
images.caption: Seasonal rivers crossed the Late Triassic lowlands of what is now the American Southwest. The Chinle Formation preserves floodplain sediments and fossil conifer wood.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: Pangaea was breaking apart. The young Atlantic opened between the continental blocks, and shallow seas flooded parts of their margins.

images.subject: Above a Morrison floodplain
images.caption: River channels and floodplains left layers of sediment across western North America. These rocks make up much of the Morrison Formation, which preserves many Late Jurassic dinosaurs.

images.subject: Triassic and Jurassic animals by size
images.caption: Compare 48 animals across three sections covering body lengths, wingspans and fossil measurements. Each section has its own size order. The full-size chart and fossil references are available from the source link.

images.subject: Triassic and Jurassic animals by size
images.caption: Compare 48 animals across three sections covering body lengths, wingspans and fossil measurements. Each section has its own size order. The full-size chart and fossil references are available from the source link.
A sparsely vegetated Early Triassic river plain after the extinction. Forest loss and erosion are recorded in rocks, but the landscape varied and some plants survived.

Lystrosaurus, a beaked and tusked plant-eating relative of mammals, on an Early Triassic river plain. Several species survived the extinction; their sizes varied and their life appearance is uncertain.

size.name: Lystrosaurus
size.note: Different published estimates; not a measured range.

images.caption: Cartorhynchus was a short-snouted marine reptile related to ichthyosaurs. The known fossil was probably a juvenile; its tail is incompletely known.

size.name: Cartorhynchus
size.note: Tail estimated; specimen was probably juvenile.

images.caption: Teleocrater was a long-necked four-legged predator from Middle Triassic Tanzania, related to dinosaurs but not itself a dinosaur. Its skull, hands, feet and tail are incompletely known.

size.name: Teleocrater
size.note: Estimates; measurements vary by individual.

images.caption: Asilisaurus, a four-legged dinosaur relative from Middle Triassic Tanzania. It was not itself a dinosaur; its skin and colouring are unknown.

size.name: Asilisaurus
size.note: Estimates; measurements vary by individual.

images.subject: Early dinosaurs in Ischigualasto
images.caption: Fossils from the Ischigualasto Formation in Argentina include the lightly built Eoraptor and the larger predatory Herrerasaurus.

size.name: Eoraptor
size.note: Length of the early fossil skeleton

images.subject: Plateosaurus in a river basin
images.caption: Late Triassic Plateosaurus was a long-necked early sauropodomorph. Its fossils are abundant at some Late Triassic sites in central Europe.

size.name: Plateosaurus
size.note: Estimated adult length; specimens vary

images.subject: An ichthyosaur and ammonite in a Jurassic sea
images.caption: Stenopterygius swam in Early Jurassic seas. Fossils preserve its streamlined body, just as ammonite shells preserve the shape of a very different swimmer.

size.name: Stenopterygius
size.note: Estimated total length

images.subject: Sauropods on the Morrison floodplain
images.caption: Long-necked sauropods and plated stegosaurs are known from the Morrison rocks of western North America. Diplodocus carried a very long tail, while Brachiosaurus stood higher at the shoulders.

size.name: Diplodocus
size.note: Estimated total length

images.subject: An early bird at a Jurassic lagoon
images.caption: Bavarian limestone preserves Archaeopteryx, an early bird with feathers, a long bony tail and teeth. Pterosaurs such as Rhamphorhynchus flew on membranes supported by an elongated finger.

size.name: Archaeopteryx
size.note: Estimated total length

images.caption: A cast of the Asilisaurus skeleton, rebuilt from at least 14 individuals found together in one Tanzanian bone bed, at the Field Museum in Chicago.
Two Plateosaurus skeletons dug from the clay pit at Trossingen, Germany, on display at the University of Tübingen.
images.note: Old mounts: the right-hand skeleton is posed on all fours, but Plateosaurus is now generally seen as walking on its hind legs. The species was then called P. engelhardti; the Trossingen animals are now P. trossingensis.

images.caption: A three-toed Eubrontes footprint from Early Jurassic rocks at Rocky Hill, Connecticut, left by a large meat-eating dinosaur.
images.note: No bones have been found with these tracks, so the exact maker is unknown.

images.caption: A fossil of Anchiornis from Liaoning with long feathers fanning out from its arms and legs.
A replica of the London specimen of Archaeopteryx, the first skeleton found (1861), with feather impressions on the wings and the long bony tail.
images.note: This is a cast at the Karlsruhe natural history museum; the original is in the Natural History Museum, London.

images.caption: A mounted skeleton of Lystrosaurus murrayi in the Natural History Museum in Paris.
images.note: Museum display behind glass.

images.caption: A nearly complete skeleton of the early ichthyosaur Chaohusaurus from Chaohu, about 248 million years old.
images.note: Scientific photograph with scale bars; the large bars are 10 centimetres.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: The Western Interior Seaway split North America into eastern and western landmasses. The Paleocene globe uses the same viewpoint, so the change in coastline is easy to see.

images.subject: Above an Arctic dinosaur floodplain
images.caption: From a ridge above the ancient North Slope of Alaska, channels wind through a wooded polar floodplain. Pachyrhinosaurus had a thick boss on its nose. Fossils of very young dinosaurs show that several groups nested at these latitudes.

images.caption: Eleven featured animals, from Patagotitan to a flower-visiting beetle. Body lengths, wingspans and fossil measurements each have their own size order. Open the full-size chart and fossil references from the source link.

images.subject: Feathers at a Jehol lakeshore
images.caption: Fossils from the Jehol Biota of northeastern China preserve the simple feathers and banded tail of Sinosauropteryx. Some Confuciusornis fossils preserve a pair of long tail feathers. This early bird was about 30 cm long by one museum estimate.

size.note: Approximate total length, including the tail

images.subject: At the feet of Patagotitan
images.caption: Bones from several Patagotitan individuals were buried in floodplain deposits in Patagonia. The skeleton gives an estimate of its length. Weight estimates depend on how the body is modeled.

size.note: Natural History Museum estimates

images.subject: A beetle among flowers
images.caption: Amber from northern Myanmar preserves Angimordella alongside flowering-plant pollen. Its exact role in pollination is debated, and the flower here represents a possible encounter.

size.name: Angimordella
size.note: Measured body length of the amber specimen

images.subject: Below the Western Interior Seaway
images.caption: Tylosaurus swam in the shallow sea that covered the interior of North America. Ammonites such as Placenticeras shared these waters. Their shells fossilize far more readily than their soft bodies.

images.caption: Quetzalcoatlus fossils come from ancient river and floodplain deposits at Big Bend, Texas. The giant species Q. northropi is known from fragmentary remains, and its span is estimated using related fossils.

images.caption: Triceratops crosses the river, Edmontosaurus moves along the far bank, and Tyrannosaurus watches from the trees. Fossils of all three are known from the Hell Creek Formation.

images.caption: The asteroid struck a shallow sea near present-day Yucatán. Drill cores record impact melt, broken rock and sediments that accumulated on the first day. The Paleocene gallery picks up with recovery.

images.caption: Waimanu fossils come from marine sediments in what is now New Zealand. Its skeleton shows early adaptations for swimming underwater with its wings.

images.caption: Fossils from western Colorado preserve the heavy limbs and large tail of Barylambda. Its exact body mass depends on which fossil and scaling method are used.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: A warm early Eocene Earth, viewed over the Indian Ocean. India was approaching southern Asia, and the Southern Ocean and Antarctica can be compared with the Oligocene globe from the same viewpoint.
images.credit: PALEOMAP PaleoDEMs · C. R. Scotese and N. M. Wright

images.subject: Above an Arctic forest
images.caption: Look down over the rivers and wooded wetlands of what is now Ellesmere Island. Fossils show that a warm temperate forest ecosystem reached high Arctic latitudes even under a polar light cycle.

images.subject: Eocene animals by size
images.caption: Eight featured animals, from a giant whale to a winged ant. Each group has its own size order. Open the source link for measurements and references.

images.subject: A tiny horse in a warming world
images.caption: At the start of the Eocene, small early horses lived in Wyoming's Bighorn Basin. Fossil teeth indicate that their average body mass fell during peak warming in the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum.

images.subject: A walking whale enters the water
images.caption: Ambulocetus lived in and around shallow coastal waters in what is now Pakistan. Its strong limbs and large hind feet help explain how this early whale could move on land and swim.

size.note: Approximate reconstructed total length

images.subject: Life around Messel Lake
images.caption: Darwinius moves through the forest above the ancient volcanic lake. The Messel deposits also preserve the early owl Masillastrix, whose stomach contents and wing anatomy suggest daytime activity. The described juvenile owl was about 12 cm long.

images.subject: A giant ant at forest-floor level
images.caption: The Messel shales preserve giant winged ants. Titanomyrma queens were several centimetres long, and their preserved wings show why they rank among the largest known ants.

size.name: Titanomyrma
size.note: Approximate body length of a large Messel queen

images.subject: Uintatherium at the water's edge
images.caption: Uintatherium was a heavy plant-eating mammal. Its skull carried six bony knobs and long upper canine teeth. Fossils from the Bridgerian of western North America preserve those distinctive features.

size.name: Uintatherium
size.note: A described fossil upper canine was about 30 cm long.

images.subject: The Valley of Whales underwater
images.caption: Basilosaurus and the smaller Dorudon lived in the shallow sea that once covered Wadi Al-Hitan, Egypt. Both whales retained tiny hind limbs. Dorudon was about 5 m long.

images.caption: Antarctica now carried a major ice sheet. The globe uses the Eocene camera angle. Paleogeographic data guide the shorelines, and ice shading shows an approximate continental extent.

images.subject: Above ancient Oregon
images.caption: Wooded hills and lakes cover the John Day Basin. Leaf fossils from Bridge Creek record cool-temperate deciduous trees and conifers as climates changed near the start of the Oligocene.

images.subject: Oligocene animals by size
images.caption: Nine featured animals, including a giant hornless rhino, an early anthropoid and a fossil dragonfly. Measurements are grouped by type, with specimen notes and sources available from the source link.

images.subject: An Antarctic glacier reaches the sea
images.caption: Growing Antarctic ice changed sea level and ocean circulation near the Eocene–Oligocene boundary. Marine sediments record the cooling and growth of continental ice. The shape of any one glacier is uncertain.

images.subject: Life on the White River floodplain
images.caption: Three-toed Mesohippus moves past the sheep-sized oreodont Merycoidodon. Hoplophoneus, a saber-toothed nimravid, crouches in cover. Fossils of these mammals are known from the White River deposits.

size.name: Mesohippus

images.subject: A river and canopy in the Fayum
images.caption: Fayum deposits in Egypt preserve the large two-horned Arsinoitherium and the early anthropoid Aegyptopithecus. This regional scene draws on fossils from different horizons. Aegyptopithecus is estimated to have weighed roughly 5–8 kg.

size.name: Arsinoitherium
size.note: Approximate adult shoulder height

images.subject: Beneath a giant hornless rhino
images.caption: A skull and lower jaw from the Linxia Basin in China establish the size and distinctive head of Paraceratherium linxiaense. The rest of the portrait draws on fossils of related giant rhinos.

size.name: Paraceratherium
size.note: Measured basal length of the type skull: 1.148 m.

images.subject: A giant penguin dives
images.caption: Long flippers and a pointed bill distinguish Kairuku, an early penguin from Zealandia. Several skeletons preserve how it was built for diving.

size.name: Kairuku
size.note: Estimated relaxed standing height

images.subject: An early toothed mysticete
images.caption: The Oregon skull of Aetiocetus weltoni preserves teeth. It belongs to an early branch on the baleen-whale side of the cetacean family tree. The fossil evidence leaves its feeding method open to interpretation.

size.name: Aetiocetus

images.caption: Fine deposits in a German crater lake preserved dragonfly wings. The measured Epiaeschna wisseri hindwing anchors the size label. The body and colours draw on related dragonflies.

size.name: Epiaeschna
size.note: Measured length of one fossil hindwing: 58.1 mm.

images.subject: Rivers below the rising Alps
images.caption: As the Alps rose and eroded, braided rivers carried gravel north and built broad fans in the basin now occupied by the Swiss Plateau. Geologists call those deposits the Molasse. The Pleistocene gallery returns to this landscape from a matching viewpoint to show the effects of ice.

images.subject: The valley before the modern Rhine
images.caption: The crust stretched and a long basin subsided between faulted shoulders in what is now the Upper Rhine Valley. Sediments record changing water environments in the rift. The modern Rhine drainage developed later.

images.subject: Earth from space
images.caption: From above the Americas, the Andes trace the western edge of South America. The following scenes move down to mountain fronts and river basins where sediment preserves evidence of landscape change.

images.subject: Above the Andean foothills and Amazon wetlands
images.caption: The rising Andes shed sediment into the lowlands of western Amazonia. Broad wetlands and changing channels formed part of a drainage system that developed in stages.

images.subject: The Amazon begins to drain east
images.caption: Marine sediments near the mouth of the Amazon carry minerals from the Andes. One study dates the onset of a transcontinental river to about 9.4–9 million years ago. The arrows show general drainage directions. The timing of the full connection remains debated.
images.credit: PALEOMAP relief and Hoorn et al. sediment evidence

images.subject: The Amazon reaches the Atlantic
images.caption: The Amazon pouring brown, sediment-laden water into the Atlantic, photographed from the International Space Station in 2018. Sediments laid down off this coast carry minerals from the Andes: one study dates the start of a river right across the continent to about 9.4 to 9 million years ago.
images.note: The dating is from Hoorn et al. 2017, Global and Planetary Change; when the river fully connected across South America is still debated.

images.subject: Himalayan rivers build the Bengal Fan
images.caption: Rivers carried sediment from the Himalayas into the foreland and on toward the Bay of Bengal. Sediment cores from the Bengal Fan record Himalayan erosion and changes in weathering. River courses continued to reorganize after the Miocene.

images.subject: Lava fills parts of the Columbia basin
images.caption: Lava poured from fissures in repeated eruptions and spread across parts of the inland Pacific Northwest. The layered basalt later became the bedrock through which Pleistocene floods cut channels and coulees.

images.subject: Three-toed horses in changing grasslands
images.caption: Horse teeth from the Great Plains record different diets as warm-season grasses expanded. Grazers, mixed feeders and browsers occupied a patchwork of open country and woodland. Several horse lineages still had three toes.

images.subject: Sahelanthropus beside an ancient lake
images.caption: Fossils from Chad preserve the skull and teeth of Sahelanthropus, a candidate for an early member of the human lineage. The lakeside scene places it in a wooded setting. How it moved and where it belongs on the family tree are still debated.

size.name: Sahelanthropus
size.note: Estimated space inside the fossil skull: 360–370 cm³.

images.subject: Earth from space as the ice retreats
images.caption: Ice still covered much of northern Canada near the end of the Pleistocene. Lower sea level exposed parts of the continental shelves. The globe combines dated ice outlines with a simplified coastline based on the lower sea level.
images.credit: PALEOMAP PaleoDEMs · NADI-1 · DATED-1 · Lambeck et al.

images.subject: Ice carves the Alpine valleys
images.caption: Alpine valley glaciers widened and deepened valleys as they advanced onto the Swiss foreland. The scene matches the Oligocene Alpine viewpoint for comparison. Local glacier advances and retreats occurred at different times.

images.subject: Meltwater gathers in the Great Lakes basins
images.caption: Repeated glaciations deepened older basins. As the Laurentide ice sheet retreated, meltwater collected against the ice margin and drained through changing outlets. Lake levels and shorelines continued to shift after the Pleistocene.

images.subject: Ice Age floods cut through Columbia basalt
images.caption: When the ice dam of Glacial Lake Missoula failed, repeated floods crossed the Columbia basin. They scoured the much older Miocene basalt and left channels, coulees and giant gravel bars. The scene returns to the Miocene basin from a matching viewpoint.

images.subject: Woolly mammoths cross the Beringian steppe
images.caption: Much of Beringia remained ice-free during the last glacial maximum. Short grasses and other plants supported woolly mammoths. Small ears and thick hair helped them live in cold, dry conditions.

size.note: Approximate adult shoulder height

images.subject: Diprotodon beside an Australian salt lake
images.caption: Lake Callabonna in South Australia preserves remains of Diprotodon. Its huge body belonged to a plant-eating marsupial. This lakeshore scene pairs with the existing skeleton photograph in Evidence.

size.name: Diprotodon
size.note: Approximate dimensions for large individuals

images.subject: Early Homo in the southern Caucasus
images.caption: Fossils and stone tools from Dmanisi, Georgia, document an early presence of Homo in Eurasia. The landscape gives a regional setting for movement. The fossil site does not record the exact route the population took.

images.subject: Homo erectus in the Turkana Basin
images.caption: The Turkana Boy skeleton from Kenya preserves much of the body of an early Homo erectus. Its long legs help show how body proportions had changed. The riverbank depicts a setting in the wider Turkana Basin.

images.subject: Early Homo sapiens in North Africa
images.caption: Fossils and dated sediments from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, provide early evidence of our species. The finds help show that human origins involved populations across Africa. The scene depicts everyday movement through that landscape.

images.subject: Neanderthals in a Eurasian river valley
images.caption: Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia through changing climates. For part of their history they overlapped with Homo sapiens. Ancient DNA shows that some populations interbred. A skull photograph is available in Evidence.

images.subject: Humans of the genus Homo
images.caption: Compare 12 Homo groups on a shared timeline and map of fossil sites. The poster marks individual finds, fossil date ranges and cases where ancient DNA confirms interbreeding.

images.subject: Skulls of our relatives
images.caption: Casts of the skulls of human relatives, arranged as a family tree at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. Several kinds of Homo lived through the Pleistocene, some at the same time; today only our own species remains.

images.subject: Humans of the genus Homo
images.caption: A jaw from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, puts early Homo in the late Pliocene about 2.8 million years ago. The poster follows the fossil record from that find through later Homo groups to the present.

stories.title: The Cambrian explosion
stories.summary: Between about 580 and 485 million years ago, life in the sea went from soft fronds and quilted mats to animals with shells, legs, eyes and backbones. Step through the fossil sites, from Newfoundland to the Burgess Shale and Morocco, that show how and when it happened, and why scientists still argue over the cause.

chapters.title: A warmer world after the ice
chapters.place: Gaskiers, St. Mary's Bay, Newfoundland, Canada
chapters.text: The Earth had come through two great freezes, the Sturtian and the Marinoan, when ice may have reached the tropics; the second ended 635 million years ago. One last, shorter ice age, the Gaskiers, left boulders dropped by melting ice in rocks at Gaskiers in Newfoundland, about 580 million years ago. It lasted only a few hundred thousand years and probably did not cover the whole planet. Meltwater rich in nutrients and a slow rise in oxygen may have helped larger living things to evolve, though how closely the ice and life are linked is debated. Within about ten million years the first large, complex organisms appear, in rocks just above the Gaskiers deposits.
species: Early sponges (known only from chemical traces)

sites.name: Gaskiers glacial deposits
sites.note: Thick beds of rubble and dropstones laid down by the short Gaskiers ice age.

chapters.evidenceNote: Boulders scratched by ice and dropped into sea-floor mud are dated by uranium-lead measurements to between about 579.9 and 579.6 million years ago.

chapters.title: Fronds on a deep sea floor
chapters.place: Mistaken Point, Avalon Peninsula, Newfoundland, Canada
chapters.text: On a dark sea floor, too deep for sunlight, stood feathery fronds and lay spindle-shaped Fractofusus, among the oldest large and complex living things known. Many were rangeomorphs, built from branches that repeat the shape of the whole, like a fern. With no mouth or gut, they may have soaked up food dissolved in the water, though some scientists think they filtered it. Falls of volcanic ash buried whole communities where they stood, and one ash layer is about 565 million years old. Mistaken Point became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

sites.name: Mistaken Point Ecological Reserve
sites.note: Whole sea-floor communities preserved under volcanic ash.

chapters.evidenceNote: The creatures left impressions in the sea floor where volcanic ash buried them, and crystals in the ash give their age.

Feathery frond fossils on a rock surface at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, with a coin for scale.

chapters.title: The first proven animals
chapters.place: Winter Coast of the White Sea, Arkhangelsk region, Russia
chapters.text: In shallow seas over what is now northern Russia, creatures lived on carpets of microbes covering the sea floor. Kimberella, up to 15 centimetres long, had a front and a back and seems to have scraped food from the mats, leaving fan-shaped scratch marks; many think it was a relative of the molluscs, though not all agree. Dickinsonia, a flat ribbed oval up to 1.4 metres long, left rows of resting marks where it fed. In 2018 Ilya Bobrovskiy and colleagues, working on ropes down cliffs 60 to 100 metres high, found that Dickinsonia fossils still hold cholesterol, a fat made by animals. That made Dickinsonia, about 558 million years old, the oldest animal confirmed by chemistry.

sites.name: Zimnie Gory cliffs, White Sea
sites.note: Volcanic ash between the fossil beds is dated to 555.3 million years; older beds hold Dickinsonia and Kimberella.

chapters.evidenceNote: Body impressions and feeding traces lie in sandstone dated by volcanic ash, and molecules extracted from the fossils show animal cholesterol, though a few scientists doubt that the cholesterol came from Dickinsonia itself.

chapters.title: The puzzle of the Ediacara Hills
chapters.place: Ediacara Hills, Nilpena Ediacara National Park, South Australia
chapters.text: The richest Ediacaran communities lived on shallow sandy sea floors like this one, where Reg Sprigg noticed fossils in 1946; the whole Ediacaran Period is named after these hills. Among quilted Dickinsonia and fronds lived Spriggina, with a shield-like head and a segmented body, and Ikaria, a worm the size of a grain of rice with a front, a back and probably a gut. Ikaria, named in 2020, is the likely maker of tiny burrows in the same rocks and one of the oldest known bilaterians, the group that includes worms, insects and us. What most Ediacaran creatures were is still argued: early animals, giant single cells, lichens, or a lost branch of life with no living relatives. Most of them disappear near the start of the Cambrian.

sites.name: Ediacara Hills (Nilpena Ediacara National Park)
sites.note: Where Reg Sprigg found the first fossils in 1946; whole fossil sea floors are exposed in the park.

chapters.evidenceNote: The fossils are clear impressions in sandstone, but their biology is argued over: many scientists see Dickinsonia, Kimberella and Ikaria as animals, while others have proposed giant single cells, lichens (Greg Retallack) or a separate extinct group (Adolf Seilacher's Vendobionta) for many of the quilted forms.

chapters.title: The first shells, and the first drills
chapters.text: Near the end of the Ediacaran, some animals in shallow seas began to build hard skeletons. Cloudina, first found in the Nama Group of Namibia, made tubes of chalky cones stacked inside one another, a few millimetres wide, like a pile of paper cups. It has since been found from Namibia and Oman to China, Spain, Brazil and Nevada. In some places up to a fifth of Cloudina tubes have small round holes bored through them, among the earliest signs of a predator attacking prey. Armour and attack had begun their long race.

sites.name: Nama Group, Zaris Formation (central Namibia)
sites.note: Cloudina occurs in the Zaris Formation, where a volcanic ash bed is dated to about 547 million years.

chapters.evidenceNote: The chalky tubes are preserved in limestones dated by volcanic ash layers in the Nama Group to about 550 to 539 million years ago; what kind of animal built them is uncertain.

chapters.title: Burrows mark the Cambrian's start
chapters.place: Fortune Head, Burin Peninsula, Newfoundland, Canada
chapters.text: Rocks at Fortune Head mark the official start of the Cambrian Period, 538.8 million years ago. The marker is not a body but a burrow, Treptichnus pedum: a chain of short tunnels dug just under the sea floor by a worm-like animal probing for food. Earlier creatures had mostly lain or crawled on the surface; now animals were digging down and stirring the mud, breaking up the microbial mats that Ediacaran life depended on. Geologists later found Treptichnus a few metres below the official boundary, so the marker is not perfect, but the change it records is real.

sites.name: Fortune Head boundary section
sites.note: The global reference point (golden spike) for the base of the Cambrian.

chapters.title: A burst of new body plans
chapters.place: Meishucun, Jinning, near Kunming, Yunnan, China
chapters.text: In the first ten million years of the Cambrian, seas around the world filled with small shelly fossils: caps, tubes, spines and plates, many only a few millimetres long, from early molluscs, sponges, brachiopods and armoured animals whose soft bodies are rarely found. At Meishucun in Yunnan they appear and quickly become abundant in phosphate-rich rocks. Within about 13 to 25 million years most of the main animal body plans alive today had appeared. Why then? Scientists point to more oxygen, the first predators and an arms race of armour, new genes that control how bodies are built, and animals reshaping the sea floor for one another; many now think several of these worked together, and a 2019 study led by Rachel Wood argued that the burst came in pulses that began in the Ediacaran.

sites.name: Meishucun section, Jinning
sites.note: Phosphate rocks where small shelly fossils suddenly become abundant; once a candidate for the base of the Cambrian.

chapters.evidenceNote: That many animal groups appear quickly in the fossil record is clear; why it happened, and whether it was one burst or several pulses (Wood and colleagues, 2019) with roots deep in the Ediacaran as gene clocks suggest, is still debated.

chapters.title: Eyes, hunters and armour
chapters.text: About 521 million years ago trilobites appear, almost at once, in Siberia, North America, Morocco and Spain. They were arthropods with jointed armour hardened with minerals, and most had compound eyes. Eyes changed life in the sea: hunters could find prey from a distance, and prey needed shells, spines and places to hide. The top hunters were radiodonts such as Anomalocaris, swimmers with a pair of spiny grasping arms in front of the mouth; fossil eyes from Kangaroo Island in Australia, about 513 million years old, some with at least 16,000 lenses, rivalling the sharpest eyes of living arthropods. Whether eyes actually set off the Cambrian explosion, as Andrew Parker's 'light switch' idea proposes, many scientists doubt.

chapters.title: Windows into an early Cambrian sea
chapters.text: At Maotianshan near Chengjiang, fine mud buried a whole early Cambrian sea floor so fast that legs, guts, gills and eyes survive. First recognised in 1984, it had yielded about 185 described species by 2006: radiodonts, trilobites with their legs and antennae, sponges, worms, spiny lobopodians and some of the first chordates. At Sirius Passet in far northern Greenland, rocks of about the same age hold a similar mix, including gilled relatives of the arthropods. In 2019 a third window opened, the Qingjiang biota on the Danshui River in Hubei, where more than half of the 101 kinds first described were new to science, among them many jellyfish and comb jellies. Together they show that busy food webs were already in place early in the Cambrian.

chapters.title: The first animals with backbones
chapters.text: Among the Chengjiang fossils near Haikou are small fish-shaped animals: Haikouichthys, about 2.5 centimetres long, and Myllokunmingia, both described in 1999. They had a head, gills, fins, a stiffening rod along the back and zigzag blocks of muscle, the body plan of every later backboned animal, from sharks to people. More than 500 specimens of Haikouichthys are known. In 2026 a study reported that these first vertebrates had four camera-like eyes, two at the sides and two smaller ones on top of the head, which may have become the light-sensing pineal organ of later animals. Whether Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia are two species or one is still argued.

chapters.title: The strange animals of the Burgess Shale
chapters.place: Burgess Shale, Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada
chapters.text: High in the Canadian Rockies, mud flows buried animals on a sea floor about 508 million years ago and kept their soft bodies as dark films. Charles Walcott found the site in 1909 and collected over 65,000 specimens; later studies by Harry Whittington and his students showed how strange many were. Opabinia had five eyes and a long trunk ending in a claw; Hallucigenia, a spiny worm on legs, was long drawn upside down and back to front; scale-covered Wiwaxia was probably a relative of the molluscs; and Pikaia, up to about 5 centimetres long, is one of the earliest known chordates. In 2012 scientists found a rich new site at Marble Canyon in Kootenay National Park, 42 kilometres away, and collected 50 animal species there in just 15 days.

chapters.title: Epilogue: the survivors of Fezouata
chapters.place: Fezouata Shale, north of Zagora, Draa Valley, Morocco
chapters.text: For a long time the strange Burgess Shale animals seemed to vanish after the middle of the Cambrian. Then, in the late 1990s, the local collector Mohamed Ben Moula showed scientists soft-bodied fossils from the hills north of Zagora in Morocco, in rocks from early in the Ordovician Period; the richest beds are about 480 million years old. They hold Burgess Shale-type animals, including Aegirocassis, a radiodont about two metres long that sieved plankton instead of hunting. Their survival suggests that much of the apparent disappearance came from a lack of rocks that preserve soft bodies, not only from extinction. Here the Cambrian explosion runs on into the next great rise in the number of species, the Great Ordovician Biodiversification.

stories.title: How the dinosaurs evolved
stories.summary: From small survivors of the Great Dying 252 million years ago, dinosaurs rose to rule the land for more than 130 million years, growing into giants and evolving feathers and flight. An asteroid ended their reign 66 million years ago, but one branch, the birds, lives on.

chapters.title: Survivors of the Great Dying
chapters.place: Karoo Basin near Graaff-Reinet, South Africa
chapters.text: About 252 million years ago the worst mass extinction known wiped out about 81 percent of species in the sea and 70 percent of land vertebrate species. In the Karoo of South Africa the rocks laid down just afterwards are crowded with Lystrosaurus, a tusked plant-eater that was one of the few survivors. Alongside it lived Proterosuchus, a sprawling, crocodile-shaped hunter up to about 3.5 metres long. Proterosuchus was one of the earliest archosauriforms, the wider group that would later produce crocodiles, pterosaurs and dinosaurs. Life on land took millions of years to recover, leaving room for new kinds of animals.

chapters.evidenceNote: Layer after layer of Karoo river mud records which animals lived before and after the extinction, and the layers just above it are dominated by survivors such as Lystrosaurus.

chapters.title: The first dinosaur cousins
chapters.text: Within a few million years of the extinction the archosaurs had split into two lines: one leading to crocodiles, the other to pterosaurs, dinosaurs and birds. Some of the oldest known members of the bird line come from the Manda Beds of Tanzania. Teleocrater, 2 to 3 metres long, was a long-necked meat-eater that still walked on four crocodile-like legs, while Asilisaurus was a slender four-legged cousin of the dinosaurs with leaf-shaped teeth and a beak-like lower jaw. Nyasasaurus, known only from an upper arm bone and a few backbones, may be the earliest dinosaur of all or a very close relative. Small footprints from Poland suggest that dinosaur relatives were already walking about 250 million years ago, though not everyone agrees who made them.

chapters.title: The first dinosaurs
chapters.place: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, San Juan, Argentina
chapters.text: The oldest dinosaurs that nearly everyone accepts come from Brazil and Argentina and are about 233 to 231 million years old, from during or soon after a spell of very wet climate called the Carnian Pluvial Episode. In Argentina's 'Valley of the Moon', Herrerasaurus was the commonest meat-eater, and Eoraptor was a lightly built dinosaur weighing about 10 kilograms. The main dinosaur lines had already split: Eoraptor is now usually placed near the start of the long-necked sauropod line, and Eodromaeus near the start of the theropods. They shared the land with many rhynchosaurs such as Hyperodapedon and mammal relatives such as Exaeretodon.

chapters.title: Dinosaurs spread across Pangaea
chapters.text: With all the continents still joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea, dinosaurs could spread almost anywhere on land. Between about 214 and 204 million years ago Plateosaurus, a long-necked plant-eater 5 to 10 metres long that walked on its hind legs, lived in large numbers in what is now Germany, Switzerland and France. Clay pits at Trossingen and Frick have yielded many complete skeletons, probably of animals that sank into soft mud and were trapped. In North America a quarry at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, yielded many skeletons of the small, fast hunter Coelophysis. Yet in many places crocodile-line reptiles and phytosaurs were still the commonest large animals.

chapters.title: Rivals vanish, dinosaurs take over
chapters.text: About 201 million years ago, as Pangaea began to tear apart, huge volcanic eruptions of the Central Atlantic magmatic province set off one of the five great mass extinctions. On land the phytosaurs and nearly all the crocodile-line reptiles died out, except small crocodile relatives, while dinosaurs, pterosaurs and mammals came through. In the rift valleys of eastern North America, footprints show large meat-eating dinosaurs appearing less than 10,000 years after the boundary. Big three-toed tracks called Eubrontes, 25 to 50 centimetres long, are common in Early Jurassic rocks such as those at Rocky Hill, Connecticut. From then on, dinosaurs were the main large land animals for the next 135 million years.

chapters.title: Feathered dinosaurs before the first bird
chapters.text: Lake beds in north-east China, laid down about 160 million years ago, preserve small dinosaurs with their feathers in astonishing detail. Anchiornis, a small relative of birds known from hundreds of specimens, had long feathers on its arms, legs and feet, giving it four wings. Tiny pigment grains in its fossil feathers show it was grey and dark with white, black-tipped wing feathers and a reddish crest. Anchiornis lived about 10 million years before Archaeopteryx, proving that bird-like feathered dinosaurs already existed before the famous 'first bird'. Whether Anchiornis itself counts as a bird depends on where scientists draw a line that is genuinely blurred.

chapters.title: Giants of the Late Jurassic
chapters.text: By the Late Jurassic dinosaurs had become giants. The Morrison Formation, river and floodplain rocks spread over 1.5 million square kilometres of the western United States, holds long-necked sauropods such as Diplodocus, about 26 metres long, as well as Brachiosaurus, Apatosaurus and Camarasaurus, the commonest of them. The plated Stegosaurus browsed nearer the ground, and meat-eaters such as Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus hunted them all. Strikingly similar animals, including the giant sauropod Giraffatitan, lived at the same time at Tendaguru in Tanzania.

chapters.title: Archaeopteryx, the famous in-between animal
chapters.text: In 1861, just two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species, a fossil feather and then a skeleton of Archaeopteryx were found in Bavarian limestone laid down in warm lagoons about 150 million years ago. It was about half a metre long with broad feathered wings, but it also had sharp teeth, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail, like a small meat-eating dinosaur. It soon became key evidence that birds evolved from reptiles, and fourteen fossil skeletons, some very incomplete, are now known. Whether it could flap and fly well or mostly glided is still debated.

chapters.title: Feathers, flowers and early birds
chapters.text: About 125 million years ago, volcanic ash repeatedly fell into the lakes of north-east China, burying animals and plants so gently that feathers, skin and even colour patterns survive. Sinosauropteryx, described in 1996, was the first dinosaur outside the birds and their closest relatives found with feathers: a coat of simple filaments, with a banded tail. Several hundred complete skeletons of Confuciusornis, a crow-sized bird with a toothless beak, show that true birds were now common. The same rocks hold Archaefructus, one of the oldest known flowering plants, an early sign of the plants that would come to dominate the land.

chapters.title: Titans on a splitting supercontinent
chapters.text: During the Cretaceous the southern continents drifted apart, and South America's dinosaurs went their own way. Titanosaurs, the most varied group of long-necked sauropods, included the largest land animals known. Patagotitan, known from at least six young adults found on a ranch near La Flecha in rocks about 101.6 million years old, was first estimated at 37 metres and 69 tonnes; later work suggests nearer 31 metres and 50 to 60 tonnes. Most of the giants, including Argentinosaurus from near Plaza Huincul, belonged to one group of titanosaurs found only in Patagonia.

chapters.title: Horned and duck-billed dinosaurs flourish
chapters.text: The main fossil beds of Dinosaur Provincial Park were laid down by rivers on a coastal plain beside an inland sea, about 76.5 to 74.4 million years ago, and 58 dinosaur species have been found there. Horned dinosaurs such as Centrosaurus and Styracosaurus and crested duck-bills such as Corythosaurus and Lambeosaurus lived alongside armoured ankylosaurs and tyrannosaurs. Different groups of species replace each other up through the rock layers, showing how quickly the plant-eating fauna changed. Some studies argue that dinosaurs overall were already producing new species too slowly by this time, but the horned and duck-billed dinosaurs were still multiplying fast.

sites.note: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979 for its badlands and fossils.

chapters.evidenceNote: The bone beds are well dated, but whether dinosaur diversity was already falling is disputed: Sakamoto and colleagues (2016) found a long decline, while Bonsor and colleagues (2020) found no strong sign of one.

chapters.title: Tyrannosaurus and the last dinosaurs
chapters.place: Hell Creek, near Jordan, Montana, USA
chapters.text: The river and swamp deposits of the Hell Creek Formation preserve some of the very last non-bird dinosaurs. Tyrannosaurus rex, about 12 metres long and weighing 5 to 7 tonnes, was the giant predator. It shared the land with Triceratops, the duck-bill Edmontosaurus, dome-headed pachycephalosaurs and armoured ankylosaurs, as well as crocodiles, turtles, lizards and small mammals. The climate was mild, with palm trees. Just above the formation lies the thin boundary layer rich in iridium, a metal rare in Earth's crust but more common in asteroids, which marks the end of the dinosaur age.

sites.name: Hell Creek Formation near Jordan, Montana
sites.note: The formation is named after exposures along Hell Creek near this town.

chapters.evidenceNote: Argon dating of volcanic ash in these rocks ties the boundary layer, and the extinction, to the Chicxulub impact within 32,000 years.

chapters.title: The asteroid strikes
chapters.text: About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 kilometres across hit the sea where Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula is now, blasting a crater about 200 kilometres wide that lies buried under about a kilometre of younger rock. Its debris forms a thin layer found all over the world, and dating ties the impact to the extinction within 32,000 years. Darkness and cold followed, halting the growth of plants and plankton, and about three quarters of plant and animal species died out, including all non-bird dinosaurs and all pterosaurs. Huge volcanic eruptions in India, the Deccan Traps, were also under way at the time; most researchers see the impact as the main cause.

sites.note: The buried crater, found in oil-company surveys in 1978 and identified in 1991.

sites.name: Deccan Traps, Western Ghats
sites.note: Thick lava flows in western India that erupted across the time of the extinction.

chapters.evidenceNote: A single layer of impact debris marks the extinction worldwide, and most studies (Schulte and colleagues 2010; Chiarenza and colleagues 2020) find the impact enough to explain it, while others argue the Deccan eruptions played a large part.

chapters.title: The dinosaurs that survived: birds
chapters.dateLabel: c. 66 million years ago and after
chapters.text: One branch of the dinosaurs made it through: the birds. A skull found in a quarry near Maastricht, about 66.7 million years old, belongs to Asteriornis, nicknamed the 'wonderchicken', a small, long-legged bird that probably lived near the shore, with features of both landfowl and waterfowl. It lived alongside toothed birds such as Ichthyornis relatives, which all died out. The impact destroyed forests across the world, and the birds that survived were probably small ground-dwellers with a varied diet. Every living bird descends from those few survivors, so dinosaurs are still all around us.

stories.title: The Great Dying and the recovery
stories.summary: About 252 million years ago eruptions in Siberia triggered the worst extinction in Earth's history, wiping out most life in the sea and much of it on land. This story follows the world before the disaster, the killing itself, and the slow recovery that ended with the first dinosaurs.

chapters.title: A Permian reef in Texas
chapters.place: El Capitan, Guadalupe Mountains, Texas, USA
chapters.text: Pangaea, the single supercontinent, stretched from pole to pole, and warm shallow seas lapped its edges. One of them, the Delaware Sea of today's Texas and New Mexico, was ringed by a great reef built mostly by lime-making algae, microbes, sponges and tiny colonial animals called bryozoans, not by corals as today. Around 260 million years ago falling sea level cut the sea off from the ocean, it dried out, and salt and mud buried the reef. Lifted by faults in the last 20 million years, the reef now stands as the cliff of El Capitan, and Carlsbad Caverns are carved into the same rock.

sites.note: The thousand-foot cliff of El Capitan is made of Capitan Reef limestone.

chapters.evidenceNote: The reef limestone, its fossils and the salt layers that buried it can be traced through the Guadalupe Mountains, the world reference section for the Middle Permian.

chapters.title: Lava in China, a first crisis
chapters.text: Around 260 million years ago lava flooded what is now south-west China, building the Emeishan Traps, named after Mount Emei. They still cover more than 250,000 square kilometres, though far smaller than the Siberian eruptions to come. At about the same time a crisis struck: big single-celled fusulinids, corals and tropical reefs collapsed in the sea, and in South Africa's Karoo the giant plant-eating and meat-eating dinocephalians vanished. How big this end-Capitanian extinction was is disputed: some count it among the great mass extinctions, others see a smaller or more local event.

chapters.title: Sabre-teeth and tusks in the Karoo
chapters.place: Karoo Basin near Graaff-Reinet, South Africa
chapters.text: In the last part of the Permian, rivers wound across the Karoo in the far south of Pangaea, lined by forests of Glossopteris, a seed-bearing tree with tongue-shaped leaves that grew across the southern continents. The commonest large animals were dicynodonts, beaked plant-eaters with two tusks, from burrowing Diictodon to much bigger kinds. They were hunted by gorgonopsians, sabre-toothed relatives of mammals up to about 3.5 metres long, such as Rubidgea and later Inostrancevia. Layer after layer of Karoo mud preserves this world right up to its end.

sites.name: Karoo Basin, Beaufort Group rocks
sites.note: River muds up to 6 kilometres thick hold one of the richest records of Permian land animals.

chapters.evidenceNote: Skeletons buried in river muds of the Beaufort Group, dated by volcanic ash layers, record the animals and plants of the late Permian.

chapters.title: Siberia bursts into flame
chapters.text: About 300,000 years before the great extinction, lava began to pour out across Siberia. Roughly two-thirds of all the Siberian Traps erupted in about 300,000 years, and their lavas still cover about 2.5 million square kilometres of Siberia, with more buried under younger rocks to the west. Just as important, sheets of magma pushed sideways underground through a basin full of coal, limestone and salt. Baking these rocks released enormous amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases, including chlorine compounds that can harm the ozone layer.

sites.note: Stacked lava flows form the step-like cliffs of this remote plateau.

chapters.evidenceNote: Uranium-lead dates on crystals from the lavas and the underground magma sheets match the age of the extinction.

chapters.title: The Great Dying at Meishan
chapters.text: In a quarry at Meishan in eastern China, limestone full of fossils gives way within a few beds to rock where most of them are gone. Ash layers dated with great precision show that the main extinction began about 251.94 million years ago and was over within about 60,000 years, a blink in geological time. Just before it, the chemistry of carbon in the sea lurched, a sign of huge amounts of carbon entering the air. Meishan is the world's reference point for the start of the Triassic, marked by the first appearance of the tiny conodont Hindeodus parvus.

chapters.title: Forests fall and the coal stops
chapters.place: Frazer Beach, Sydney Basin, New South Wales, Australia
chapters.text: On the coast near Sydney the last Permian coal seam is capped by grey lake mud: the Glossopteris forests that made the coal died out here a few hundred thousand years before the extinction in the sea. Worldwide about 81 percent of marine species and about 70 percent of land vertebrate species were lost. It was also the greatest known extinction of insects, and perhaps the only one that cut their diversity deeply. No coal at all is known from the earliest Triassic anywhere: peat-forming swamp forests took millions of years to return.

chapters.evidenceNote: Fossil pollen and spores in rock layers dated by zircon crystals show the Glossopteris flora vanishing from the Sydney Basin before about 252.1 to 252.3 million years ago.

chapters.title: Too hot, too acid, too breathless
chapters.place: Nanpanjiang Basin, Guizhou and Guangxi, China
chapters.text: Oxygen in the tiny teeth of conodonts from south China works like a thermometer, and it suggests tropical seas warmed to around 40 degrees Celsius, with peaks that came and went for millions of years. Warmer water holds less oxygen while animals need more, and models suggest this alone explains over half of the losses in the sea. Shell chemistry also points to a sharp drop in ocean pH as the extinction began. How much each of these mattered, and whether the acid was global, is still disputed; ozone loss, acid rain and mercury poisoning may have added to the toll on land.

sites.note: About 15,000 conodonts from rocks here were used to track Early Triassic sea temperatures.

chapters.evidenceNote: Oxygen isotopes in conodont teeth and boron isotopes in brachiopod shells record heat and acid, but how severe and how widespread each was is argued over.

chapters.title: Lystrosaurus inherits the Earth
chapters.text: On land one survivor stood out: Lystrosaurus, a stocky dicynodont with a beak and two tusks, most kinds half a metre to a metre long. For a while about 95 percent of the backboned land animals in South Africa's earliest Triassic rocks were Lystrosaurus, something no other land animal has ever matched. Its bones turn up in South Africa, India, China and Russia, and in 1969 to 1970 Edwin Colbert's team found them at Coalsack Bluff in Antarctica, strong evidence that these lands were once joined. Growth marks in Antarctic tusks suggest it could slow down through the dark polar winters, a lifestyle that may have helped it survive.

chapters.title: A slow and patchy recovery
chapters.place: Paris Canyon, Bear Lake County, Idaho, USA
chapters.text: For millions of years many seas were dominated by a few hardy survivors, such as the thin-shelled clam Claraia, and recovery kept stalling as new heat spikes and a further extinction about 249 million years ago struck. Yet some places bounced back early. Near Guiyang in south China a full food web of fish, shrimp and ammonoids was living about 250.8 million years ago, only a million years after the extinction, though some researchers doubt it lasted. At Paris in Idaho, rocks about 249 million years old hold sponges, ammonoids, fish and early squid relatives. Small reefs built by animals came back after a few million years, but corals of the modern kind appeared only in the Middle Triassic, about ten million years after the Great Dying.

chapters.title: Reptiles go back to sea
chapters.text: Within a few million years reptiles had taken to the emptied seas. At Chaohu in eastern China, rocks about 248 million years old hold Chaohusaurus, a metre-long early ichthyosaur, including a mother with babies, one apparently being born head first. Beside it lived Cartorhynchus, about 40 centimetres long with flipper-like limbs and a short snout, a close cousin of the ichthyosaurs that may still have crawled onto land. Tail bones from Spitsbergen about 250 million years old show ichthyosaurs already at sea, and their finders suggest the group began even before the extinction.

chapters.title: Ruling reptiles and dinosaur cousins
chapters.text: As the land recovered, the archosaurs, the 'ruling reptiles' that include crocodiles and dinosaurs, spread fast; sail-backed Ctenosauriscus lived in Germany about 247 million years ago. The Manda Beds of Tanzania show how early the dinosaur line split off. They hold Teleocrater, one of the oldest known reptiles on the bird and dinosaur side of the family, Asilisaurus, a slender silesaurid one to three metres long and close cousin of the dinosaurs, and Nyasasaurus, perhaps the earliest dinosaur of all. These rocks are usually dated to about 245 million years ago, but some scientists argue they are millions of years younger.

chapters.title: Rain falls and dinosaurs spread
chapters.text: About 234 million years ago huge eruptions in what is now western North America warmed the planet, and for one to two million years the dry Triassic world turned rainy. Marine life suffered again, but on land the old plant-eaters such as most dicynodonts and rhynchosaurs declined. In the Dolomites, footprints show no dinosaurs before the rains, about 40 percent dinosaur tracks near their end, and over 90 percent in the layers above. The oldest well-dated dinosaur skeletons, in Brazil and at Ischigualasto in Argentina, come from just this time: 20 million years after the Great Dying, the age of dinosaurs was beginning.

stories.title: How humans evolved
stories.summary: From the first apes that may have walked upright about 7 million years ago to the end of the last Ice Age, this story follows the fossils, footprints, tools and DNA that show how our family tree grew and branched. Many kinds of humans lived at the same time, met and sometimes mixed, until our own species was the only one left.

chapters.title: The first upright apes?
chapters.text: DNA suggests that our line and the line leading to chimpanzees parted somewhere between about 13 and 5 million years ago. The oldest fossil that may belong on our side is Toumaï, a skull found in the Djurab Desert of Chad in 2001 and dated to about 7 million years ago. The hole where its spinal cord left the skull sits further forward than in apes, a hint that it held its head over an upright body. Orrorin from Kenya, about 6 million years old, and Ardipithecus from Ethiopia, 5.6 to 4.4 million years old, also seem to have walked upright on the ground while still climbing trees. Toumaï's brain was slightly smaller than a chimpanzee's.

chapters.title: Lucy's kind walks upright
chapters.text: About 3.66 million years ago, at Laetoli in Tanzania, upright walkers left trails of footprints in wet volcanic ash that soon hardened. Found by Mary Leakey's team in the 1970s, they are widely accepted as the oldest footprints made by a creature walking on two legs. They were most likely made by Australopithecus afarensis, the species of Lucy, a skeleton found at Hadar in Ethiopia in 1974 and about 3.2 million years old. Lucy's kind had brains not much bigger than a chimpanzee's and long arms with curved fingers for climbing, but hips and legs built for walking. A second trail at Laetoli, cleaned and studied again in 2019, has a different shape, so two kinds of upright walkers may have shared the area.

chapters.title: The first stone tools
chapters.place: Lomekwi, west shore of Lake Turkana, Kenya
chapters.text: In 2011, on the west shore of Lake Turkana in Kenya, a team led by Sonia Harmand found stone cores, flakes and heavy anvils in layers dated to about 3.3 million years ago. That is about half a million years older than the oldest fossils of our own genus, so the toolmakers may have been Australopithecus or Kenyanthropus, whose fossils come from the same area. Some archaeologists doubt the date, arguing that the tools could have been washed down a slope from younger layers. The oldest tools of the Oldowan kind, sharp flakes struck from pebbles with a hammerstone, come from Nyayanga in western Kenya, about 2.9 million years old. They lay among butchered hippo bones and teeth of Paranthropus, a big-toothed cousin of ours.

chapters.title: The first of our genus, Homo
chapters.text: In 2013 Chalachew Seyoum found half a lower jaw at Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, lying in silts dated by volcanic ash to about 2.8 million years ago. Its shape leans towards Homo, making it the oldest known fossil of our genus. Teeth reported from the same area in 2025 show that early Homo and a new, still unnamed kind of Australopithecus lived there side by side between about 2.8 and 2.6 million years ago. Nearby, at Bokol Dora, toolmakers struck sharp-edged Oldowan tools between 2.61 and 2.58 million years ago. Later came Homo habilis, the 'handy man', named in 1964 from fossils found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania from 1960 on.

chapters.title: Homo erectus: a body like ours
chapters.place: Drimolen cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa
chapters.text: A small child's skull, rebuilt from more than 150 fragments dug from Drimolen cave near Johannesburg, is the oldest known fossil of Homo erectus, about 2 million years old. The same cave held the skull of Paranthropus robustus, so Homo, Paranthropus and Australopithecus all lived in South Africa at the same time. Homo erectus had long legs and shorter arms, a body like ours made for walking long distances on open ground. By about 1.76 million years ago, toolmakers at Kokiselei in Kenya were shaping hand-axes, and finds from Melka Kunture in Ethiopia, reported in 2023, push the first ones back to about 1.95 million years. The Turkana Boy, a nearly complete skeleton from Nariokotome in Kenya, about 1.5 to 1.6 million years old, was already about 1.5 metres tall when he died as a child.

chapters.title: The first humans leave Africa
chapters.text: By about 1.8 million years ago, humans had reached Dmanisi in Georgia, in the hills between the Black Sea and the Caspian. Five skulls and more than 10,000 simple stone tools have been found there, dated by volcanic rock and magnetic signals to between 1.85 and 1.77 million years ago. The Dmanisi people had small brains, 546 to 775 cubic centimetres, and are usually counted as an early form of Homo erectus. One old man had lost all but one tooth years before he died, so others may have helped him to eat. Stone tools from Shangchen in China are even older, about 2.1 million years, so the first journeys out of Africa may have begun earlier still.

chapters.title: Homo erectus reaches Java and China
chapters.text: Homo erectus reached Java by about 1.3 million years ago, and no earlier than 1.5 million. That date for the Sangiran fossil beds comes from tiny volcanic crystals in the layers above, below and among the bones, and it replaced older estimates of up to 1.7 million years. On the way east, hand-axe makers had reached Attirampakkam in southern India by about 1.5 million years ago. In northern China, the oldest 'Peking Man' fossils from Zhoukoudian near Beijing are about 770,000 years old; the original bones were lost in 1941. Homo erectus lived on in Asia for a very long time, perhaps until about 110,000 years ago.

chapters.title: Early Europeans and the Neanderthal line
chapters.text: Humans were in Spain by 1.4 to 1.1 million years ago: part of a face from Sima del Elefante, in the Atapuerca hills, is the oldest human face yet found in western Europe. Nearby at Gran Dolina, Homo antecessor lived about 900,000 to 800,000 years ago. In a deep pit in the same hills, Sima de los Huesos, lie the bones of at least 28 people, about 430,000 years old. Their faces already have Neanderthal features, and DNA from their bones shows they belonged to the Neanderthal line. Further north, the Mauer jaw from Germany, about 609,000 years old, gave its name to Homo heidelbergensis.

chapters.title: Our species appears in Africa
chapters.text: Skulls, jaws and teeth from Jebel Irhoud, an old cave in Morocco, are the oldest known fossils of our own species, Homo sapiens, about 315,000 years old. They were dated using flint tools found with them that had been heated in fires. Their faces look like ours, but their braincases were longer and lower, so the modern head shape came together only gradually. The Omo I skull from Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, at least 233,000 years old, looks fully modern. Together the finds suggest that our species took shape across Africa, not in one spot.

chapters.title: Many kinds of humans at once
chapters.place: Rising Star cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa
chapters.text: Deep inside the Rising Star cave system near Johannesburg, excavations from 2013 recovered the bones of at least 15 individuals of a new species, Homo naledi. They lived between about 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, yet had a mix of old and new features: shoulders and hips like Australopithecus, hands and feet more like ours. The Kabwe skull from Zambia, about 299,000 years old, belongs to yet another group, often called Homo heidelbergensis. So Africa held at least three kinds of humans at the same time, early Homo sapiens among them, while Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo erectus lived in Europe and Asia. The team that found Homo naledi argues that it buried its dead on purpose, but other scientists say the evidence does not show this.

chapters.title: Denisovans: humans found by DNA
chapters.text: In 2010, DNA from a young girl's tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed a kind of human that nobody had known about: the Denisovans. They were close relatives of the Neanderthals, and another girl from the cave, nicknamed Denny, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Denisovan DNA in the cave's layers goes back about 217,000 years. A jaw from a cave high on the Tibetan Plateau, at least 160,000 years old, and a nearly complete skull from Harbin in China, at least 146,000 years old, have been identified as Denisovan from ancient proteins and DNA, at last giving them a face. Denisovans also had children with our species: up to about 5 percent of the DNA of some people in New Guinea, Australia and the Philippines comes from them.

chapters.title: Small humans on the islands
chapters.text: In 2003, in Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores in Indonesia, scientists found the skeleton of a tiny adult, about 1 metre tall with a brain of about 380 cubic centimetres. The species, Homo floresiensis, lived there between about 100,000 and 60,000 years ago. Jaws, teeth and an arm bone from Mata Menge on the same island show that very small humans were on Flores by about 700,000 years ago. In 2019 another small species, Homo luzonensis, was named from bones and teeth in Callao Cave in the Philippines, found in a layer about 67,000 years old. Whether these island people came from Homo erectus that shrank over time, or from an older and smaller kind of human, is still argued.

chapters.title: Across the sea to Sahul
chapters.place: Madjedbebe rock shelter, Arnhem Land, Australia
chapters.text: Our species spread out of Africa and along southern Asia to Sahul, the single landmass that joined Australia and New Guinea when the sea was low. Even then, reaching it meant crossing stretches of open sea between the islands of Wallacea. At Madjedbebe, a rock shelter in northern Australia, stone tools, grinding stones and ground ochre lie in layers dated to about 65,000 years ago by measuring light-sensitive signals in sand grains. Other researchers argue that this dating is unreliable and that people arrived closer to 50,000 years ago. A 2025 study of mitochondrial DNA from living people supports arrival about 60,000 years ago, although many geneticists favour the later date.

chapters.title: Meeting and mixing with Neanderthals
chapters.text: As our species spread into Europe and western Asia, it met the Neanderthals, who had lived there for hundreds of thousands of years. Bones from a cave at Ranis in Germany, about 45,000 years old, are among the oldest Homo sapiens in Europe, and their DNA carries Neanderthal pieces from a mixing that happened about 45,000 to 49,000 years ago. Genomes of more than 300 ancient and living people show that most of this mixing happened in one long period between about 50,500 and 43,500 years ago. A person from Peștera cu Oase in Romania, who lived 37,000 to 42,000 years ago, had a Neanderthal ancestor only four to six generations back. Today people in Europe and Asia carry about 1 to 3 percent Neanderthal DNA.

chapters.title: The last Neanderthals
chapters.text: Careful radiocarbon dating of 40 sites from Russia to Spain shows that the Neanderthals' way of making stone tools ended across Europe by about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago. They had shared Europe with incoming modern humans for several thousand years (2,600 to 5,400 by a 2014 estimate, at least 5,000 by a 2025 one), and disappeared at different times in different places. At Gorham's Cave in Gibraltar, researchers argued in 2006 that Neanderthals survived until about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago. But when other late sites in southern Spain were re-dated with cleaner methods they turned out at least 10,000 years older, so most researchers now doubt such late survival. The Neanderthals themselves are gone, but pieces of their DNA live on in most people today.

chapters.title: Into the Americas as the ice melts
chapters.place: Blackwater Draw, near Clovis, New Mexico, USA
chapters.text: Most researchers think that during the last Ice Age people from north-east Siberia crossed Beringia, a land bridge exposed by the low sea, into the Americas. When they first arrived is fiercely argued. Human footprints at White Sands in New Mexico are dated to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago; critics questioned the first radiocarbon dates, but pollen and luminescence dates published in 2023 agreed with them. Monte Verde in Chile, long accepted at about 14,500 years old, was argued in 2026 to be no older than about 8,200 years, a claim its excavators reject. By about 13,000 years ago the Clovis people, named after finds near the town of Clovis in New Mexico, were hunting mammoths across North America, and, as far as the evidence shows, ours was the only kind of human left on Earth.

stories.title: Life moves onto land
stories.summary: Between about 470 and 300 million years ago the bare continents were taken over, first by tiny plants and millipedes, then by forests, four-legged animals, flying insects and the first egg-layers on dry land. This story follows that conquest from the earliest spores to the collapse of the great coal rainforests.

chapters.title: First spores on a bare land
chapters.text: For most of Earth's history the land was bare rock, sand and mud, with no more life on it than thin films and crusts of microbes; fossils from lake beds a billion years old show such life on land. Plants grew out of green algae that lived in fresh water. The first sign of them is their spores: tiny grains with tough walls, about 470 million years old, found in rocks in Argentina and, about ten million years later, in Saudi Arabia and Czechia. The plants that shed them were probably small and low, and their bodies do not turn up as fossils for another 40 million years.

chapters.title: Cooksonia, the first plants with pipes
chapters.text: Cooksonia was a plant only a few centimetres tall: a bare stalk that forked a few times, with no leaves and no roots, each branch tipped with a little capsule of spores. In at least one kind a dark strand runs up the middle of the stem, the earliest known tissue for carrying water. Water pipes like these would later let plants grow tall. Some of the oldest Cooksonia come from Ireland and Wales, where tiny zircon crystals dated in 2024 show the rocks are no older than about 426 to 427 million years; a Cooksonia from Czechia may be about 432 million years old.

chapters.title: Millipedes and scorpions creep ashore
chapters.place: Isle of Kerrera, near Oban, Scotland
chapters.text: Animals followed the plants onto land. Kampecaris, a small millipede from old lake beds on the Scottish island of Kerrera, about 425 million years old, is one of the oldest land animals known and may have fed on rotting plants, as most millipedes do today. A younger millipede from Stonehaven, Pneumodesmus, about 414 million years old, has breathing holes along its body, so it must have breathed air. Scorpions were around even earlier: Dolichophonus, from the Pentland Hills near Edinburgh and 436 to 428 million years old, is the oldest scorpion known, though nobody can yet say whether it lived on land or in water.

chapters.title: A whole world frozen in stone
chapters.text: Near Rhynie in Scotland, hot springs rich in silica flooded a marshy plain and turned its life to stone where it stood, down to single cells. The plants, such as Rhynia and Aglaophyton, were leafless green stems, and inside them are the oldest known mycorrhizal fungi, the partner fungi that live in plant roots to this day. Mites, springtails, harvestmen and spider-like trigonotarbids lived among the stems. Rising a metre or more above everything else was Prototaxites, a trunk-like column long thought to be a giant fungus; a 2026 study argued that it was neither fungus nor plant but a lost branch of life.

chapters.evidenceNote: Silica from the springs filled the cells before they could rot, so thin slices of the chert show plants, fungi and animals under the microscope; only Prototaxites' place in the tree of life is still argued over.

chapters.title: The first forests rise
chapters.place: Sea cliffs near Minehead, Somerset, England
chapters.text: In 2024 scientists described fossil tree trunks, fallen branches and roots in sandstone cliffs on the Somerset coast, about 390 million years old: the oldest forest yet found. Its trees, Calamophyton, looked a little like tree ferns, with a crown of twigs on a slender trunk up to about 4 metres tall, and the branches they shed littered the forest floor. A few million years later forests at Cairo and Gilboa in New York State held Wattieza trees 8 metres or more tall and Archaeopteris, whose extensive, spreading roots were much like those of modern trees. Roots broke up rock and carried carbon deeper into the soil, and as forests spread, carbon dioxide in the air fell steeply.

chapters.title: A fish with a neck and wrists
chapters.text: Shallow streams in what is now Arctic Canada, then close to the equator, were home to Tiktaalik, a fish up to about 2.7 metres long. It had scales, fins and gills, but also a neck, strong bones like a wrist inside its front fins and probably simple lungs, so it could prop itself up in shallow water. Found in 2004, it shows the body of four-legged animals taking shape inside a fish. It was a cousin of the first four-legged animals rather than their ancestor: footprints in a Polish quarry, about 390 million years old, suggest that animals with legs were already walking more than ten million years earlier, though some experts think fish made the marks.

chapters.title: Crisis in the Devonian seas
chapters.text: About 372 million years ago, and again about 359, the seas ran short of oxygen and black, lifeless mud settled on the sea floor. The first crisis, named after the Kellwasser valley in Germany, wiped out the great reefs built by corals and sponge-like stromatoporoids and perhaps 40 percent of sea species; the second ended the armoured placoderm fishes. One idea blames the new forests: deep roots broke up rock, rivers carried the freed nutrients to the sea, and blooms of algae used up the oxygen. Tiktaalik's kind, the fish with necks and wrists, died out, while the true four-legged animals came through.
