chapters.title: Many-toed legs in Greenland
chapters.text: After the crisis four-legged animals spread. In the mountains of East Greenland, in rocks about 365 million years old, lie Acanthostega, about 60 cm long with eight webbed fingers on each hand and gills like a fish, and Ichthyostega, about 1.5 metres long with seven toes on each hind foot. Acanthostega probably spent nearly all its life in shallow, weedy water, which suggests that legs with toes first evolved for water, not for walking. Ichthyostega could drag itself over flat ground on its strong front legs, moving more like a seal than a salamander.

chapters.title: Seeds free plants from water
chapters.text: Spore plants have a weak spot: their sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg, which ties them to damp ground. Seed plants got round it. The oldest known seeds, about 365 million years old from West Virginia, belong to Elkinsia, whose young seeds sat in small cup-shaped cases. A seed wraps a baby plant and its food in a coat that keeps it from drying out, so it can wait for rain before it sprouts, and pollen carries the sperm through the air. Seed plants could now grow on dry slopes where spore plants failed, and their descendants dominate the land today.

sites.note: Young seeds of Elkinsia, the oldest known seed plant.

chapters.evidenceNote: Seeds with their cup-like cases are preserved in Late Devonian rocks; Runcaria from Belgium, about 385 million years old, shows an earlier, not yet fully wrapped stage.

chapters.title: Insects become the first flyers
chapters.place: Bitterfeld and Delitzsch, Saxony-Anhalt and Saxony, Germany
chapters.text: Insects were the first animals to fly. The oldest fossils of winged insects are about 328 to 324 million years old, and they already come in several kinds, so flight probably began earlier. One of the oldest, Delitzschala from eastern Germany, had wings spanning just 2.5 cm, still showing their spots. By the end of the Carboniferous, griffinflies such as Meganeura from France had wings spanning about 70 cm, among the largest flying insects ever. A popular idea is that oxygen-rich air let them grow so big, but some recent studies doubt the link.

chapters.evidenceNote: Wings are the toughest part of an insect and are pressed into the rock with their veins; gene-based estimates put the start of flight much earlier, near 400 million years ago, but no such fossils are known.

chapters.title: Eggs for dry land at Joggins
chapters.place: Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Nova Scotia, Canada
chapters.text: At Joggins in Nova Scotia, sea cliffs cut through a coal forest of giant clubmoss trees up to 30 metres tall. Inside their hollow fossil stumps lie small animals that seem to have fallen in and been trapped, among them Hylonomus, a lizard-like animal about 20 to 25 cm long that probably ate millipedes and early insects. It was long called the oldest reptile. Reptiles, mammals and their kin, the amniotes, lay eggs with a shell and inner bags of fluid that keep the young from drying out, so they could breed far from water. A 2025 study placed Hylonomus just outside the amniotes, so who laid the first such eggs is an open question again.

sites.note: Fossil tree stumps holding early four-legged animals.

chapters.evidenceNote: Hylonomus's bones are well known, but whether it was a true amniote is argued over, and 350-million-year-old clawed footprints from Australia, claimed in 2025 as amniote tracks, may have been made by other animals.

chapters.title: A coal-swamp shore in ironstone
chapters.place: Mazon Creek, near Morris, Illinois, USA
chapters.text: By now swamp forests of giant clubmosses, ferns, horsetails and seed ferns covered the warm lowlands, and their buried remains became the coal that gave the Carboniferous its name. At Mazon Creek in Illinois, plants and animals that washed into a muddy bay about 309 million years ago were quickly sealed inside ironstone nodules. Split open, the nodules show more than 400 kinds of plants and over 320 kinds of animals: insects, the giant millipede relative Arthropleura, early four-legged animals and the strange Tully monster. Few places show so fully what lived in and around a coal forest.

sites.name: Mazon Creek and the Braidwood strip mines
sites.note: Ironstone nodules from the Francis Creek Shale.

chapters.evidenceNote: Bacteria rotting the buried bodies made the iron mineral siderite, which cast them in hard nodules, often with their soft parts.

chapters.title: The coal rainforests break apart
chapters.place: Former Riola and Vermilion Grove coal mines, near Danville, Illinois, USA
chapters.text: In coal mines near Danville, Illinois, miners and geologists found a whole fossil forest of giant clubmosses, tree ferns, seed ferns and horsetails spread over about 1,000 hectares, drowned when the ground dropped below sea level. Not long afterwards, around 305 million years ago, a short, sharp ice age dried and cooled the tropics, and the great rainforests broke up into patches. The giant clubmoss trees almost vanished and tree ferns took over. Many amphibians died out, while amniotes, with their shelled eggs, coped better with the drier world, and among them were the first synapsids, the line that would one day lead to mammals.

stories.title: The age of mammals
stories.summary: Mammals spent their first 140 million years small and in the shadow of the dinosaurs, then came through the asteroid strike 66 million years ago and spread into the empty world. In the ages that followed they took to the trees, the sea and the grasslands, crossed between continents and grew into the giants of the ice ages, most of which vanished in the last 50,000 years.

chapters.title: Small mammals in a dinosaur world
chapters.text: Mammals appeared at almost the same time as the dinosaurs: shrew-sized Morganucodon, about 205 million years old, is usually counted among the first. For the next 140 million years most mammals stayed small and were probably active mainly at night. Yet they were more varied than once thought: by about 160 million years ago there were swimmers like the beaver-tailed Castorocauda, as well as gliders and diggers. About 125 million years ago, in what is now Liaoning, the opossum-sized Repenomamus even ate young dinosaurs, and one fossil shows it locked in combat with a Psittacosaurus when a volcanic mudflow buried them both.

chapters.title: Mammals rebound after the asteroid
chapters.place: Corral Bluffs, near Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA
chapters.text: The asteroid that struck 66 million years ago wiped out about 93 percent of the mammal species known from western North America; the survivors were mostly common animals no bigger than a cat. Within about 140,000 years rat-sized Purgatorius, an early relative of the primates, was climbing trees in Montana. At Corral Bluffs, mammal skulls found inside egg-shaped stones show how fast the recovery went: mammal diversity doubled within about 100,000 years, and by 300,000 years pig-sized plant-eaters such as Carsioptychus lived in palm forests. By about 700,000 years, when the first bean pods appear, there were wolf-sized Eoconodon and Taeniolabis, a plant-eater of 34 to 56 kilograms, a hundred times heavier than the survivors.

chapters.title: A hothouse brings primates and horses
chapters.text: About 56 million years ago a huge release of carbon warmed the world by about 5 to 8 °C in less than 20,000 years, an episode called the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum. In this heat the first primates of modern type appear on all three northern continents, along with the earliest horses and some of the earliest even-toed hoofed animals, such as the deer-like Diacodexis. The tiny primate Teilhardina seems to have spread from Asia through Europe to North America in about 25,000 years. In Wyoming's Bighorn Basin the first horse, Sifrhippus, shrank by about 30 percent, to about 4 kilograms, as temperatures peaked and grew again as the climate cooled; about a third of mammal species there became smaller.

chapters.title: Windows on Eocene forests
chapters.place: Messel Pit, near Darmstadt, Hesse, Germany
chapters.text: In the warm Eocene, lakes in Wyoming and Germany buried animals whole in fine mud. Fossil Lake in Wyoming, about 52.5 million years old, holds Onychonycteris, one of the oldest bats known from complete skeletons; it had claws on all five fingers and may have flown before bats could hunt by echolocation. The Messel Pit, a volcanic crater lake about 47 million years old, preserves early bats, small early horses, including a mare with her unborn foal, and the primate Darwinius, with the outline of her fur and the remains of her last meal of fruit and leaves. Why so many animals died in the lake is debated: volcanic gases and poisonous algae have both been suggested.

chapters.title: Whales walk back into the sea
chapters.text: Whales descend from land mammals: their closest living relatives are hippos, and early whales share the double-pulley ankle bone of even-toed hoofed animals. About 49 million years ago in what is now Pakistan, wolf-sized Pakicetus lived in and around water on four legs but already had the ear bones of a whale. A little later Ambulocetus swam like an otter in coastal waters, and Maiacetus, found with a fetus lying head first, may still have given birth on land. By about 40 million years ago Basilosaurus, up to about 18 metres long, and the smaller Dorudon swam in the sea that covered Egypt's Wadi Al-Hitan, keeping only tiny hind legs.

chapters.title: Grasslands and the grazers
chapters.place: Ashfall Fossil Beds, Antelope County, Nebraska, USA
chapters.text: As the world cooled and dried, open grassland spread: tiny silica bodies from grasses show grass-dominated country on the Great Plains between about 26 and 22 million years ago. Grass is tough and gritty, and horses evolved high-crowned teeth to grind it; Merychippus, which appeared about 16 million years ago, is the first horse known to have grazed. About 12 million years ago ash from a huge eruption in what is now south-western Idaho, nearly 1,450 kilometres away, fell on a Nebraska waterhole. More than 100 barrel-bodied rhinos, along with three-toed horses, camels and birds, died there over days and weeks, and fossil grass seeds are still lodged between the rhinos' teeth.

sites.note: A waterhole buried in volcanic ash, with over 200 complete skeletons, found in 1971.

chapters.evidenceNote: Tooth shapes and fossil grass silica show the shift from forest to grassland, and the Ashfall skeletons lie in pure volcanic ash that dates and seals the scene.

chapters.title: Two continents swap their animals
chapters.place: Santa Fe River, northern Florida, USA
chapters.text: For tens of millions of years South America was an island continent with its own animals, such as ground sloths, armadillos, armoured glyptodonts and giant flightless 'terror birds'. Once the Isthmus of Panama joined the Americas, the main exchange began about 2.7 million years ago, although ground sloths and raccoon relatives had already crossed over water millions of years earlier. Fossils 2.6 to 2.3 million years old from Florida's Santa Fe River show southern newcomers: the terror bird Titanis, about 1.5 metres tall, the glyptodont Glyptotherium, ground sloths and armadillos. Going the other way, horses, camels, tapirs, deer, cats, dogs, bears and elephant relatives moved south, and they did far better: northern immigrants make up nearly half of South America's land mammal species, while many native South American hoofed mammals died out.

chapters.title: Giants of the mammoth steppe
chapters.text: During the later ice ages a cold, dry grassland called the mammoth steppe stretched from Spain across Asia to the Yukon in Canada, once the most extensive kind of landscape on Earth. It fed woolly mammoths, steppe bison, horses, reindeer and woolly rhinoceroses weighing up to about 2 tonnes, with front horns over a metre long, all hunted by cave lions, wolves and sabre-toothed cats. In 2020 the frozen body of a three-week-old cub of the sabre-tooth Homotherium was found in permafrost by the Badyarikha River. It died about 36,000 years ago and still has thick dark brown fur, paws and claws, and its small ears and wide paws suggest an animal built for the cold.

chapters.title: The ice-age giants disappear
chapters.place: Rancho La Brea, Los Angeles, California, USA
chapters.text: Between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago most of the world's largest land mammals died out, among them mammoths, woolly rhinos, giant ground sloths and sabre-toothed cats. At La Brea, new radiocarbon dates on 169 fossils show that sabre-toothed cats, dire wolves, American lions, ground sloths, horses, bison and camels had all vanished from southern California by about 12,900 years ago, within about 300 years of a thirty-fold jump in wildfires as the climate warmed and dried and human numbers grew. The last reliably dated woolly rhinos lived in north-east Siberia about 14,000 years ago, and mammoths died out on the mainland about 10,000 years ago, but a small herd survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago. How much hunting by people, climate change or both were to blame is still argued, and the answer probably differs from place to place.

sites.name: Rancho La Brea tar pits
sites.note: Natural asphalt that trapped animals for tens of thousands of years; its dated bones and charcoal record the end of the giants.

sites.name: Wrangel Island
sites.note: Arctic island cut off by rising seas about 10,000 years ago, where the last woolly mammoths lived.

chapters.evidenceNote: Radiocarbon dates on the last bones of each species are compared with signs of fire, climate and people; at La Brea fire, drying and people acted together, while elsewhere some researchers stress hunting and others climate change.

forces.title: Volcanism
forces.line: Lava and volcanic gas warm the planet, and sometimes wreck it.
forces.text: Volcanoes carry heat and gas from the Earth's interior to the surface. Over millions of years the carbon dioxide they release, balanced by rain slowly washing it out of the air into rock, works like a thermostat that keeps the climate mild, and gas building up under the ice probably ended the Snowball Earth freezes. Rarely, lava floods cover areas the size of a country: the Siberian Traps left about 4 million cubic kilometres of basalt 252 million years ago, and their gases are the leading suspect for the worst mass extinction. Several other great lava floods coincide with extinctions, though how much each one caused is debated.

forces.title: Water
forces.line: Oceans, rain and rivers carve the land and steady the climate.
forces.text: Liquid water appeared early, probably in the Earth's first half-billion years, and the ocean still covers about 71 percent of the surface. Rain and rivers wear mountains down and carry away the sand and mud that become new rock. Rain also dissolves rock in a slow reaction that pulls carbon dioxide out of the air, which over millions of years helps keep the climate steady. When seas are cut off or break through, change can be sudden: the Atlantic refilled the dried-out Mediterranean within perhaps a few months to two years.

forces.title: Oxygen
forces.line: Microbes, then plants, filled the air with oxygen.
forces.text: The early air had almost no free oxygen. Cyanobacteria, microbes that use sunlight to split water, began to release it, and between about 2.46 and 2.06 billion years ago oxygen built up in the air for good, rusting iron out of the seas and probably helping to trigger ice ages. It rose again before the first animals appeared and once more as plants and forests spread over the land. Today oxygen makes up about 21 percent of the air, nearly all of it made by living things.

forces.title: Ice
forces.line: Ice ages lock up water, lower the seas and carve landscapes.
forces.text: For most of its history the Earth has had little or no permanent ice, but at least five great ice ages broke the warmth. In two of them, about 2.4 billion and 717 to 635 million years ago, ice may have reached the equator, a 'Snowball Earth', though how complete the freeze was is disputed. For the last 2.6 million years or so, ice sheets have grown and melted in the north in step with small changes in the Earth's orbit. At the last peak, about 21,000 years ago, ice covered a quarter of the land and the sea stood about 125 metres lower than today.

forces.title: Drifting continents
forces.line: Moving plates build mountains, open oceans and shuffle continents.
forces.text: The Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Over hundreds of millions of years that is enough to gather the continents into a supercontinent and break it up again, a cycle that takes roughly 300 to 500 million years. Collisions raise mountains such as the Himalayas and the Alps, rifts open new oceans such as the Atlantic, and the shifting map changes sea level, ocean currents and climate, and splits or joins groups of living things. When the plates first began to move is still argued over.

forces.title: Impacts
forces.line: Rocks from space made the Moon and ended the dinosaurs.
forces.text: The young Earth was struck again and again as the planets grew, and most scientists think one giant collision, about 4.5 billion years ago, threw off the debris that became the Moon. Later impacts left huge scars, such as Vredefort in South Africa and Sudbury in Canada, about two billion years old. Today an asteroid about a kilometre across hits the Earth on average once every 500,000 years. The last known one about 10 kilometres wide struck Chicxulub in Mexico 66 million years ago, leaving a crater about 180 kilometres across and helping to end the age of the dinosaurs.

forces.title: Evolution
forces.line: Living things remake the air, the land and each other.
forces.text: Life has changed the planet as much as the planet has changed life. Microbes built layered mounds 3.5 billion years ago and later filled the air with oxygen; animals diversified in the Cambrian explosion from about 539 million years ago, and plants spread onto land from about 470 million years ago and later grew into forests. Mass extinctions cleared the way for new groups again and again, and the species alive today are fewer than one in a hundred of all that have ever lived.

forces.title: People
forces.line: One species now reshapes the land, life and climate.
forces.text: Humans became a force on the planet only very recently. Spreading modern humans probably helped wipe out many large animals in the last 50,000 years, though climate change may share the blame. Farming, which began about 11,700 years ago, turned forests and grasslands into fields. Burning coal, oil and gas has raised the carbon dioxide in the air from about 280 parts per million before industry to more than 420 today, higher than at any time for at least 3 million years.
